Russian forces use group of civilians as 'human shields' near Kupiansk, fire at them afterwards, Ukraine's military says
Russian forces led a group of civilians toward a gas pipeline, using them as human shields, and afterwards opened fire at them near the front-line city of Kupiansk in Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian military said, providing alleged drone footage of the incident.
The group included two women, a child, and several men who were being led toward the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk gas pipeline, according to Ukraine's 13th Khartia Corps. The group came under repeated mortar and artillery fire as it moved.
Drone footage recorded by Ukrainian reconnaissance units showed casualties among the civilians, Khartia said, adding that Ukrainian troops had not opened fire. Based on the impact patterns, the strike originated from the eastern bank of the Oskil River, where Russian forces are positioned, the corps said.
Khartia called the strike a "deliberate provocation" and warned that Russian media could use footage from the incident to falsely accuse Ukraine of attacking civilians. The corps said it would hand over the materials for a war crimes investigation.
"Civilians are used as human shields by the Russians, and then become their target for disinformation campaigns," Khartia wrote.
Ukraine's Joint Forces grouping separately said on Oct. 13 that Russian forces had struck a column of civilians leaving Kupiansk during what it described as a forced evacuation. The military said it was still establishing the number of casualties.
According to the Joint Forces grouping, Russian troops had conducted similar operations in recent weeks, using civilians as human shields to cover the withdrawal of some of their soldiers.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
read also
Russian drone strikes university building in Rivne, injures 25
A Russian drone struck a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people, Rivne's National Police branch said on Oct. 13.
Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said.
Ukraine's Education and Science Minister Andrii Butenko said that a fire broke out in a building of Rivne State Humanitarian University as a result of the Russian drone strike. The Faculty of Music building was almost completely gutted by the fire, while neighboring teaching facilities had windows smashed, he added.
Oleksandr Koval, head of Rivne Oblast Military Administration, said on Oct. 13 that the drone strike damaged the second floor of the building. The fire in the building had been contained, and emergency services were on site.
"All victims are receiving medical assistance. Rescuers, police, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and municipal services are working at the scene," Koval said.
According to the university, all students were in shelters at the moment of the attack. There were casualties amongst the university's administrative staff.
At around 10:35 a.m., Ukraine's air force had reported a jet-powered drone flying over Rivne. The air alert was issued in the city at 10:10 a.m.

articles.title: Russia’s Rassvet Satellites Could Give Drones Space-Based Control, Former HUR Official Warns
articles.body:
Russia’s growing Rassvet satellite network could eventually allow its forces to control long-range drones over Ukraine in real time, a former senior Ukrainian intelligence official warned on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) from 2015 to 2020, made the remarks in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He cautioned against writing off the project because of problems with its first satellites, arguing that the real question is whether Moscow can make the system reliable enough to support regular military communications over Ukraine. The network, he said, could also be used as another tool for hybrid warfare against NATO countries.
“For Europeans, this is a direct threat,” Pavlenko said, explaining that Russia is moving its jet drone factories underground. This could further limit Ukraine’s ability to break manufacturing cycles or destroy the drones – already hard to intercept due to their speed – before they can even be deployed.
“Fitted with a compact Rassvet terminal, such a drone, launched from a civilian vessel in the English Channel or from a rented trailer in Europe, will be able to strike targets in London or Paris unhindered, controlled directly from the Kremlin,” Pavlenko continued, arguing that Europe simply does not have enough Patriot interceptors to repel Russia’s large-scale attacks conducted by cheap satellite drones.
Ukrainian Startup Zvook Secures Investment From Czech DEPO Ventures
Rassvet – Russia’s domestic attempt of Starlink
Built by the Russian company Bureau 1440, Rassvet is a low-orbit satellite broadband service that users can connect to through dedicated terminals that relay data to satellites overhead.
As such satellites sit far closer to Earth than geostationary ones, the signal’s travel time is significantly shorter, which could improve performance. According to Pavlenko, a satellite at about 500 kilometers (approximately 311 miles) could offer delays of roughly 30 milliseconds, compared with close to 70 at the planned 800 (roughly 497 miles).
The only trade-off is that each satellite passes quickly over any given spot, so continuous coverage of a large area requires hundreds of them. Higher orbit, although with possible delays in speed, could allow each satellite to cover more ground.
Bureau 1440 says the finished system will operate at an altitude of about 800 kilometers (497 miles), deliver speeds of up to 1 Gbps with delays of up to 70 milliseconds, and use 5G non-terrestrial network standards and laser links between satellites.
Actual speeds in combat would also depend on network load, routing, ground stations and the number of users sharing a channel, Pavlenko noted, so the advertised 1 Gbps should not be read as what each terminal will receive.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify these figures.
Russia carried out two launches of 16 Rassvet-3 satellites each in 2026, both on Soyuz-2.1b rockets from the Plesetsk cosmodrome. However, not all of the roughly 32 spacecraft are working as intended, Pavlenko said; one dropped out of its orbit, while others failed to climb to their planned altitude.
Moscow aims to launch 292 satellites in 2027 and 924 by 2035, according to The Moscow Times.
What this means for Ukraine
Russia’s push for its own satellite system sped up after it launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine in February 2022, particularly because Starlink proved its value to Ukrainian Defense Forces on the battlefield.
For the Russian military, a secure satellite link would mean sharing data between units, streaming video and reaching platforms operating beyond ground networks.
A small constellation can still be military useful, Pavlenko said. Even without constant coverage, a satellite passing over the right area at the right time opens a short “access window” that may be enough to send a video feed, issue a command or adjust a drone’s mission.
That scenario has already been tested, according to Ukrainian intelligence sources cited by Janes in August 2026, who said Russia used its first batch of Rassvet satellites to communicate over Ukraine for several hours.
The biggest concern is drones. Most Russian long-range drones today fly preset routes or rely on civilian mobile networks via a SIM card. With a satellite link, an operator could watch live footage and change a drone’s course or target mid-flight.
Pavlenko said large strike drones, particularly jet-powered models, are the most likely candidates since they can carry the necessary terminals.
Russia began using jet-powered drones extensively in recent months, as they can reach speeds of up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (roughly 250-370 miles per hour), making them significantly harder to intercept.
He identified three main risks for Ukraine: drones gaining a communication channel independent of ground networks, better coordination between dispersed units, and smaller future terminals that could fit on more types of weapons.
There are limits, however. Each drone would need a compatible terminal, antenna, power supply and software, and a satellite link alone would not improve navigation or protect a drone from electronic warfare or air defenses.
Countering the system
Jamming Rassvet will not be so simple, Pavlenko said, noting that effective countermeasures require detailed knowledge of its frequencies, protocols and terminal design – much of which is not public.
Terminals with electronically steered antennas can track satellites quickly and hold a steadier connection, while reprogrammable chips let engineers update satellites with new software after launch.
And shooting down satellites is not much easier. A large constellation can absorb the loss of a few spacecraft, and destroying them creates debris that endangers other objects in orbit, Pavlenko said.
On Aug. 28, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced that Kyiv has petitioned the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) to exclude Ukraine’s territory from the service areas of Rassvet, arguing that the system is used solely to support Russia’s war effort.
“The purpose for Russia to use such satellites over the territory of Ukraine is absolutely clear and it has nothing to do with civilian purposes,” Sybiha said, adding that Moscow intends to use the system to support its war effort and commit “genocidal crimes.”
The following day, the Digital Transformation Ministry, the Foreign Ministry and the Ukrainian State Center of Radio Frequencies filed objections to the Rassvet-1 and Rassvet-3 systems.
Nonetheless, Pavlenko acknowledged that the ITU cannot enforce its decisions. But, if Rassvet’s registration were to be revoked, the system would effectively operate illegally, strengthening the case for jamming it and striking its ground infrastructure.
Risks beyond Ukraine’s front line
Rassvet’s reach could extend well beyond Ukraine’s frontline, Pavlenko said, warning that Russia is planning to sell the system’s access in 70 countries across the Global South.
This could essentially put the service in the hands of criminal groups, including Somali pirates using unmanned boats against merchant ships and Latin American cartels trying to evade US surveillance.
Ukrainian intelligence also believes Russia deliberately registered Rassvet on frequencies that overlap with Iridium, a satellite system used by the Pentagon. If so, any Western attempt to jam Rassvet could disrupt allied military communications as well.
China’s growing role
Amid sweeping sanctions imposed by the EU, Russia has already shifted from Western components obtained through grey-market channels to primarily Chinese electronics.
That is a demanding switch for space hardware, which must withstand radiation and extreme temperatures and cannot be repaired after launch. New components would also mean reworking software and testing equipment, Pavlenko said.
Beyond sales, Beijing gains much from the arrangement as Russia’s war offers a live testing ground for Chinese technology and imposes a steady demand for electronics, optics and communications gear.
Pavlenko singled out Shanghai Fudan Microelectronics, a Chinese chipmaker the US Commerce Department added to its Entity List in September 2025 for supplying technology to Russian military end users. There is no evidence, however, that its components are used in Rassvet satellites.
He also linked the acceleration of Russia’s defense industry to Andrei Belousov, who became defense minister in May 2024.
According to Pavlenko, Belousov was given authority over the wider defense industry and reoriented it toward Chinese chips, optics, thermal imagers and carbon fiber.
He claimed that 90% of the Russian defense sector’s financial settlements now run through the yuan and Chinese banks, although the figure could not be independently verified.
President Volodymyr Zelensky separately warned on Monday, Oct. 12, that Beijing is assisting Russia’s efforts in building Rassvet.
“We know that China works on satellites, works on the possibility of helping Russia with a system similar to Starlink,” he told the Financial Times, adding that “they are getting closer, and they are passing it on to Russia.”
A delegation of bipartisan US lawmakers has backed expanding Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network and urged an effort to win over the company’s owner, Elon Musk, during their visit to Kyiv on Oct. 9.
Musk has repeatedly refused to allow its use inside Russia over fears of nuclear escalation.
Currently, SpaceX allows Ukraine to use Starlink on Ukrainian-controlled territory, including Russian-occupied areas such as Crimea. However, the service inside Russia is completely blocked.

articles.title: Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
articles.body:
Ukraine has loosened its reliance on Washington but still depends on the United States in three military areas that let US President Donald Trump keep pressuring Kyiv, The Telegraph wrote on 12 October. That pressure now centers on the energy ceasefire Trump declared on 11 October, with US officials reportedly warning Kyiv not to hit Russian energy during the truce. Kyiv backs a mutual truce, but Moscow has not confirmed it, and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s grid have continued.
The paper named three such ties: satellite intelligence, Patriot interceptors, and American weapons bought with European money. A pause in any of them would hit just as Russia’s winter campaign begins. Ukraine says an intercepted document reportedly lays out up to 1,000 Russian missiles, drones, and bombs for 60 critical sites this winter, so any pause in US intelligence, interceptors, or PURL deliveries would land as that campaign gets under way.
Satellite intelligence: the US still holds the key
The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and other US services still pass precise satellite data that help Ukrainian forces hit targets inside Russia, by the paper’s estimate. Trump briefly suspended that flow in March 2025 to pressure Zelenskyy. A Ukrainian official told Axios that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened during 9 October talks in Miami to cut off US intelligence.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
Patriot interceptors: no quick substitute
The Telegraph called interceptor missiles the second and probably sharpest dependency. Only American Patriot systems can down Russia’s most powerful missiles, which strike Ukrainian cities daily, the paper wrote. Kyiv’s PAC-3 stocks ran dry mainly because US reserves were diverted to the Middle East after America’s war against Iran, the paper added. Kyiv had warned in March that a long Middle East war would squeeze its PAC-3 supply.
Five European defense firms—Destinus, MBDA Deutschland, Safran, Airbus, and Thales—signed a letter of intent in July to develop a joint interceptor, but a testable prototype is not expected before next year, the paper wrote. Ukraine is also building its own interceptor with European allies under the FREYJA program.
The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal
US arms bought with European money
The third is buying American arms with European money through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a NATO-run purchasing scheme. US officials have reportedly warned Europe that Trump may halt those supplies if Ukraine keeps striking Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Russian Rassvet satellite system threatens Ukraine, Europe and global security – Maj Gen Pavlenko
articles.body:
The Russian Rassvet satellite network is being developed not only for the war against Ukraine, but also as a tool for carrying out provocations, illegal schemes, and hybrid aggression against NATO countries and the international community, Deputy Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense from 2015 to 2020, Major General Illia Pavlenko said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
According to Pavlenko, the creation of an autonomous satellite infrastructure will allow Russia to covertly carry out sabotage operations anywhere in the world.
"This is a direct threat to Europeans. The enemy is moving its jet-powered UAV production facilities underground. Equipped with a compact Rassvet terminal, such a drone, launched from a civilian vessel in the English Channel or from a rented trailer in Europe, will be able to strike targets in London or Paris unhindered, guided directly from the Kremlin. Europe simply won't have enough expensive PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot system to repel massive attacks by cheap satellite-guided drones," the major general said.
Pavlenko identifies Russia's plans to sell network access in 70 countries of the Global South as a separate risk. "Somali pirates will undoubtedly use this connection to guide unmanned boats toward civilian vessels, and drug cartels in Latin America will use it to circumvent U.S. surveillance systems. Giving them such a tool is effectively like giving an enemy nuclear weapons," he said.
In addition, the general noted that the Russian developers of Rassvet have chosen an operating frequency band that completely overlaps with the frequencies of the American Iridium satellite system used by the Pentagon, creating a risk of interference and complicating the use of electronic warfare (EW) capabilities.
"This is a major threat to the Americans and NATO countries. By jamming Rassvet's frequencies in the event of a hybrid conflict or the fight against smuggling, they risk completely crippling their own communications and the command and control of their warships or units," a former high-ranking military intelligence official said.

articles.title: 11 sailors missing off Bulgaria in ship attacks, as Trump tries to ‘soften’ Putin with diesel deal
articles.body:
Two merchant ships were struck by drones Tuesday in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, sinking one vessel and leaving 11 sailors missing, as the NATO member suggested Russia could be responsible but stopped short of directly accusing Moscow.
The attacks came exactly one week after another cargo ship was sunk by drones off the Bulgarian coast, raising concerns about the growing threat to commercial shipping near NATO territory. They also coincided with fresh diplomatic tensions over President Donald Trump's efforts to bring Russian President Vladimir Putin back to peace negotiations, including a controversial agreement allowing Russian diesel exports.
Bulgarian officials said the two vessels were attacked roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the country's coast. The ship that sank, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, went down off the village of Krapets. Five crew members were rescued, while 11 remained missing.
The second vessel, the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, was struck by three drones overnight. All 15 crew members, seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, were rescued, with five suffering minor injuries.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency security meeting Tuesday morning and described the attacks, which occurred close to his country's territorial waters, as "absolutely unacceptable."
Radev said Bulgaria was seeking greater assistance from NATO and the European Union to strengthen maritime and airspace surveillance. Although he did not directly accuse Russia, he suggested Moscow stood to benefit from the attacks.
"We have no clear evidence to accuse any of the parties," he said, adding that logic suggested the outcome served Russia's interests.
Bulgaria subsequently summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who said after meeting Radev that she had received no information from the Russian Defense Ministry about the attacks. She also suggested they could have been a provocation by a third party. Moscow did not immediately comment on the incidents. Ukraine, however, explicitly blamed Russia.
"Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Sybiha urged Ukraine's international partners to increase pressure on Moscow, accusing Russia of attempting to disrupt global food supplies by targeting commercial vessels in one of the world's most important grain-export corridors.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also condemned the attacks, saying the Black Sea had become another front of escalation in Russia's war against Ukraine.
Tuesday's attacks followed a series of similar incidents that have heightened concerns about the security of shipping routes near Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members.
On October 6, two cargo vessels came under drone attack off Bulgaria. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sustained catastrophic damage and sank, leaving its 10 crew members, nine Syrians and one Egyptian, missing. Bulgarian authorities subsequently suspended the search without establishing their fate.
The second vessel, the Palau-flagged Able, caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued, including two who suffered serious injuries. Both vessels were operated by Turkish companies.
A day earlier, the Turkish-owned cargo ship Royad Mammadov, which was carrying grain, was struck off Romania's coast and later sank. Romanian authorities reported two deaths and 11 survivors. Ukraine accused Russia of launching the drone attack.
Russia and Ukraine are among the world's largest grain exporters, and the war has repeatedly threatened international food supplies by disrupting Black Sea shipping.
Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukrainian Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River facilities and shipping routes running close to the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts. Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up attacks on Russian vessels involved in grain exports elsewhere in the Black Sea and in the Sea of Azov, near the mouth of the Don River.
The maritime escalation has added another dimension to the economic confrontation between Moscow and Kyiv, with both countries seeking to disrupt the other's trade and sources of revenue. The latest attacks unfolded as Trump sought to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending the war, while increasing pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt drone strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian energy infrastructure for contributing to rising global diesel prices, although energy experts say the war involving Iran has been the principal driver of the increases. On Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced what he described as an energy ceasefire under which Russia and Ukraine would stop attacking each other's energy facilities.
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed that a formal agreement had been reached, and Ukraine subsequently accused Russia of continuing its attacks.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian refineries and other energy facilities for the two days following Trump's announcement, but Moscow had not reciprocated.
"Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire," Zelensky said. "However, Russia did not heed the American president," he added, accusing Moscow of attacking Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure. He said 19 Ukrainian regions had come under attack during the two-day period.
Zelensky said the strikes demonstrated that Moscow had no intention of exercising similar restraint. He insisted Ukraine remained prepared to take reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, but argued that meaningful progress required stronger international pressure on Russia. "Wars end when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war," he said.
Zelensky also warned that easing pressure on Moscow, delaying military assistance to Ukraine or making it harder to defend civilians against ballistic missiles would not advance peace.
His comments came amid reports that Washington was threatening to suspend the mechanism through which European countries purchase American weapons for delivery to Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped targeting Russian refineries.
The dispute has intensified following Trump's agreement with Putin to permit Russian diesel exports to international markets despite existing sanctions. The arrangement, intended to ease fuel shortages and slow rising diesel prices, has drawn sharp criticism from Ukraine and several European countries, which fear it will provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance its war.
Zelensky previously described the agreement as "a weak decision by strong partners." The deal would release more than 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel onto U.S. and international markets. Some energy experts have questioned whether the relatively limited volume would have a meaningful effect on global prices.
According to a Reuters report, the diesel agreement was not merely intended to address fuel prices but was also part of an American attempt to persuade Putin to resume negotiations over ending the war.
Three people familiar with discussions between American and Ukrainian officials said Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, explained the strategy during a meeting in Miami on Friday.
Two of the sources said Witkoff and Kushner told Ukrainian representatives that Putin was currently unwilling to negotiate an end to the war and that the diesel deal could help restart three-way talks involving Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
A third source said the United States believed the agreement could help "soften" Moscow's position by signaling Trump's willingness to pursue cooperation with Russia.
The strategy was intended to demonstrate that Washington was prepared to offer Moscow economic incentives while encouraging Kyiv to suspend its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, potentially creating conditions for renewed negotiations.
The Ukrainian delegation left the Miami meeting without formally agreeing to the proposals, according to Reuters, although officials indicated they were open to an energy ceasefire if Russia also observed it.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not explicitly deny the Reuters report Tuesday but said he saw no "direct connection" between the diesel agreement and Moscow's willingness to participate in peace negotiations.
He described the arrangement as mutually beneficial cooperation between Russia and the United States that served the interests of both countries and international energy markets.
Against this backdrop, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha delivered a pointed remark about Washington's changing demands on Kyiv during a security conference in Warsaw on Tuesday. "In less than two years, we have gone from 'You don't have the cards' to 'Don't play your cards.' This is an achievement," he said.
The remark referred to Trump's confrontation with Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025, when the American president told his Ukrainian counterpart that he lacked leverage in negotiations with Russia.
Now, as Washington urges Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure, Sybiha suggested the administration was effectively acknowledging that Kyiv possessed strategic leverage, but was asking it not to use it.

articles.title: Iran fortifies nuclear sites, prepares for renewed war: report
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for renewed US war: report
Iran is strengthening its nuclear and military facilities, mobilising supporters and threatening a wider regional conflict as it prepares for the possibility of renewed war with the United States, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
Iranian leaders believe US President Donald Trump could launch fresh attacks after the 3 November midterm elections, prompting Tehran to reinforce sensitive sites and warn Washington that another offensive would trigger a more devastating response, the newspaper reported on Tuesday.
Citing Iranian officials and people familiar with regional communications, the WSJ said Tehran had issued both public and private warnings that renewed US strikes could lead to attacks on American interests and Gulf allies.
Satellite imagery has shown Iran strengthening defences around nuclear facilities and border areas, while authorities have stepped up pro-government rallies and promoted military training for civilians.
Iran's limited ability to counter advanced US fighter jets, high-altitude bombers and cruise missiles has pushed Tehran to rely increasingly on threats of wider retaliation to deter Washington, according to the report.
Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at London-based Chatham House, said the prospect of war also served Iran's leadership as it grappled with diplomatic, economic and political deadlock.
Iran threatens Gulf infrastructure and US warships
Iranian officials have raised the possibility of launching ground incursions into neighbouring countries in response to further US attacks, according to people familiar with Tehran's warnings.
Senior Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates could be targeted, along with regional data centres and internet cables.
Tehran has also warned Arab officials that critical infrastructure, including Saudi oil facilities, could come under attack if fighting resumes, the WSJ reported.
The threats come as Saudi Arabia faces mounting attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds, according to the newspaper, which described it as the deadliest attack on the US or its Gulf allies during the conflict linked to the war with Iran.
Iran has also told intermediaries that it could respond more forcefully against American military personnel, including by attempting to sink US warships and inflict casualties among their crews.
The warnings highlight the risks to the Gulf's vital economic infrastructure if Trump orders another round of strikes.
US sends more military assets to Middle East
The US military is also preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities, with a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine unit heading towards the region according to the outlet.
The Pentagon is considering sending more air defence systems and ammunition to American bases across the region.
Trump ruled out launching an attack before the midterm elections last week but publicly raised the possibility of striking Iran's Mount Pickaxe nuclear site.
US officials said the military was developing several options for renewed strikes.
Direct fighting between Washington and Tehran has eased considerably since late July, when Trump backed away from plans for a major escalation, partly over concerns about dwindling interceptor missile stocks needed to protect American and regional targets.
The lull has nevertheless allowed both sides to prepare for another confrontation.
Iran has used the period to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its weapons stockpiles, while Washington has intensified economic pressure on Tehran.
Meanwhile, attacks on commercial shipping and tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz have increased.
At least three merchant vessels came under attack over the weekend, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
A drone strike on the Emirati tanker Petro Dolphin near Oman on Sunday sparked a fire aboard the vessel and left two Indian sailors missing.
Iran reinforces nuclear sites and mobilises civilians
Satellite images taken by Vantor and analysed by the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security show Iran constructing new defensive barriers around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities.
The measures, introduced last month, include makeshift earthworks designed to obstruct potential ground raids.
Iranian officials have also sought to demonstrate the country's readiness for another war.
Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, who oversees Iran's contingency planning, said in late September that airports, seaports and power plants had been equipped with shelters and emergency supplies to maintain operations during a conflict.
State media have meanwhile intensified coverage of pro-government demonstrations, with residents reporting that rallies have grown larger and spread to more locations in recent weeks.
Billboards in Tehran have advertised civilian training courses in the use of shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles and sniper rifles.
Last month, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps released footage of women undergoing training in guerrilla warfare, firearms and drone operations through its Basij paramilitary force.
In the northeastern city of Sabzevar, Revolutionary Guard personnel visited a kindergarten to recount stories of earlier fighting and display a US-made Tomahawk missile they claimed to have intercepted.
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran programme at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Tehran's political rhetoric and military preparations indicated it was actively preparing for another confrontation.
He described the measures as serving both deterrence and war planning.

articles.title: What is known about West providing Ukraine with no intel on Russian missile launches
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Ukrainian air defense systems were unable to intercept Russian ballistic missiles in time due to a lack of necessary data from Kiev’s Western partners, Ukrainian air force spokesman Yury Ignat said.
Vladimir Zelensky later confirmed this information.
TASS has summarized the key facts about the situation.
Lack of data
- Ukrainian air defense systems were unable to respond to Russian ballistic missile launches in time due to a lack of necessary data from Kiev’s Western partners, Ukrainian air force spokesman Yury Ignat said.
- He blamed the shortfall on "technical issues," noting that this was not the first time such an incident had occurred.
- Earlier, the Ukrainian air force confirmed that the country’s air defenses had been unable to receive data on Russian ballistic missile launches in time, adding that the ballistic targets were only detected by radar systems as the attack on Kiev was underway.
- The Ukrainian air force also said that the cause of the incident was being determined.
- On the evening of October 12, Ukrainian media reported that explosions were heard in Kiev before an air raid alert was issued.
- Later, Vladimir Zelensky said that Ukraine had not received intelligence from its partners before the overnight explosions.
- He called intelligence one of the most critical issues.
Possible reasons
- Ignat told the Rada television channel that specialists would investigate the incident and coordinate with Western partners to resolve the problem.
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation under the National Security and Defense Council said on its Telegram channel that it was looking into the reasons for the disruption in the transmission of intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches as various theories circulated online.
- The center noted that one possibility was that the transfer of intelligence to Ukraine had been suspended, although official details were still being verified.
- The European edition of Politico reported that US President Donald Trump could cut off US intelligence to Ukraine or pressure entrepreneur Elon Musk to disconnect Starlink satellite internet, on which the Ukrainian military depends heavily.
- The Financial Times newspaper reported, citing unnamed European officials, that the US administration was threatening to suspend the weapons procurement program and the provision of intelligence to Ukraine.
- Meanwhile, the Ukrainian news outlet Strana noted that there had been no official information confirming that the United States might have halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga also said that Kiev continues to receive intelligence from the United States.
- The European Commission has received no notifications from Washington regarding a suspension of intelligence sharing with Kiev, EC Spokesman Christian Wigand said at a briefing in Brussels.
- Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the US Senate Armed Forces Committee, also stated that the United States was sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Opinions
- Ukrainian lawmaker Galina Yanchenko previously said that if the transfer of US intelligence to Kiev were suspended, Ukrainian authorities would be unable to obtain timely information on Russian ballistic missile launches.
- US journalist Tucker Carlson described US intelligence sharing with Kiev as the only reason the Ukraine conflict has not yet ended.
- Ukrainian authorities risk being unable to reach a bunker in time during Russian missile strikes without US intelligence, Andrey Klintsevich, head of the Center for the Study of Military and Political Conflicts, told TASS.
Russia-US agreements, Zelensky’s position
- According to Politico, the recent Russia-US diesel agreements came "in a difficult month for Ukrainians, with a bitterly cold winter fast approaching."
- This made Vladimir Zelensky think about "how angry he could actually afford to be."
- Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9 during which they discussed petroleum product supplies, among other things.
- The Russian leader said that Moscow had reiterated its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the United States and global markets.
- According to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Russia is lifting its ban on diesel exports earlier than planned and is ready to supply 300,000 tons of diesel in October, raising the volume to 500,000 tons in November and one million tons in December. Monthly supplies could subsequently reach three million tons.
- The US administration, in turn, issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027.
- Zelensky criticized Trump for agreeing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel supplies, describing the move as "obvious weakness."

articles.title: North Korea's Kim showcases missile capable of reaching US as Trump signals possible meeting
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a defense industry museum displaying an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States, state media KCNA showed on Tuesday.
The report came a day after US President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia. Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in mid-November.
Kim, accompanied by his daughter, known as Ju Ae, and wife Ri Sol Ju, attended the opening of the newly opened Defence Revolution Museum on Sunday, KCNA said.
The museum displayed weaponry developed under Kim's leadership ranging from drones to the Hwasong-20 intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), KCNA photographs showed.
A display in front of the Hwasong-20 launcher appeared to show a multiple warhead design and a world map depicting ranges extending beyond the US mainland to the Middle East, Australia and South America, said Shin Jong-woo, Secretary General of the Korea Defence and Security Forum.
"The exhibition appears intended to highlight the achievements of Kim's defense science development program," Shin said. "It gave the impression of propaganda aimed at gaining a strategic advantage ahead of a potential North Korea-US summit."
North Korea shows off military developments
Analysts said the museum also reflected a broader effort by Kim to elevate North Korea's weapons displays into lasting symbols of the regime's military accomplishments.
"By turning what were once temporary weapons exhibitions into a permanent museum, Kim is institutionalizing his military achievements and portraying North Korea's nuclear and missile buildup as a completed and enduring legacy," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
Separately, North Korea said it test-fired a tactical ballistic missile on Monday to confirm the successful technical upgrade of an unspecified key component.
KCNA said the upgrade marked an important step in improving the performance of all offensive weapons systems, without providing further details.
South Korea's military said on Monday that North Korea had fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast. The launch was Pyongyang's fourth in a month, following Seoul's recent test of a hypersonic missile.

articles.title: Allies failed to warn Ukraine of impending missile attack, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Allies failed to warn Ukraine of impending missile attack, Zelensky says
- Ukraine says allies gave no warning before a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, and Zelensky called the strike “particularly vile” as five missiles hit civilian infrastructure.
- Trump said the US is still sharing intelligence and working with Kyiv and Moscow, while Ukraine said it has stopped attacking Russian refineries since his “energy ceasefire” announcement.
- Russia hit transport and logistics instead of energy sites overnight, killing four in Kharkiv and wounding many, as Ukraine warned that US early-warning intelligence is vital to save lives.

KYIV - Ukraine received no prior warning from its Western partners about a Russian ballistic missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13, as Kyiv comes under intense US pressure to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight for the first time since US President Donald Trump’s surprise Oct 11 announcement of an “energy ceasefire”, but hammered transport and logistics with ballistic missiles and drones.
Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes, experts and officials say.
Speaking to reporters on Oct 13, Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine and is working with both Kyiv and Moscow to bring an end to the war. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he said.
Trump was asked whether Russia had violated the ceasefire and answered: “I’ll let you know about that later.”
Asked if Russia could use proceeds from the diesel deal to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s a diesel deal, not for us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us.”
Zelensky said Ukraine had not targeted Russian refineries since Trump’s announcement on Oct 11.
He said Kyiv had not received the usual warning from allies of ballistic missile launches before a “particularly vile” attack on Kyiv overnight, in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives,” Zelensky said on X, “and this is one of the most critical issues.” He stopped short of linking the lack of warning to any US threats.
Air raid alerts sound in Kyiv only after blasts are heard
Air alerts sounded in Kyiv on the night of Oct 12 only after several explosions had already ripped through the city.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha tried to calm anxiety by saying Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, he said the delay had been due to the specifics of the weaponry that Russia had used.
As Ukraine fights a larger, richer and better-equipped enemy, Kyiv sees the strikes on Russian oil refineries as one of its few instruments to reduce Moscow’s ability to fight.
Yet Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks - which prompted Moscow to suspend diesel exports - for a sharp rise in US fuel prices this year, a headache for his Republican party ahead of Congressional midterm elections in three weeks.
Most analysts, however, say Trump’s war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise.
Russia had struck six Ukrainian energy sites on Oct 12. It was unclear whether Moscow had deliberately avoided energy infrastructure overnight and on Oct 13.
A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details.
Ukraine says it now has cards to play
Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine’s second city, Kharkiv, and dozens were wounded across the country, Ukrainian officials said.
The Ukrainian air force said it was investigating the failure to receive surveillance warnings before the attack.
Fabian Hoffmann, missile expert at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, said Ukraine’s European allies had “very limited” ability to replace US early-warning intelligence about Russian missile strikes:
“Ukraine relies on the so-called Space-Based Infrared System which the US deploys - and the US system is really second to none and only the United States can provide that.”
Sybiha said the US request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine’s position had strengthened, alluding to Trump’s comment to Zelensky in a tense Oval Office meeting in 2025 that “you don’t have the cards”.
“In less than two years, we have gone from ‘having no cards’ to ‘not playing your cards’. That is an achievement,” Sybiha said.
Zelensky reiterated Ukraine’s position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia. REUTERS

articles.title: “Now it’s your turn”: US envoys planned to show Moscow a refinery pause and a diesel deal, then ask for something back, a source tells Reuters
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s envoys told Kyiv that letting Russia sell diesel could draw Moscow back to peace talks, Reuters reported. In the same meeting, they said Russia’s leader was not ready to negotiate. Since then, Moscow has offered nothing in return, and Trump has brushed off claims that Russia helps Iran.
Washington is pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries and offering Moscow economic incentives to return to peace talks, even though Russia has made no commitment in return. Yesterday, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before air raid sirens sounded, amid disputed warnings that the US could cut intelligence support. Meanwhile, Ukraine is being asked to halt its long-range campaign against the oil infrastructure that fuels and finances Russia's war.
The pitch: a diesel deal as a signal to Moscow
Trump’s Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met the Ukrainian delegation in Miami on 9 October. They described Russian President Vladimir Putin as unprepared to negotiate but said the diesel deal could help restart three-way talks, two of the sources said.
The third source said the deal could “soften” Moscow because it “sends a signal that Trump is open to do things” with Russia. One of the sources described the plan:
“The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say ‘See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you this deal. Now it’s your turn to do something.’”
Ukraine’s part was to stop hitting Russian refineries. Kushner repeated Trump’s request at the meeting, noting the administration had made it several times, two sources said.
EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow
Kyiv was asked to hold its fire on Russian oil
The Ukrainians agreed to nothing formally, Reuters’ sources said. They signaled they would accept an energy ceasefire if Russia did the same, but saw the US approach as an attempt to appease Russia with business deals.
Two days later, Trump declared an energy ceasefire, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready if Russia reciprocated. Euromaidan Press has monitored official and unofficial Ukrainian and Russian sources and found no reports of new Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries after Trump’s announcement. One of the last, on the night of the diesel announcement, knocked out more than half the tanks at a fuel-export terminal in Rostov-on-Don.
Trending Now
Three sources told Reuters the envoys did not threaten to cut US support over the refinery strikes. A Ukrainian official told Axios, however, that the envoys warned Trump could cut Ukraine off from US intelligence, which a US official denied. US officials are also believed to have told European allies that Trump would halt PURL, the NATO scheme for Europe-funded US weapons for Ukraine, unless the strikes stopped, according to FT.
Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly
What Moscow has offered in return
A person close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin would return to the table only when he gets “the remaining 11% of Donbas.” Ukraine refuses to cede more land. During the 9 October call that produced the deal, Putin declined to commit to resuming talks, his aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, Axios reported.
Moscow has not confirmed the energy ceasefire either. Trump insisted on 12 October that the sides had agreed “because I said they agreed,” RFE/RL reported. On the evening of 12 October, Russian munitions collapsed an apartment stairwell in Kharkiv, killing four people. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak, meanwhile, claimed diesel exports could reach 3.0–3.5 million tons a month by year-end, above the volumes Trump announced.
“Too much to lose”: Trump on Russia and Iran
Late on 12 October, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he did not believe Russia and China were helping Iran, since they have “too much to lose.” In March, he told Fox News that Putin “might be helping them a little bit.” Asked about Russia’s possible support for Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on 2 September that his message to everyone was to “stay away.” That month, a Financial Times investigation found Russia secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles that could threaten US warships.

articles.title: NATO Unveils “Theory of Victory” to Stop Russian Attack With Drones and Missiles
articles.body:

- World
NATO Unveils “Theory of Victory” to Stop Russian Attack With Drones and Missiles
NATO has outlined a new defense strategy, dubbed the “Theory of Victory,,” designed to repel a potential Russian attack by halting its initial offensive, preventing further advances, and systematically weakening enemy forces.
According to The Wall Street Journal on October 12, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, presented the strategy during the Warsaw Security Forum, revealing that its classified version had been finalized three months earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Drawing on lessons from Ukraine’s battlefield experience, the strategy prioritizes investment in what Grynkewich called “affordable mass,” focusing on relatively low-cost drones to supplement NATO’s advanced weapons systems, according to the publication.
Under the plan, NATO’s immediate priority in the event of a Russian attack would be to stop the initial assault.
“Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed,” Grynkewich said.
The NATO commander emphasized that the Alliance’s objective would not be to defeat Russia as a state or undermine its government, but rather to repel any attack against NATO territory.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the strategy builds on earlier work by General Chris Donahue, a former commander of US Army forces in Europe and NATO’s Allied Land Command.
The approach is intended to address concerns that Russia’s geographical advantages and extensive defense industry could enable it to launch an offensive against the Baltic states, Poland, or other NATO members before the Alliance could organize a substantial military response.
A central element of the strategy involves establishing a large autonomous zone in which unmanned aerial vehicles and ground-based robotic systems would be deployed to disrupt and suppress Russian attacks while minimizing casualties among allied forces.
At the same time, NATO would use long-range missiles to strike Russian command centers and air defense systems in the Kaliningrad exclave, near St. Petersburg, and in Belarus. According to The Wall Street Journal, these operations would aim to weaken Russia’s ability to control the airspace, creating conditions for the US Army’s V Corps and other NATO ground forces to launch counterattacks.
NATO air forces would also move rapidly to target Russian reinforcements approaching the battlefield and strike additional military assets behind enemy lines.
The operations would be supported by a secure information-sharing network known as a “data backbone,” allowing NATO forces to exchange classified targeting data almost instantaneously through a cloud-based system. According to reports, components of the network have already been tested in the Middle East during the US war with Iran.
The broader concept, known as the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, is intended to strengthen NATO’s ability to respond rapidly to potential Russian aggression.
According to US military officials cited by The Wall Street Journal, the initiative ultimately aims to deter Russian leader Vladimir Putin from launching an attack against the Alliance.
The strategy also reflects NATO’s broader shift toward integrating emerging technologies into military operations, particularly those that have demonstrated their effectiveness on Ukraine’s battlefield.
On August 12, Bild reported that NATO was increasingly prioritizing drones, satellite technology, advanced sensors, and artificial intelligence as part of its efforts to modernize its military capabilities.
The move toward greater automation draws on Ukraine’s experience deploying AI-powered drone swarms capable of identifying targets, coordinating their movements, and conducting strikes autonomously, even when Russian electronic warfare disrupts communication with human operators.

The U.S. reportedly threatened to cut intelligence sharing once again last week if Kyiv does not stop stricking Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy did not publicly confirm the threat, but has backed down.

“The Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine. Nineteen regions of our country have come under attack in these two days alone,” he added.

Russia has not yet commented on the ballistic strikes, but issued a general statement saying it had struck military and weapons production facilities across Ukraine.
However, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Monday that Zelenskyy did not deserve a pause in fighting in response to the energy ceasefire: “I don’t think that he deserves a break. I don’t think that we will buy assurances and promises again,” he said.

articles.title: Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian president described the attack on Monday as “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.
“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote on social media. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.
US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv.
On Tuesday, however, Trump denied intelligence sharing had stopped. He told reporters: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and Russia on getting the war to end.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.
Asked on Tuesday whether Russia could use proceeds from the sale to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s a diesel deal, not for us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us,” he said.
Earlier the president claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me”. Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.
The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said.
“Russia did not heed the president … the Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted on Tuesday.
Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.
In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. Ukraine has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.
According to the Financial Times, the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.
The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.
Speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation with the US was continuing and said the lack of warning about the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.
On Monday, Russia also bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.
Meanwhile, 11 sailors were missing after their ship was sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria. The incident prompted Bulgaria to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but the prime minister, Rumen Radev, said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House.
Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.
“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.

Estonia’s prime minister has already urged Europe to help Ukraine destroy those refineries instead.
A stairwell gone in Kholodnohirskyi district
Russian munitions hit Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district repeatedly from around 21:17, and Mayor Ihor Terekhov preliminarily identified them as Banderols. At 22:21, he said one strike had hit a residential building, possibly trapping people. He then added in a follow-up post: “Very serious destruction—an entire stairwell has collapsed.”
The strike destroyed an entrance of the four-story building, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. It counted 11 injured across the city’s evening strikes, and a rescuer was hospitalized, while Terekhov put the number at 10. By 06:56 on 13 October, rescuers had found a third body. Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov confirmed three dead and said the search continued. Experts will check whether the building is still fit to live in, he added.
Over 24 hours, Russian attacks killed three people in Kharkiv and injured 37, including two children treated for acute stress, Syniehubov reported.
“I realize I’m on fire”: two residents recall the strike
Larysa Maksimenko had just put her bedridden husband to sleep when the strike hit, she told Suspilne Kharkiv. She suffered a head wound and burns.
“I went to the kitchen to switch on the kettle for myself, to have some coffee. I realize I’m on fire. Then glass fell on me. I came to, and I’m buried under everything. All covered in blood,” she said.
The window bars were broken, and medics carried her husband out through the window. Rescuers later found a woman under the rubble in her apartment, likely a neighbor, Maksimenko said. All she wants now, she said, is to get to her husband in hospital.
Viacheslav Chibitko, who lives on the second floor next to the collapsed entrance, saw a flash, and then everything blew out. He got his three dogs out, but five cats are still inside. During the clearing, a concrete slab fell on a rescuer, Suspilne’s correspondent reported. Crews pulled him out and handed him to medics.
Kyiv’s toll rises, and strikes hit other cities overnight
The evening drone strike on a 25-story building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district killed two people, Kyiv prosecutors reported. The second victim was found dead in a car near the building. Prosecutors counted at least seven injured, including a 17-year-old girl, while Mayor Vitali Klitschko counted 11 in the capital.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
From 18:00 on 12 October, Russia launched five ballistic missiles, nine loitering munitions, and 108 attack drones, Ukraine’s Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 88 drones. A Russian drone attack injured four patients at a medical facility in Khmelnytskyi Oblast, oblast head Serhii Tiurin said. In Dnipro, a Russian attack injured a 64-year-old man, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported. A downed Russian drone set two houses on fire in Murovane near Lviv, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
On 12 October, a Russian Smerch rocket with a cluster warhead hit a house in Cherkaske, Donetsk Oblast, killing three people, including a 13-year-old girl, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Russian attacks killed more than 150 people in the week to 11 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russian bombs killed at least 20 people in Zaporizhzhia on 10 October, by the oblast’s count. On 9 October, the US waived its sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. The White House expects Kyiv to halt refinery strikes under its proposed energy ceasefire.

articles.title: Trump slams ‘radical lunatics’ over claims Russia and China aid Iran
articles.body:
Trump slams ‘radical lunatics’ over claims Russia and China aid Iran
Russia and China are not likely to be providing assistance to Iran in its conflict with the US and Israel because they have “too much to lose,” US President Donald Trump has said. He dismissed allegations that the two countries are supporting Tehran, insisting that Washington would quickly detect any significant involvement.
The remarks come as US officials and Western media outlets claim that Russia and China are providing military and intelligence assistance to Iran, despite both countries calling for an end to the conflict.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump lashed out at political opponents he accused of spreading claims that Russia and China are helping Iran, while acknowledging that limited assistance cannot be ruled out.
“I see so many comments from the Radical Left Morons and Lunatics that China and Russia are helping the ‘wonderful’ Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote.
“If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!” he added.
Trump’s statement follows earlier claims by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that Russia and China are helping Iran in different ways. Speaking at a Senate hearing in July, Hegseth said both countries were “at different levels, enabling some of the things Iran is doing,” but declined to elaborate, citing classified information.
Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine also refused to discuss the extent of any involvement, saying it would reveal sensitive US intelligence.
Washington has sanctioned Chinese companies accused of supplying the Iranian military. In June, the US Treasury targeted Chinese- and Hong Kong-based firms allegedly involved in procuring weapons for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Defense Ministry.
Further sanctions in July targeted entities in China, Russia, and elsewhere accused of supporting an Iranian airline linked to weapons shipments.
The Wall Street Journal also reported that Chinese entities supplied Iran with satellite imagery, dual-use electronics, and components used in missiles and drones. China has denied providing military assistance to Iran.
Trump’s remarks follow a series of high-level contact with Moscow and Beijing focused on energy and economic cooperation.
At a meeting in September with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, Trump discussed Iran, trade, and energy, urging Beijing to boost refined fuel production to help stabilize global markets.
On Friday, Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease soaring fuel prices, after his administration repeatedly urged Kiev to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
The US subsequently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 2027. Moscow pledged to supply 300,000 tons in October, 500,000 in November, and 1 million in December. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said monthly shipments could eventually reach 3 million tons, with Russia lifting its export restrictions ahead of schedule.

Russia launched more than 100 aerial weapons against Ukraine from the evening into the following day, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy wrote on X on October 13.

Kharkiv was among the hardest-hit cities. A Russian strike destroyed an apartment building, prompting an overnight rescue operation as emergency workers searched through the rubble. Four people were killed and 41 others injured in the city, according to Zelenskyy.
