articles.title: Iran may be digging in for next war, raising stakes for US, Israel and Gulf allies - analysis
articles.body:
Satellite images show that Iran is fortifying various locations as it may be preparing for renewed war, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.
“Iran is fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against the US and its Gulf allies as it prepares for potential American attacks after the midterms and seeks to deter them,” the article noted.
This comes amid a flurry of other reports suggesting that the US or Israel could return to fighting Iran.
Maariv said over the weekend that the United States had pressured Israel to carry out strikes against Iran. Both Israel and the US have upcoming elections. Any strikes could affect the elections.
PBS reported on Sunday that “Iran has continued to reject a deal with the US. The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States ‘insufficient’ as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along.”
The picture being painted is of an Iran that continues attempting to rebuild its missile and drone program.
Netanyahu said Iran can no longer produce ballistic missiles
In March, Israel’s prime minister said that the Islamic Republic could no longer produce ballistic missiles due to its hammering by US and Israeli strikes. There was also an optimistic assessment about how many Iranian launchers had been destroyed and how many missiles were “corked” in their depots by collapsing routes to the missiles.
In April, The New York Times reported that Iran was repairing its missile bunkers. The regime has shown it can rebuild capabilities.
The WSJ report noted that “Iran has also reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. Last month, it built passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces, according to Vantor satellite images analyzed by the Institute for Science and International Security, a Washington, DC, nonprofit.”
The report quoted Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “In both word and deed, the Islamic Republic is actively preparing for the next war,” Ben Taleblu said.
Iran is a huge country, around 75 times the size of Israel and 150 times the size of Lebanon. Israel has struggled to defeat Hezbollah in Lebanon and remove all its threats. This illustrates the challenge of locating all the Iranian threats. The new report at the WSJ is concerning in this respect.
“Satellite images show Iran is strengthening sensitive locations, including nuclear sites and border areas, to make them more resilient to attacks. The government is also preparing Iranians for renewed war, sending paramilitary forces to read war stories to kindergartners, advertising training in firing shoulder-mounted anti-aircraft missiles, and holding rallies,” the report added.
It also said that Iran is prepared to defend against various types of airstrikes. It has likely learned some lessons from the 12 Day War in June 2025, as well as the round of strikes that began in February 2026 and lasted until May.
Iran continues to threaten shipping via the Strait of Hormuz. The US has been working to make sure that ships can pass the Strait. It is trying to make sure that the crisis with Iran doesn’t affect energy prices too much. However, all the levers the US has tried to pull still leave the conflict with Iran as an open-ended problem.
The WSJ noted that “Iranian officials have hinted that their forces could conduct land incursions into neighboring countries, according to people familiar with the warnings.”
With US forces having withdrawn from Iraq on September 30, this could give Iran some opportunities. It could try to infiltrate via Iraq or use Iranian-backed militias in Iraq to conduct more attacks. Those militias have already attacked a key pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
While US Central Command (CENTCOM) and Saudi Arabia carried out retaliatory strikes in July, there is reticence in Riyadh to confront the militias in Iraq and the Houthis at the same time.
Could renewed strikes produce different results?
This is why the WSJ report is important. It notes that “Tehran has separately warned Arab officials that it could strike regional targets, including Saudi oil facilities, in the event of a renewed conflict, some of the people said.”
Saudi Arabia is already weighing how to deal with the Houthi threat, which has targeted Saudi airports in recent days, killing and wounding people.
The question now is whether a return to fighting by the US or Israel will lead to better results than in the past.
Iran is seeking to rebuild; this means increasing its drone arsenal as well. The regime has had some success in attacking US bases in the region. It can read the same media reports as everyone else about how those attacks damaged facilities and airplanes and caused the US to reposition assets.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine did not receive early warning from partners on overnight strikes in Kyiv
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that his country did not receive an early warning from its partners on overnight Russian strikes on the capital Kyiv.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy claimed that over 100 different weapons were used in overnight strikes by Russia, including ballistic missiles, hitting civilian infrastructure.
“Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said.
Commenting on an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv announced by US President Donald Trump, Zelenskyy said Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or on the country’s energy sector in general for the two days since the announcement.
“But Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine,” Zelenskyy added.
He said Ukraine’s readiness for “reciprocal steps toward de-escalation” has not changed, arguing “effective” pressure on Russia is needed for de-escalation, and that wars end “when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war.”
“Global pressure on Russia contributes to exactly that – bringing peace closer. But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed,” he added.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said in a separate Telegram statement that one person was injured in a strike that affected a residential building in the capital’s Darnytskyi district, as Ukraine claimed downing 88 out of 108 drones launched by Russia overnight.
In a statement, the country’s Air Force added that Moscow launched five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles against Ukraine from the Russian border region of Bryansk.
Separately, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told a panel of the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland that Kyiv continues to receive intelligence data from the US.
“Yes, we continue this cooperation (with the American side). And, also, it is true that yesterday’s attack, or night attack, (the) air raid alert was launched with a delay. But it is because of (the) special type of the weaponry which was used by (the) Russian side,” Sybiha said.
The Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported over the weekend that US envoys, in talks with their Ukrainian counterparts on Friday, raised the possibility of cutting off intelligence sharing to Kyiv if it did not heed Washington’s warning to halt energy strikes in Russia.

articles.title: From no cards to many: Europe warns Trump not to waste Ukraine’s leverage
articles.body:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (L) and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha (R) listen to US President Donald Trump address the 81st United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters in New York, USA on September 22, 2026. | Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images
WARSAW — Ukraine has more leverage than a year ago — and European leaders are warning Donald Trump not to squander it by pressuring Kyiv to ease up on Russia.
"In less than two years we went from the stage of no cards to the stage of don't play your cards," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told an audience at the Warsaw Security Conference. "That's a true achievement."
Last year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was ambushed in the Oval Office by Trump, who ridiculed him for having "no cards" to play against Russia.
Advertisement
Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight.
Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin's ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump's desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war.
Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine's European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel.
The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland's status as a key U.S. ally.
"Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians," said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity.
"You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.
Advertisement
His German counterpart Johann Wadephul underlined that Berlin is pushing the Trump administration to fully impose energy sanctions approved by the U.S. Congress.
On Sep. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, codifying existing US sanctions against Russia and expanding the scope for applying secondary sanctions, tariffs and restrictions, including against the energy sector.
"This is not the time to lower the sanctions regime, but to strengthen it," Wadephul said.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband echoed that call, saying Trump should exert pressure on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire under which both warring nations would stop hitting each other's oil, gas, electricity and other assets.
Russia has so far refused to take such a step.
"Let us take seriously this issue of the energy ceasefire that President Trump has talked about, not simply a refinery ceasefire but a broad energy ceasefire, because in the last week alone we've seen 200 Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure," Miliband said.
Advertisement
Trump pressures Ukraine
The U.S. president said on Monday that Putin is keener to end the fighting than Zelenskyy — despite the Kremlin not agreeing to any ceasefire.
"I think actually Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy," Trump said.
Since Trump announced an energy ceasefire — blindsiding both Kyiv and Moscow — Ukraine has paused bombing Russian refineries even as Russian attacks continue.
While Trump wants the attacks to stop, Ukraine's European allies are keen to cripple Russia's war effort.
"Ukraine is attacking refineries, which is having an effect, and data centers, which is also having an effect," Sikorski said. He also called on Poland's MAGA-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to use his influence with Trump "to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression."
Wadephul added that he had talked to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month, and saw no interest from him in ending the war.
Advertisement
"A lot of people in Europe and especially in Germany were asking us and me, 'Why don't you talk to the Russians?' So now I had that conversation, and you saw the result," he said. "It's a very dire result. And it shows that Russia right now is not ready for ceasefire."
During the same Warsaw event, Sybiha was forced to deny rumors that Washington may have stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv in retaliation for its campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil refineries.
"You are asking me if we are getting intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said.
Concerns about a potential cut-off in U.S. intelligence grew on Tuesday after Ukraine's threat detection system failed to detect ballistic missiles that battered Kyiv overnight. Sybiha said the failure was due to a "special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side."
Zelenskyy also underlined the need for continued intelligence sharing. "There was also a rather treacherous ballistic missile strike on Kyiv — five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives."
Sybiha stressed that Kyiv needs to continue strengthening its ability to fend off Russia's constant air attacks while Ukraine's troops push back against Russian forces on the front lines.
Advertisement
"The future of Europe and the global security architecture is now being decided in Ukraine," he said.
Chris Lunday and Laura Kayali contributed to this report.

articles.title: Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Iraq faces a potential six-month gap in its air defences following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces, with new systems not expected to arrive until early next year.
The coalition completed its military withdrawal at the end of September, removing air defence systems that had helped protect parts of the country, including the Kurdistan Region.
Baghdad says agreements have been reached to purchase new equipment, but the first systems could take up to six months to arrive.
The transition has taken on added urgency after two drones targeted a camp for Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of Iraq's armed forces, said Baghdad had made "tangible progress" in acquiring new air defence systems.
He said the first batch would arrive within six months and be deployed across the country.
The package would include advanced radar systems, interceptor weapons and aircraft, he said, as part of a wider plan to strengthen Iraq's control over its airspace.
Numan said the country's security situation remained relatively stable and that Iraqi forces were maintaining a high level of readiness.
However, the announcement leaves questions over Iraq's ability to detect and intercept aerial threats before the new systems become operational.
Iraq has long struggled with limited and ageing air defence capabilities, while drones and missiles have become an increasingly prominent security threat.
A Defence Ministry official nevertheless played down the prospect of an immediate security vacuum.
"The available Iraqi air capabilities are not at a high level, and there is no denying that, but the security situation in the country is relatively calm," the official told The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The official said Iraq retained "reasonably good capabilities" and that there were currently no expectations of major security breaches.
Concerns are particularly acute in the Kurdistan Region.
Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said on Monday that both federal Iraq and the autonomous region required effective air defence coverage.
"Let us be realistic. The Kurdistan Region and Iraq as a whole need an air defence system," he told the MERI Forum in Erbil.
Barzani said an earlier agreement negotiated under former prime minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani with the United States had included plans to provide air defence capabilities covering Kurdistan.
"Air defence is not only a need for the Iraqi state. The Kurdistan Region also needs it," he said.
He also stressed that weapons should remain under state control.
Military expert Aqil al-Shammari warned that the process could take longer than the six months announced by the government.
He said another three months could be required to integrate the equipment, establish command-and-control systems, train personnel, arrange maintenance and complete deployment.
"Owning the system does not mean providing complete air coverage," the former brigadier general told The New Arab.
Shammari said the transition period would be a major test of Baghdad's ability to protect Iraqi airspace.
Kurdish officials had warned before the coalition withdrawal that removing foreign forces and their air defence systems without an immediate replacement could leave the region vulnerable.
The withdrawal forms part of a wider transition towards a new security relationship between Baghdad and Washington focused on training, technology and military co-operation without a direct US combat presence.
They have argued that protecting Kurdistan's airspace is ultimately the responsibility of the federal government because it forms part of Iraq's national airspace.
Those concerns intensified after two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
No casualties were reported, but the attack renewed fears that gaps in Iraq's air defences could leave the Kurdistan Region vulnerable to further drone strikes.
The withdrawal has also raised wider questions over whether Baghdad can manage its security without the coalition's military presence.

articles.title: As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now

As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
A police officer photographs the engine of a Shahed drone in front of a multistory residential building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Despite the recent failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The attack came as Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the U.S. to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, in turn, publicly said that intelligence sharing with the Americans continued, saying on Oct. 13, "Yes, we continue this cooperation."
Multiple sources told the Kyiv Independent that there was no decision to cut intelligence sharing. The incident instead appears to have involved a failure to detect or communicate the missile launch in time to warn Kyiv.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either."
The S-400 is a Russian air defense system with secondary ground-attack capabilities. Since 2022, Russia has repeatedly used the system, as well as its older version, the S-300, to strike Ukrainian cities.
One senior Ukrainian official familiar with the matter said Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said.
"The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The official alleged that the incident might have been "a game" to test Ukraine's reaction. Ukraine's military leadership also warned senior officials that if similar incidents became a pattern, they could indicate that Washington was using intelligence assistance to pressure Kyiv.
There is, however, no evidence in the information provided that the incident resulted from a deliberate decision to withhold intelligence.
Detection of ballistic missile launches is largely carried out by a network of sophisticated infrared detecting spy satellites, which identify the thermal spikes caused by the launch of ballistic missiles, Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
The system is generally extremely reliable but not infallible, Hoffmann said, explaining that certain environmental conditions, such as dense, unusually high cloud coverage, could impair its functioning.
Like any system, Hoffmann said, it was susceptible to "human or technical failure" or "extraordinary circumstances" that could impair its functioning.
Missile attacks on Kyiv, which precede air raid warnings, are uncommon but have occurred several times since 2022. In almost all cases, it was the ballistic missiles, which fly at extremely high speeds, that escaped detection by radar.
"Friends, this is not the first time that the intelligence services of our partners have not recorded the launch of the S-400," Zelensky's advisor, Sergey Beskrestnov, said on Oct. 12. "You should not draw conclusions prematurely."

articles.title: Zelensky says Western partners didn’t warn Ukraine about Russian ballistic missile launches before latest attack on Kyiv
articles.body:
Zelensky says Western partners didn’t warn Ukraine about Russian ballistic missile launches before latest attack on Kyiv
Ukraine received no intelligence from its Western partners about Russia’s October 12 missile strike on Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
“Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed,” he said on social media.
Russia attacked Kyiv with five ballistic missiles on the evening of October 12. Ukrainska Pravda reported that radar detected the missiles during the attack, and the city’s air raid alert sounded only after the first explosions. The Ukrainian Air Force said it had received no information about missile launches from Russian territory.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha attributed the delayed alert to “a particular type of weapon used by Russia.” He said Kyiv and Washington continue to share intelligence.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said similar situations had occurred before. “Sometimes this information doesn’t get through. This isn’t the first time… If there were some technical issues this time, I think the specialists will figure it out. And they’ll work with our partners to fix this problem,” he said.
Serhii Beskrestnov, the president’s adviser on technological innovation in the Ukrainian armed forces, said the incident did not mean the United States had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Friends, this isn’t the first time our partners’ intelligence services have failed to detect an S-400 launch. There are some details to consider. We shouldn’t jump to conclusions.
Beskrestnov said he did not believe Kyiv and Washington would stop sharing intelligence, since civilians’ lives were at stake.

articles.title: Germany works to organize a Coalition of the Willing meeting as Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy sector
articles.body:
Germany is preparing a new meeting of the Coalition of the Willing to coordinate further support for Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 12 October following a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump’s claim that Moscow has agreed to an energy truce. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is initiating a meeting of European leaders to discuss assistance to Ukraine in this situation.
Kyiv and Berlin have also agreed to hold a meeting of national security advisers in the E3 format, with Ukraine participating, according to the statement. The format involves an informal grouping of three leading European countries: the United Kingdom, France and Germany.
Zelenskyy and Merz discuss energy truce and support for Ukraine
During the conversation, the two sides also discussed US President Donald Trump’s proposal for an energy truce and Russia’s subsequent actions. Russian forces continue to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy noted.
“This is exactly how the Russians behave when pressure eases. It is very important that Europe continue to act on principle,” Zelenskyy stressed.
Germany is coordinating preparations for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, the Ukrainian president noted. The two sides also discussed support for Ukraine’s financial stability. Further steps are to be coordinated in greater detail during a meeting scheduled for this week, Zelenskyy said.
The Coalition of the Willing seeks additional support for Ukraine
The Coalition of the Willing was initiated by the United Kingdom and France, which held talks with representatives of 37 countries in March 2025 on supporting Ukraine in the event of a peace agreement. The initiative envisaged financial assistance and the deployment of troops, air forces or naval forces to protect Ukraine against renewed Russian aggression, Bloomberg reported.
The latest meeting of the Coalition of the Willing took place on 24 August and was the 16th meeting, according to a statement on the website of the President of Ukraine. Zelenskyy called on partners to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense and provide at least 300 missiles for Patriot systems for the winter, the statement said.
The president also proposed bringing forward part of the European loan financing planned for 2027 so that Ukraine could receive the funds this year. He separately stressed the need to find a mechanism for using frozen Russian assets to defend Ukraine and to unblock the maritime corridor in the Black Sea.
“We value this format—the Coalition of the Willing. It brings together countries that are ready not only to talk about security but also to act. We need this—to act and build real security together,” Zelenskyy stressed.
A ceasefire in words, but fresh attacks on energy infrastructure in practice
Ukraine and Russia had allegedly agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on 11 October. However, at the time of publication, neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed such an agreement, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
Ukraine supports the ceasefire and is awaiting details from the US side, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X the same day. Russia must also agree to halt the strikes, he stressed.
Ukrainian forces had received the relevant orders, and Kyiv was ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure provided Russia reciprocated, Zelenskyy said in his evening address on 11 October.
Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure after the ceasefire was announced, including striking a gas production facility and a petrol station, Zelenskyy said on his official Telegram channel on 12 October. Moscow had shown no willingness to abide by the ceasefire, the president added.

articles.body:
Zelensky: Partners did not warn of ballistic missile strike on Kyiv
The head of state made this announcement on Facebook while summarizing the consequences of yet another Russian strike on Ukraine, according to Ukrinform.

Summarizing the consequences of yet another Russian strike, the President recalled that from the evening until now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different types of weapons: jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles. A significant portion of these weapons was successfully intercepted. But, as Zelenskyy noted, unfortunately, not all of them.
He noted that an ordinary residential building in Kharkiv was destroyed, and the rescue operation lasted virtually all night. Four people were killed in this strike on the building. The President noted that in a single evening, and in Kharkiv alone, 41 people were wounded.
As reported, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, starting at 6:00 p.m. on Monday, October 12, the enemy attacked Ukraine with five “Iskander-M”/S-400 ballistic missiles from the Bryansk region, nine “Banderole”/“Dan-T” loitering munitions, and 108 Shahed-type strike UAVs (74 of which were jet-powered), “Gerbera,” and “Parody”-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russian Federation), the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk, and Hvardeiske (temporarily occupied Crimea).
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 a.m. on Tuesday, October 13, air defense forces shot down or neutralized 88 drones. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, and downed targets (debris) were found at seven locations.

articles.title: North Korea unveils copy of Canadian armored vehicle
articles.body:
- Kim Jong Un opened a new underground-style defense museum displaying the Hwasong-20 ICBM, new missiles and drones.
- Among the exhibits is a new 4x4 armored vehicle closely resembling the Canadian Roshel Senator used by Ukraine in Kursk.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has opened a new national defense museum packed with the country’s missiles, rocket launchers and drones, and among the exhibits is a previously unseen 4×4 armored vehicle that closely resembles the Canadian-made Roshel Senator used by Ukraine.
State news agency KCNA reported on Oct. 13 that Kim attended the opening of the Defense Revolution Museum, run by the Second Economy Commission that oversees North Korea’s arms industry, on Oct. 11 and vowed to keep developing the country’s weapons. KCNA quoted him calling the museum a “precious monument” and did not give its size or location, though photos suggest at least part of it was built underground, with weapons lined up in long, tunnel-like halls.
The new armored vehicle shown in KCNA photos shares the overall layout and several hull details of the Senator, a Canadian armored car built on a Ford F-550 truck chassis that Roshel has supplied to Ukraine in large numbers. The North Korean version appears to have a lengthened body, suggesting it has been adapted to carry more troops in the back. KCNA did not name the vehicle or give any details about its protection, engine or how many are in service.
North Korean troops know the Senator from the battlefield. Ukrainian units used Senators during their incursion into Russia’s Kursk region in August 2024, where thousands of North Korean soldiers later fought alongside Russian forces to push Ukraine out. Russian troops have captured several Senators intact or lightly damaged, including one taken by naval infantry in the Kursk region that month, and a captured vehicle may have been handed to North Korea, which now appears to be building its own version. Roshel has delivered more than 2,000 Senators to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, and open-source tracking project Oryx had documented 182 in Mrap version and 83 Senator IMV of them destroyed, damaged or captured by the end of 2025.
The museum’s largest exhibit is the Hwasong-20 intercontinental ballistic missile, which North Korea has displayed but not yet flight-tested, shown with a world map suggesting it could reach the United States and beyond. Visitors also see a new submarine-launched ballistic missile, the 600 mm super-large multiple rocket launcher and a range of drones developed under Kim’s rule.
Kim opened the museum a day after North Korea test-fired what KCNA described as a tactical ballistic missile, which state media said brought “an important change” in improving all of the country’s weapons systems. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi condemned the launch. The museum opening also came as U.S. President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia in mid-November.

articles.title: Defense forces shoot down and suppress 88 out of 108 enemy drones; hits recorded at 17 locations – Air Force
articles.body:
Overnight into Tuesday, air defense forces shot down and suppressed, using electronic warfare measures, 88 out of 108 drones of various types used by Russian troops to attack Ukraine, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on its Telegram channel.
"Overnight into October 13 (starting from 18:00 on October 12), the enemy launched an attack using 5 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk region, 9 Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and 108 strike UAVs, including Shahed types (74 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoy drones launched from the directions of Orel, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), as well as the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk and the Autonomous Republic of Crimea (Hvardeiske)," the message notes.
According to preliminary military data, as of 08:00, air defense units had shot down or suppressed 88 enemy UAVs, including Shahed types (58 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types.
"Enemy air attack assets were recorded striking 17 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at seven other sites. Additionally, loitering munitions struck the city of Kharkiv, though some failed to reach their targets," the command reported.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
As of this morning, the attack is ongoing, with several enemy drones remaining in the airspace.

articles.title: Wes Streeting might be an unlikely defence secretary – but he’s still a better bet than Penny Mordaunt
articles.body:
When Andy Burnham announced his first cabinet in July, few would have had Wes Streeting marked down as a likely defence secretary. Not even Wes. And no one is more bullish about Wes’s life chances than Wes. It just didn’t seem a natural fit. Defence secretaries tend to be more the unsmiling types who operate in the shadows. Politicians like John Healey, with the pallor of someone who has spent too long in underground bunkers with military chief of staffs. People who slide in and out of rooms without making a fuss.
Wes has always been someone who likes to be noticed. Enjoys the theatre of Westminster. The first to arrive at a party and the last to leave. A natural gossip. “Psst – you’ll never guess what Zelenskyy just said to Trump.”
But in the past few months, Wes has had something of a personality change. At the recent Labour party conference, he kept his appearances distinctly low key. No longer the life and soul of Liverpool, out till 2am before getting up to do the media round just four hours later. It can’t be long before we see him driving a tank somewhere near the Russian border. Wes is gonna be Wes.
He also has the distinct advantage of not being Penny Mordaunt, the former Tory minister who has done more to terrify a nation than any living defence secretary. A few weeks ago, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians in which Michael Gove was cast as the prime minister and Penny as defence secretary. The set up was that Russia had torpedoed a ship off Scotland, with the politicians and the military placed in a mock-up Cobra meeting and left to come up with responses as the situation developed.
This could have been the moment to restore faith in our democratic institutions. To admire the insight and clarity with which our leaders handle a crisis. To see how they repay the trust and power which we bestow on them. In which case, you should think again. What actually emerged is that politicians are no brighter than the rest of us. They just have egos which make them believe they are the right people in the right place at the right time. And that we are lucky to have them.
To put it bluntly, The War Game was a total shitshow. Just one bad decision after another. For the first two episodes, The Govester was like a rabbit in the headlights. Completely clueless as the UK came under increasing levels of attack. The best he could offer was to repeat back the last thing that was said to him and bark “ASAP!”
Penny, though, was a total menace to herself and the country from the word go. If this is really how defence secretaries behave, we should all be out digging bunkers in open land and stocking up on tinned food. Not that it would do much good. From the outset, Penny was hell-bent on escalating the conflict despite being told Britain’s military defences were totally threadbare and that the UK was only a middle-ranking global power. She couldn’t wait to use up the UK’s arsenal of weapons, and by the end two nuclear warheads were 20 minutes away from annihilating two major cities. Bye bye Britain. Still, at least she would go down as our last ever defence secretary.
So Streeting’s first appearance before the defence select committee was, first and foremost, a moment to give thanks he wasn’t Penny and that we are all – more or less – still here. And Wes looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD. He now talks mainly in letters – SDR, DIP and NAD – and jargon that is designed to be unintelligible to most mortals. Mostly, he wanted to get through the entire session by saying as little as possible and to send any stray reporters who had wandered into the committee room by mistake to sleep. He’d have liked to be more open, he said. But if he was, he’d have to kill us. For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets. If not exactly his happiest place, then still a happy one.
Wes began by telling the committee that the UK and its Nato allies were facing their gravest threat since the cold war. Given that, you could understand why he wan’t particularly keen on telling us just how unprepared we were for some kind of an attack as our enemies might be listening. When Streeting had taken on the defence job he had spent most of the first week telling the media that he would – like his predecessor – resign if he thought the money being allocated was inadequate.
Three months on and he was rather dancing on the head of a pin. He couldn’t say how, when or even if the commitment to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 would be met. We just had to keep the faith that somehow it would all work out OK. John Healey said it would all end up OK, and if John Healey said so then we ought to believe him. After all, it wasn’t just a question of spending more money – it was also about spending the money he did have better.
It also turned out that some of our defence capacity was largely illusory. Both because it took six years for most military contracts to be delivered, by which time there was a fair chance the hardware would be obsolete, and because much of the increased spending had been backloaded until after the next election. Politicians never tire of passing on costs to future governments.
The MoD’s permanent secretary, Jeremy Pocklington, spent at least five minutes trying to persuade the committee that backloading wasn’t really backloading even if it looked like backloading. For that kind of mind-numbing bullshit, Jezza has been awarded the Companion of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath. Still, Wes did say at one point that he “wasn’t keen on fighting a war”, which I suppose is a start. Gives him the edge over Penny at the very least.

articles.title: Poland urges Europe to switch to 'war-mode' defense production
articles.body:
Jo Harper
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Poland’s Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on Tuesday urged Europe to put weapons and ammunition production on a wartime footing to counter Russia's military build-up, Polish state news agency PAP reported.
He also urged the EU to allow urgent defense purchases from NATO allies outside the bloc.
Speaking in Warsaw following talks with European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius on strengthening European military capabilities, accelerating arms production and securing defense supply chains, Kosiniak-Kamysz said, "I personally favor switching to wartime mode in the production of weapons and ammunition throughout Europe.”
He argued that Russia was already operating in that way, without waiting for others, while Europe could no longer afford to remain complacent.
Kosiniak-Kamysz identified three priority areas for European defense investment: affordable long-range precision-strike capabilities, drones and counter-drone systems, and artificial intelligence.
He urged greater flexibility in European defense procurement, arguing that urgent purchases should be opened to NATO allies outside the EU when European manufacturers could not supply the necessary equipment quickly enough.
"We also propose that, in the case of critical purchases requiring rapid delivery, when it is not possible to obtain this equipment in the European Union, we should open up to our NATO allies who will be able to help us," he said.
The proposal highlights tension in European defense policy between efforts to strengthen the EU's domestic arms industry and the immediate need to acquire military capabilities in response to Russia's war against Ukraine.
It could also have implications for defense manufacturers in non-EU NATO countries, including Türkiye, Britain and the US, although the Polish minister did not identify specific countries or suppliers in his remarks.

articles.title: Who is Yuki Imai, the Japanese journalist Russia has arrested on espionage charges?
articles.body:
Who is Yuki Imai, the Japanese journalist Russia has arrested on espionage charges?
A Japanese journalist has been detained on suspicion of espionage on Sakhalin, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said. The agency identified him as a Japanese national and a correspondent for the newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun but did not release his name. He was detained in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk shortly before he planned to leave Russia and taken to Moscow.
The FSB released footage of the operation with the detainee’s face blurred. Officers appear to have seized him at a hotel. The footage shows officers forcing him to unlock his devices, and he appears surprised when they accuse him of espionage.
The FSB said the journalist was gathering information about Russian military personnel on instructions from Japanese intelligence. According to the agency, he was collecting data on the number of Kuril Islands residents mobilized for the war in Ukraine and on residents who volunteered to fight.
The detainee is 34-year-old Yuki Imai, according to the case record from Moscow’s Lefortovsky District Court. On October 13, the court ordered him held in custody in an espionage case under Article 276 of Russia’s Criminal Code. He faces up to 20 years in prison.
Imai had been visiting Russia since 2014. His most recent visit began in the summer of 2026, according to the news outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti (1, 2). He studied at St. Petersburg State University and posted photographs from his trips around Moscow and St. Petersburg. He said he had “a bit of an interest in Soviet military equipment,” as well as Russian culture — classical music, ballet, and Soviet cinema. The footage of his detention showed a book by Ivan Bunin in his suitcase.
According to Ostorozhno, Novosti, Imai had recently published articles about the State Duma elections and the unveiling of a monument in Khabarovsk commemorating the Soviet Union’s victory over Japan. He also wrote about Russia’s strengthening ties with North Korea.
During his most recent trip, Imai visited Primorsky Krai, with stops in Vladivostok and Nakhodka and a visit to a children’s arts center there. He interviewed Russian-speaking residents of Japan and took an interest in life in the Russian Far East, the Soviet-Japanese War, and friendship between Russia and Japan.
Imai’s most recent article, published on October 5, is a report from Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk about the presence of North Korean nationals in the region.
News of Imai’s detention came amid reports that Tokyo had extradited a member of the Russian group Qilin to Germany, according to the news outlet Agentstvo. Japanese authorities detained the 28-year-old Russian national in May on suspicion of involvement in a September 2024 cyberattack on a logistics company in Germany. Qilin is ransomware used by hackers, including those linked to North Korea.
The last time a Japanese journalist was detained in Russia on espionage allegations was in 2019. He was accused of trying to obtain classified materials about Russia’s military capabilities in the Far East and was expelled from the country.
Russian authorities use detained foreigners in exchanges for Russians facing prosecution abroad. For example, in 2023, Russia charged Wall Street Journal correspondent Evan Gershkovich with espionage. A court sentenced him to 16 years in a penal colony. Gershkovich was freed in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.
Relations between Russia and Japan deteriorated after Putin made his first trip to the Kuril Islands in August, visiting Iturup. In response, Japan summoned the Russian ambassador and lodged a “strong protest.”

articles.title: Russian forces destroy over 260,000 military drones in Ukraine operation — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russian forces have destroyed over 260,000 Ukrainian military drones since the start of the special military operation in Ukraine, according to the latest report released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
"In all, the following targets have been destroyed since the start of the special military operation: 674 aircraft, 284 helicopters, 260,703 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,216 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,787 multiple rocket launchers, 36,713 field artillery guns and mortars and 74,402 special military motor vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Kiev loses 1,285 troops along engagement line in past day - latest figures
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,285 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 270 troops, a tank and a field artillery gun in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, roughly 230 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and about 160 troops and four armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost roughly 345 troops and seven armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, over 240 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and about 40 troops and two field artillery guns in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russia’s Battlegroup North fighting for three communities in pocket of encirclement in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North forces are fighting for the liberation of three communities in the Kharkov Region and tightening the ring of encirclement of Ukrainian troops in that area, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units are tightening the ring of encirclement in the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. In the pocket of encirclement, they are fighting for the liberation of the communities of Nikolayevka, Varvarovka and Nefyodovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army lost roughly 60 troops, a motor vehicle and five ground robotic platforms in the pocket of encirclement, it specified.
Battlegroup North forces are expanding the outer area of control and continue battles for taking control of the settlements of Prikolotnoye, Kotovka and Gogino in the Kharkov Region, the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 270 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup North forces inflicted more than 270 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy tank and a field artillery gun in its areas of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
In the Kharkov direction, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Velikiye Prokhody, Khotomlya, Pogoreloye, Russkaya Lozovaya, Tsirkuny and Veliky Burluk in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.
In the Sumy direction, Battlegroup North units struck formations of two mechanized brigades of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Glukhov, Yuryevo, Barilovka, Maryino, Konotop and Nikolskoye in the Sumy Region and the city of Sumy, it said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 270 personnel, a tank, eight motor vehicles, a field artillery gun and an electronic warfare station in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts 230 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted roughly 230 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup West units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Grushevka, Blagodatovka, Berezovka, Maliyevka and Osinovo in the Kharkov Region and Volchy Yar in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 230 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 17 motor vehicles, three artillery guns and four electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts 160 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted roughly 160 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed four enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Kramatorsk, Semyonovka, Slavyansk and Nikolayevka in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 160 personnel, four armored combat vehicles, 31 motor vehicles and an artillery gun in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center forces liberate 286 buildings in Dobropolye over past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center forces liberated 286 buildings in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic and destroyed roughly 65 Ukrainian troops over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, assault groups of the 51st Army advanced in the town’s central and northwestern parts. Some forces jointly with marine infantry formations continued mopping up the town’s quarters they had seized and the territory of the Dobropolskaya coalmine," the ministry said.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup Center units liberated 286 buildings, including three production structures and eliminated roughly 65 Ukrainian troops in Dobropolye, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts 345 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted roughly 345 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed seven enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Center units inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, an airborne brigade of the Ukrainian army and two National Guard brigades in areas near the settlements of Liman, Verovka, Belozerskoye, Svyatogorovka, Vesyolaya Gora, Maryevka and Novoyavlenka in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 345 personnel, seven armored combat vehicles, eight motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and a Grad multiple rocket launcher in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 240 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 240 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup East units continued their advance deep into the enemy’s defenses and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an air assault brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Gavrilovka and Tarasovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Dudnikovo, Zalivnoye, Blakitnoye and Volnyanka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 240 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, eight motor vehicles and an artillery gun in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 40 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 40 Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy field artillery guns in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.

articles.title: North Korean missile launches may be response to South's hypersonic test, Seoul says
articles.body:
North Korea's launch of multiple ballistic missiles towards the East Sea appears to be an apparent response to South Korea's successful test of a hypersonic glide vehicle last week, the South Korean military has confirmed.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches originating from the Pyongyang region.
At least one projectile flew more than 900 kilometres, Yonhap News Agency said.
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the firing could also demonstrate technical advances under Pyongyang's five-year defence modernisation blueprint.
Jang declined to confirm whether the weapons tested were hypersonic systems or intermediate-range ballistic missiles, noting that further technical analysis is ongoing.
The launches followed South Korea’s inaugural test of a hypersonic glide vehicle on Thursday.
Regional reactions
Japan's defence authorities confirmed detecting two suspected ballistic missiles, reporting that the projectiles landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone.
The US Pacific Command issued a statement confirming close consultations with regional allies: "Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies."
The command reiterated Washington's ironclad commitment to defending regional partners.
The missile tests unfold amid friction along the inter-Korean border following a September 21 landmine detonation inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers, two critically.
Seoul accused North Korean forces of deliberately laying the explosives following a joint inquiry with the UN Command.
Pyongyang rejected the findings as fabricated and warned it would retaliate against any countermeasures.
Pyongyang has not issued an official public statement regarding Monday's launches.

North Korea Revives Russia’s Forgotten Missile Project—and Gives It a Deadlier Upgrade
North Korea has unveiled a new missile system capable of striking targets up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) away, combining a rocket booster with a glide bomb in a design resembling Russia’s long-delayed Hermes missile project.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 13, the previously unnamed system was displayed during a North Korean exhibition highlighting the country’s technological developments. Military equipment researcher Andrii Tarasenko drew attention to the weapon, which appears to incorporate several significant changes compared with its Russian counterpart.
One of the most notable differences is its ammunition. Unlike the Russian Hermes design, North Korea’s system reportedly uses a glide bomb as the second stage of its rocket, potentially allowing the weapon to travel toward its target after separating from the initial booster.
The launcher configuration also differs substantially. The North Korean system features 22 launch tubes, compared with six on the Russian Hermes launcher. Its reported range is 100 kilometers, while the Russian project was designed with longer-range configurations in mind.
The weapon is not entirely new. North Korea conducted its first publicly reported test launches of a similar system in May 2026, although its official designation and detailed technical specifications have not been disclosed.
Defense Express noted that the combination of a rocket booster and glide bomb resembles the concept behind the US-developed Ground-Launched Small Diameter Bomb (GLSDB), previously supplied to Ukraine.
The GLSDB uses a rocket motor to launch a precision-guided glide bomb from the ground, extending its reach beyond that of conventional air-dropped munitions. However, the system has faced operational challenges, and Defense Express reported that questions remain about whether its technical problems have been fully resolved.
The Russian Hermes project dates back to the 1990s and was intended to provide precision strikes against targets at extended ranges. Despite years of development and testing, the system has not entered widespread operational service, with the latest significant public updates dating to 2023.
According to Defense Express, North Korea’s newly displayed weapon may represent a further development of the original Russian concept rather than a direct copy. The outlet also noted that Moscow’s apparent decision not to pursue Hermes remains unexplained.
Earlier, in March 2025, North Korea unveiled its first airborne early warning and control aircraft, based on the Soviet-designed Il-76 and closely resembling Russia’s A-50 radar plane.
Pyongyang also showcased its Saetbyol-4 drone, which bears a striking resemblance to the US-made RQ-4 Global Hawk, raising questions about North Korea’s use of foreign military designs in developing its own weapons systems.

articles.title: How the Yandex ‘Russian bots’ lie fell apart
articles.body:
How the Yandex ‘Russian bots’ lie fell apart
Did Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers destroy the Kremlin’s pro-MAGA bot army? Or are Vladimir Zelensky and his European patrons insulting their citizens with remedial-grade propaganda? RT takes a trip down the rabbit hole.
Ukrainian forces hit three Yandex (Russia’s equivalent to Google) data centers with long-range drones between October 8 and 11. Yandex confirmed that operations were “completely halted” at the facility struck on October 8, and temporarily halted at the center struck on October 11. This much is true, but the story that followed veers into NAFO fiction.
How did the ‘Russian bots’ story begin?
On October 8, American cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler posted a Cloudflare graph showing a dramatic drop in “bot traffic” after the first Yandex center was hit. As Yandex is primarily a search company, its bots crawl the internet indexing content for users. All search engines function in this way, but Fowler – either through malice or ignorance – conflated this search bot activity with social media bot activity, claiming that the drop in traffic could “disrupt the midterm elections in the US.”
The story spread, hitting the mainstream media on October 11 when Tom’s Hardware published an article claiming that “Russian disinformation bot traffic” had been “nearly eliminated” after the strikes. The word “disinformation” was later pulled from the headline, but the tale had already taken on a life of its own.
That same day, an AI-created graph began circulating, claiming that “Russian bots” were making 56% fewer posts in support of Germany’s right-wing AfD party in the aftermath of the strikes. The graph, which was unsourced and had one axis unlabeled, measured the “decline in activity of Russian bots” up to October 15, four days in the future at the time it appeared online.
Regardless, the graph was shared by a Green Party councillor in Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia, and by Czech MEP Tomas Zdechovsky. “This is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets,” Zdechovsky wrote on social media. “So much talk about German patriotism… then the connection from Russia goes down.”
Who spread the lie?
By October 12, the story had been reported by Germany’s Der Standard and Focus. That morning, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky spread it further, claiming at the Warsaw Security Forum that his strikes on Yandex data centers had made it “a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms.”
“A lot of people noticed it, and there was less hate, less division and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots,” Zelensky continued. “And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from. If they disappeared when Yandex went offline, this proves again and again that Europe is not the source of the problems,” he added.
Speaking on the sidelines of the forum, Polish minister Tomasz Siemoniak claimed that the country’s domestic intelligence agency was “observing a significant, radical decline in Russian bot activity online,” while Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said that “we should ask Mr. Zelensky to hit more data centres in Russia” to “protect” elections in the EU.
Anti-Kremlin activist and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov weighed in, claiming that “the Russian troll bots” in his X feed had “dropped dramatically,” while former US ambassador Michael McFaul thanked the Ukrainian weapons industry for granting him reprieve from “daily” harassment by “armies of Russian bots.”
The Russian troll bots in my own feed have dropped dramatically already. MAGA's online support may soon reflect Trump's approval rating!
— Garry Kasparov (@Kasparov63) October 11, 2026
The only problem was none of this was true, and based on the replies to McFaul’s tweet, nobody was buying it.
How was the bots story debunked?
The story didn’t take long to fall apart. Common Consultancy, a Scandinavian NGO that has previously accused Russia of orchestrating social media influence campaigns, concluded that there was “no visible effect” on pro-MAGA or pro-AfD social media posts after the Yandex strikes. Leonid Volkov, an anti-Kremlin activist associated with deceased opposition figure Alexey Navalny, slammed Zdechovsky for spreading “nonsense and falsehood.”
CeMAS, a liberal German think tank, stated that it was “not seeing a drop in the number of posts that could be explained by an attack on data centers.” The Hasso Plattner Institute and Polisphere, two tech nonprofits, concurred, and German newspapers began quietly editing their articles on Monday night.
Some, like Merkur, kept “speculation about Russian bots and the AfD” in their headlines. Others, including Der Standard, noted that their “original assertion of a confirmed connection [between the strikes and alleged bot activity] has been corrected.” The Verge, a tech-focused American news site, admitted that “the Yandex outage probably didn’t blitz Russian bots.”
Is this hybrid war?
By the time the story was debunked and corrected, the damage was done. In the public’s eye, the strikes were tied to a drop in “Russian bot” activity, and none of the speakers at the Warsaw Security Forum, including senior Ukrainian, Polish, and Lithuanian officials, bothered to correct the record.
These same leaders have spent the last two months amping up their accusations of “hybrid war” – acts of sabotage, disinformation, and cyber-harassment that do not rise to the level of actual war – against Russia, with Berlin’s foreign intelligence chief warning last week that Moscow’s supposed “shadow war” against the West could see Germany “becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia.”
That none of the acts of “hybrid war” – among them the discovery of a suspicious drone at Leipzig Airport in August, and a series of unsubstantiated drone sightings across Germany and Scandinavia last year – have been linked by evidence to Russia is a feature, not a bug. “Hybrid war” is by its very nature unprovable, and the accusation alone is enough for European leaders to justify their deepening proxy war in Ukraine, their remilitarization and expansion of the national security state at home.
Furthermore, the accusations themselves are a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, analyst Thomas Fazi argued last week. “Europeans,” he wrote, “are being subjected to a sustained campaign of cognitive or psychological warfare aimed at conditioning them to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia.”
Who stands to gain?
For Germany’s ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), accusations of ‘hybrid warfare” and “AfD bots” serve a much more petty and venal political end. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is less popular now than at any point in his political career, and with the AfD trouncing the CDU in state elections and leading his party by ten points in opinion polls, Merz has taken every opportunity available to tie his opponents to Russia.
“We in Germany will not allow ourselves to be divided, not by hybrid attacks, not by Moscow-bot-driven hate speech on social media, and – if I may say so – not even by the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers,” the chancellor said in a speech earlier this month.
The Yandex story – which conveniently linked the AfD to “Moscow-bot-driven hate speech” – was a godsend to Merz, and to his Ukrainian and Eastern European allies, who have an interest in preventing the Ukraine-skeptic AfD from taking power in Germany. Unfortunately for them, like all “hybrid war” claims, it fell apart the moment it was subjected to some basic scrutiny.

Trump said he does not believe Russia and China are helping Iran
