articles.title: Critics warn of espionage risks, loss of trust within NATO as Slovakia restores military-diplomatic representation with Russia
articles.body:
Concern as Slovakia restores military contacts with Russia
October 13, 2026
When Robert Fico sat opposite Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin in May, the Slovak prime minister said relations between their countries should extend beyond energy supplies.
He told the Russian president that steps had already been taken to restore military attaches at their respective embassies.
Five months later, the arrangement is now taking shape.
Slovakia has sent two military officers — Brigadier General Slavomir Staviarsky and his deputy, Colonel Ivo Gahir — to Moscow and is preparing to receive a Russian military attache in Bratislava, restoring military-diplomatic representation for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
What has Slovakia to gain?
The move has prompted criticism from opposition politicians, who question what Slovakia stands to gain.
They warn that Russia could use the arrangement to strengthen its intelligence operations.
"One additional military attache does not fundamentally change that broader picture; the appointment's main significance is the political signal it sends," Martin Poliacik, a former Slovak MP affiliated with the opposition Progressive Slovakia party, told DW.
"NATO allies should be concerned both about the activities of the incoming officer and about the political environment in which he will operate," he went on.
The appointments were reported by Slovak news website Aktuality.sk on October 8. Both officers appear on the Slovak Defense Ministry's published list of military diplomats serving abroad.
According to public broadcaster STVR, Staviarsky has been in Moscow since the beginning of August.
Meanwhile, opposition defense experts quoted by Aktuality.sk named the incoming Russian officer as Maxim Verezan.
Verezan has received Slovak approval, according to the opposition sources cited by the website, but was not yet listed among accredited military attaches.
Aktuality.sk says that the Defense Ministry has not answered its question as to when Verezan is due to arrive in Bratislava.
Fear of espionage and disinformation
The prospect has revived memories of a Russian espionage scandal involving Sergei Solomasov, the Russian embassy's deputy military attache in Bratislava, a few years ago.
Solomasov was filmed recruiting and handing over money to Bohus Garbar, a contributor to the pro-Russian website Hlavne spravy, in 2021.
Solomasov was expelled from Slovakia the following year. Garbar was subsequently convicted of espionage and bribery.
Opposition experts told Aktuality.sk that a Slovak attache in Moscow would be closely watched and obtain little useful information, while the reciprocal Russian posting could facilitate espionage in Slovakia.
They warned that the incoming officer could conduct influence and disinformation operations, questioning what Slovakia would receive in return.
Government defends the move
The Slovak government and its supporters have defended the renewal of contacts as a means of gathering information and maintaining diplomatic representation.
In a statement reported by Slovak public broadcaster STVR, Slovak military intelligence said Staviarsky's role was to assess the security and military-political situation and keep the Defense Ministry informed.
Richard Gluck, a member of Fico's Smer party who chairs parliament's defense and security committee, pointed to the presence of American, British and French military diplomats in Moscow.
"We were losing a great deal of information," Gluck told STVR, arguing that ending Slovakia's military diplomatic presence in Moscow had been a mistake.
'A very serious step'
For retired Lieutenant General Pavel Macko, however, the circumstances in which the previous contacts ended are crucial.
"This is a very serious step taken by the Fico government," said Macko, a former Slovak deputy chief of defense and once the highest-ranking Slovak general in NATO's command structures.
"Nothing has changed [since 2022], just the opposite," he went on.
"Russia's adversarial activities continue to grow in Slovakia and in the region. The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine continues with high intensity, so do the hostile hybrid activities against Slovakia and its neighbors," Macko said.
He pointed to a foiled plot to burn down a Ukrainian-owned drone factory in eastern Slovakia and suspicions that incidents in Munich and Leipzig were linked to Russian operations based in Slovakia.
Macko also warned that political influence over Slovakia's intelligence services and the government's pro-Russian policies could further damage intelligence-sharing and trust among allies, despite the presence of "a significant number of very professional and trustworthy officers."
One eye on next year's election?
Martin Poliacik, meanwhile, said he suspected political motives lay behind the decision to restore the military attache posts, which comes as Prime Minister Fico eyes his chances of re-election next year.
"[Fico's] best chance of building a credible narrative for the next election is to claim that everyone else is dragging us into war and he alone wants peace," Poliacik told DW.
"I believe he will argue that he is best placed to talk to Putin about ending the war, and that this requires an exceptionally close relationship with him," he went on, adding that Fico tried to keep quiet about the major role played by Slovak arms manufacturers in supplying Ukraine with ammunition.
The ammunition is supplied under commercial contracts, rather than as military aid from the Slovak government.
Poliacik, too, distinguished between Slovakia's formal commitments and confidence in its political leadership. In his view, Western partners have become accustomed to Fico's behavior.
"Slovakia is formally fulfilling its NATO commitments," he went on.
"Formal compliance does not, by itself, settle the question of political trust," Poliacik added. "Predictability, however, is not the same as reliability."
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

articles.title: The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal
articles.body:
A drone strike on 10 October put more than half of the large fuel tanks out of action at an oil-loading terminal in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don, Russian news Telegram channel Astra found. The terminal loads fuel onto river and sea tankers for export, and it burned for two days while a local channel wrote that reeds might be on fire. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow has officially acknowledged the hit. It came hours after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Russia has spent the autumn hammering Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Ukraine’s long-range drones keep hitting the refineries, depots, and terminals that fuel Russia’s army and earn it export revenue. Every burned tank turns that revenue into repair bills, while Moscow is already subsidizing its own fuel pumps. A refinery-only truce of the kind the White House described a day after the strike would shield the Russian plants that feed terminals like this one.
Seven of 12 tanks out of action
Astra’s analysts concluded from eyewitness footage that at least seven of the terminal’s 12 large tanks had been knocked out. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ counted seven burned-out tanks and one more scorched by the fire.
The fire was still burning in the early hours of 12 October. Local channel Rostov Glavny posted video of the burning tank farm, passing on rumors that reeds were on fire and noting the city’s second day under smoke, The Moscow Times reported. Footage filmed in the daytime on 12 October showed no more open flames, only gray smoke, according to Astra.
A terminal that loads fuel for export
The site is the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant, formerly known as Yug Rusi, in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny District. It receives, stores, and transships fuel onto river and sea tankers, including for export, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said.
The terminal also supplies fuel to the Russian army and earns Moscow hard currency, ZN reported. The Moscow Times put its loading capacity at 3.5 million tons a year and its tank farm at about 60,000 cubic meters, roughly 16 million gallons.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
The refinery itself stands in the town of Novoshakhtinsk near the border with Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast. The terminal sits on the Don River with access to the Sea of Azov, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi noted. Ukraine hit the refinery in June, and Ukraine’s General Staff reported striking the Yug Rusi terminal on 9 July, placing it in Bataysk.
A night of drones over the region
Exilenova+ posted images of the burning terminal in the early hours of 10 October. It presented them as the site after Trump’s phone call with Putin. The channel later shared NASA satellite fire data showing the blaze.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar claimed the attack injured six people. Slyusar further stated air defenses downed more than 100 drones over the region. Radio Liberty’s Russian Service noted that neither side had officially confirmed the hit on the terminal.
Hours after the US-Russia diesel deal
The strike came hours after Trump announced on 9 October that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury then cleared the trade with a sanctions license.
On 11 October, Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Under it, he expects Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, a White House official told Axios.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that evening that Ukraine’s armed forces had received all relevant orders. Neither Ukrainian monitoring channels nor Russian officials have reported a new strike on a Russian oil facility since. On 13 October, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to guarantee an energy ceasefire if Russia took matching steps.

articles.title: Zelensky claims West gave no warning of latest Russian strike
articles.body:
Zelensky claims West gave no warning of latest Russian strike
Ukraine received no advance warning from its Western partners ahead of an overnight Russian missile strike, Vladimir Zelensky claimed on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian Air Force first raised the issue earlier in the day, saying it detected incoming missiles only during their final approach, without receiving advance intelligence from the West.
Footage circulating online appeared to show at least six ballistic missiles striking Kiev, with air raid sirens sounding only after the impacts.
Zelensky echoed the complaint, saying Ukraine had received no warning from its “partners” about the impending attack. He did not single out any country but stressed that Western intelligence on planned Russian strikes remains “one of the most critical issues” for Kiev.
The presumed lack of the early warning sparked speculation that the US might have stopped sharing intelligence with Kiev. The two countries have been engaged in a public spat over the past few days. Zelensky condemned the US decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel as a “weak decision by strong partners,” while US President Donald Trump suggested it is time for Ukraine to get a “new president” instead of Zelensky, whose tenure has long ended but no elections have been held under the pretext of the conflict with Russia.
Trump has appeared to reject the allegations that Washington stopped sharing intelligence with Kiev, stating the US has been working with both Russia and Ukraine “on getting the war to end.”
“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” Trump told reporters.
Kiev usually receives early missile warnings through the Battlespace Command and Control Center, a system used by the US military and the NATO bloc. Media reports have suggested the presumed lack of warning overnight was an isolated technical incident rather than a political decision. A source familiar with the matter told Politico that the US had told Ukraine that there was “no warning because of bad weather conditions.” Kiev, however, was reportedly unsatisfied with the explanation and that a “growing number of people” are concerned that there were other reasons behind the lack of warning.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: No warning from partners about Russian ballistic strike on Kyiv
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: No warning from partners about Russian ballistic strike on Kyiv
Commenting on Russia's recent attacks on Ukrainian cities, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine received no warning from its partners about the ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of 12 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy noted that starting that evening and continuing into 13 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with more than 100 different weapons, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles. A significant proportion were shot down, but not all of them.
"There was also a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv – five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike," Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that intelligence about Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives and is one of the most critical issues.
"This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," the president added.
Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine has not struck Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for two days since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
"During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine. [...] Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to make de-escalation happen. Wars end when the aggressor realises that it cannot prolong the war," Zelenskyy stressed.
He added that international pressure on Russia contributes to bringing peace closer.
"But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- Earlier, it was reported that during talks with the Ukrainian team in Florida on Friday 9 October, Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine because of Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
- Reuters sources denied that any such threats had been made.
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, has said that Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the United States.

articles.title: Putin wants Ukraine deal more than Zelensky – Trump
articles.body:
Putin wants Ukraine deal more than Zelensky – Trump
Russian President Vladimir Putin is more eager than Vladimir Zelensky to reach a deal to end the Ukraine conflict, US President Donald Trump has said. Trump’s comments came after he suggested it is time for Ukraine to get a “new president.”
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump claimed both Moscow and Kiev support the energy ceasefire which he announced on Sunday. Neither Russia nor Ukraine has confirmed the truce.
“I think they want to make a deal, but they don’t know how. But we’re going to get them to make a deal,” Trump said.
“I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky,” he added.
Trump also rejected criticism of his decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel following a phone call with Putin on Friday, stressing that the agreement benefited the wider world and American farmers and ranchers. 
“Zelensky has to focus on making a deal, not talking about that,” he stressed, referring to the Ukrainian leader’s criticism of the agreement.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire.” Zelensky said the announcement “was news for me,” but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has declined to confirm the agreement, saying contacts were ongoing. While praising the efforts of American negotiators, Peskov stressed that Moscow is seeking long-term peace rather than a temporary ceasefire. Russian officials have long argued that a truce would only help Ukraine to reinforce its battered military and receive more Western-made weapons.
According to the New York Times, Ukrainian officials were informed of the US-Russia diesel deal during tense negotiations in Miami. The US delegation subsequently demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries, and when Kiev’s representatives asked what they would receive in return, the Americans reportedly argued that Washington already provided substantial assistance, including intelligence sharing. Some participants interpreted this as a veiled threat to withdraw support, the article said.
Following his conversation with Putin and Zelensky’s angry reaction to the diesel deal, Trump suggested that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Zelensky’s presidential term expired more than two years ago, although the Ukrainian leader has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Russia has declared Zelensky “illegitimate,” highlighting his dubious legal status as a major obstacle to a peace agreement.
After a war of words with Trump, Zelensky signaled he was ready to hold an election but demanded a 60-day ceasefire with Russia. Moscow responded by stressing that “if Kiev genuinely wants to hold elections… then the president of the Russian Federation… will be ready to issue an order not to carry out strikes against Ukraine on the election day specifically.”

articles.title: Fact check: Russia turns to AI to push fakes about 'women's draft' in Ukraine
articles.body:
Fact check: Russia turns to AI to push fakes about 'women's draft' in Ukraine
Servicewomen of the “Fighting Witches” mobile group of Ukraine’s Air Defense Forces practice shooting at a base in Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Nov. 2, 2024. (Yevhenii Vasyliev/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Russian disinformation yet again targets the sensitive topic of mobilization in Ukraine — this time, pushing falsehoods about an alleged forced draft of women.
Pro-Kremlin social media accounts and Russian media have spread AI-generated images alleging that Ukrainian women are being lured to join the Armed Forces by targeted recruitment posters, while others claim they are being outright called up for military service.
But though tens of thousands of Ukrainian women enlisted in the army as volunteers, these claims are false — there is no mandatory draft of women in place, nor is it being prepared.
Telegram channels have once again proven to be fertile ground for such fabricated stories, with both Ukrainian- and Russian-language channels involved in spreading them.
One fake post from Sept. 15 alleged that posters featuring women in military uniforms had appeared around Odesa, a city in southern Ukraine. Other channels reposted identical photographs but claimed they had been seen around Lutsk, in western Ukraine.
The banners' message was intended to show how domestic chores hardly differ from tasks at the front, reading, "You figured out the washing machine — you'll figure out FPVs (first-person-view drones) too."
"There were no such banners, and an AI verification tool indicates they were AI-generated," Roman Osadchuk, the director of Threat Intelligence at the LetsData tech company, told the Kyiv Independent.
LetsData spotted the campaign in mid-September as it began circulating on social media.
A similar fake image was posted on the Telegram channel of Russian state TV presenter Olesya Loseva on Sept. 29. The post featured a bogus advertisement she claimed had been displayed in one of Kyiv's shopping centers.
The image features a young woman standing over a baby and a gun, with the Ukrainian-language caption reading: "A real Ukrainian woman can do these things in 40 seconds!"
When the Kyiv Independent ran this image through Hive Moderation, a platform that detects AI-generated or synthetic content, it returned a near-certain verdict — 99.9% likely to be AI-generated.
"This narrative is recurring and gets amplified from time to time, meaning that it comes and goes, sometimes using 'new tools' like AI-generated imagery," adds Osadchuk.
While disinformation and propaganda have long been central to Moscow's arsenal, Russia is now harnessing AI to spread falsehoods faster and more widely.
"Russia-linked actors have mostly used AI tools to amplify existing tactics, such as producing inauthentic content at scale and spreading content to reach broader audiences and fuel polarization," the European Center of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats reported in March.
read also
Besides Telegram, the narrative has also appeared on X, where a post by Donbass Segodnya, a pro-Russian news outlet, featured images of a woman apparently holding summons papers, implying that a mass call-up of women has begun.
Women can indeed receive summonses, but only if they are in the military register, which is mandatory only for women with relevant medical or pharmaceutical education.
Even then, this does not mean they can be mobilized against their will. The women are simply added to the register and can be summoned to update their personal data or undergo a medical examination.
No mobilization of women in Ukraine
Since 2022, Ukraine has been carrying out a large-scale draft of military-age men to boost its army's ranks and resist Russian aggression — a topic repeatedly targeted by Russian disinformation and propaganda.
Women have also joined the military as volunteers, with about 76,000 being part of Ukraine's Armed Forces, including 57,000 serving in military roles. However, Ukraine has not instituted a mandatory draft for women.
"There are no decisions to mobilize women in Ukraine," said Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, a body at the country's National Security and Defense Council, on Aug. 26.
"The parliamentary committee on national security, defense, and intelligence officially stated that there are no legislative initiatives, draft laws, or internal discussions concerning the introduction of such mobilization.
Moscow launched this latest disinformation campaign just as rumors of women's conscription circulated in Ukraine.
Former Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov raised the issue in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) on Aug. 20, arguing that requiring women to serve in the military would "immediately double the mobilization pool."
Separately, former U.S. Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg said on Aug. 24 that he believed women should be mobilized to help Ukraine's manpower problem since "they (women) fight no worse than men."
The Ukrainian parliament reacted by saying that the comments "do not reflect the actual legislative work."
With no draft law on the table, the mobilization of women remains confined to AI-generated content.

articles.title: Russian strike injures dozens at Rivne University as ballistic missiles hit Kyiv
articles.body:
Russian strikes caused injuries and deaths across Ukraine on Tuesday, including at a university in Rivne and civilian infrastructure in Kyiv.
At least 25 people were injured after a Russian strike hit an educational institution in Ukraine's Rivne on Tuesday, local authorities said.
Police said two people who are in a serious condition are undergoing surgery, while three more people were being treated by medical staff.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said five ballistiv missiles also hit civilian infrastructure in the country's capital Kyiv, adding that Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about the attack.
Zelenskyy characterised the barrage on the capital as “particularly vile,” and emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine's partners on such ballistic missile attacks “helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues.”
"This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning.
Strikes on Kharkiv kill 4, injure 41
Zelenskyy said that in addition to four deaths in a strike on an apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city in one evening alone.
A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the Kyiv city military administration said, while a Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said.
One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.
Russia's war in Ukraine hasn’t seen major shifts on the ground since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Moscow's intensified aerial attacks on cities that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. Among the damage was a residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv that was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said.
Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the 4 1/2-year war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Tuesday's strikes came ahead of a key summit of the European Council in Brussels on Friday, 16 October, where Zelenskyy is expected to attend.

articles.title: Ukraine’s largest steelworks begins cold shutdown after extensive damage from Russian strikes, saying safe operation is impossible while war continues
articles.body:
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has begun the process of placing its plant in cold shutdown following four Russian missile attacks, the company said on 10 October. The attacks killed six workers, injured more than 18 others, and forced the suspension of primary steel production.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is Ukraine’s largest steelworks, so its shutdown adds to the pressure on an industry already hit by Russian attacks and disrupted exports.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company’s priority was to protect workers and industrial assets. He said the ArcelorMittal Group would remain in Ukraine, but that its assessment was that safe operation was impossible while the war continued.
Workers and the city
As of July, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and its subsidiaries employed about 17,000 people, local outlet Pershyi Kryvorizkyi reported. On 29 September, the outlet reported that the company had not said how many workers could lose their jobs and was assessing its staffing needs after production stopped. It also said municipal water and heating utilities had about 1,000 vacancies and had been instructed to help ArcelorMittal workers find jobs. The outlet noted that it was unclear whether the vacancies were new and that the announcement did not specify the roles or salaries.
In late September, Kryvyi Rih defense council head Oleksandr Vilkul wrote on Telegram that the city would cut spending and stop a number of projects as tax revenues fell. He attributed the pressure to Russian attacks and the inability to export through seaports, and said several major industrial facilities were idle, including ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and three mining and ore-processing plants.
September steel output down 4.7-fold
Ukraine’s steel production fell 4.7-fold year on year in September, to 131,000 tons, the steelmakers’ association Ukrmetalurhprom said, NV reported. Metinvest chief operating officer Oleksandr Myronenko told Forbes Ukraine on 15 September that the group would declare force majeure on some contracts after Zaporizhstal and Kametstal halted operations.
An expected $1 billion impairment
The ArcelorMittal Group said on 25 September that it expected to record a non-cash impairment of about $1 billion, mostly related to property, plant, and equipment. It also said it had provided more than $700 million in financial support to its Ukrainian business.

Ukraine Hunts Down Russian Buk-M3 Air Defense System Worth $45 Million, Video
Ukrainian forces have identified and struck a Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile system valued at approximately $45 million, according to Ukraine’s 15th Artillery Reconnaissance Brigade, known as Chornyi Lis, on October 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The brigade released footage of the operation, showing its personnel targeting the Russian air defense system.
“We are systematically blinding enemy air defenses and making Russia’s military-industrial complex poorer,” the brigade stated.
The Buk-M3, which entered service with the Russian military in 2016, is an advanced medium-range surface-to-air missile system that forms part of Russia’s multilayered air defense network. It is capable of intercepting aircraft, cruise missiles, drones, and other aerial threats at distances of up to 70 kilometers (43 miles) and altitudes of up to 35 kilometers.
Unlike its predecessors, the Buk-M3 uses sealed launch containers to house its missiles. Each launcher can accommodate up to six ready-to-launch missiles and operate in coordination with dedicated transport and reloading vehicles.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian forces targeted a Russian Iskander-M missile system repair facility, a radar installation, logistics infrastructure, and concentrations of Russian troops in a series of strikes carried out on October 12 and during the night of October 13.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the operations on October 13, reporting that multiple Russian military targets had been struck both inside Russia and across Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.

articles.title: Baltic state bets on films and video games in militarization push
articles.body:
Baltic state bets on films and video games in militarization push
Estonia’s Defense Ministry has launched a funding competition for films and video games intended to strengthen public willingness to go to war, as Tallinn and the other Baltic states continue their military buildup citing a supposed Russian threat.
The scheme has a total budget of up to €250,000 ($280,000) and covers feature films, documentaries, animation, television series, and narrative video games, public broadcaster ERR reported on Tuesday. Applications close November 18, with the money available for use next year.
Tallinn is specifically looking for audiovisual productions that align with national defense goals and can reach different generations and make military issues accessible to a wider audience, ministry spokesman Thomas Melli explained to the outlet.
Director Ilmar Raag, who previously received ministry funding for a documentary, urged officials to favor credible portrayals over simplistic messaging, warning that overt propaganda could backfire. “Those people who give money in the ministry must see that if a filmmaker’s mind moves towards an overly simplistic propagandistic vision, it can actually have a negative backlash,” he told ERR.
The initiative comes alongside region-wide preparations for what have officials have claimed could be a confrontation with Russia by the end of the decade. The Financial Times reported earlier this month that Estonia wass acquiring missile systems capable of reaching St. Petersburg and deploying additional troops along the Russian border, particularly near the Kaliningrad exclave.
Defense Minister Martin Herem “joked” last month that if Estonia mobilized and Russia did not attack, it would be “economically more correct to attack ourselves” rather than keep troops waiting. “Then at least we will know when it will start, and we will not waste food and air in vain,” he said.
Despite already allocating a combined €9.4 billion to defense this year, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have recently sought an additional €500 million from the EU for military drones, citing the possibility of Russia testing NATO.
The Baltic states have also pursued a sweeping crackdown on Russian language, media, and culture. Estonia and Latvia are phasing out Russian-language schooling, while all three countries have banned Russian television channels. Latvia has gone further, targeting books, video games, toys, clothing, and other goods produced in Russia and Belarus.
NATO has separately spent years researching online influence techniques. Published experiments examined fake social-media profiles, targeted advertising, and purchased engagement. The bloc described the work, examined in RT’s America Now, as defensive research.
Moscow has repeatedly denied plans to attack Estonia or other NATO members, accusing Western governments of using the supposed threat to justify militarization and restrictions on Russian culture and Russian-speaking residents.
Russian officials have warned, however, that attacks on Russian territory or attempts to blockade Kaliningrad could provoke a military response involving all weapons in the country’s arsenal.

articles.title: Washington’s diesel deal: A door in the sanctions wall
articles.body:
On Friday, President Trump described his phone call with Vladimir Putin as “highly successful.” By Monday, oil traders had reason to agree. Kyiv had reason to feel betrayed.
In a single weekend, Washington dismantled part of the sanctions architecture it had spent four years building against Russia, all to shave a few cents from the price of diesel three weeks before an American election.
The mechanics are straightforward. Russia banned its own diesel exports on 8th July after Ukrainian drone strikes crippled its refineries and constricted domestic supply. That ban, combined with the disruption the Iran war inflicted on Gulf shipping, helped drive diesel prices toward record highs worldwide.
On 9th October, Trump announced that Putin had agreed to release diesel back onto the market: 300,000 tons “immediately,” another 500,000 in November, a million more “immediately thereafter,” and as much as 4.8 million tons in total, depending on how quickly Russia’s bombed refineries could recover.
The US Treasury moved just as swiftly. It issued a waiver suspending American sanctions on Russian diesel until 7th April 2027. Moscow, however, authorized only 500,000 tons for the time being, a smaller and slower first step than Trump’s announcement had implied.
Trump portrayed the agreement as a triumph of personal diplomacy, linking it to the other front of his energy strategy.
“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” he wrote on Truth Social.
Markets moved on the headline. Diesel futures fell more than 4 percent on the day of the announcement. Within hours, the US diesel refining margin had dropped by more than six dollars a barrel.
Yet the scale of what was promised tells a different story.
READ: Trump’s national security team holds unannounced Camp David talks on Iran war, Yemen: Axios
At roughly 7.45 barrels per ton, the first 300,000-tonne tranche amounts to about 2.2 million barrels. That is roughly 14 hours of American distillate consumption and about 2 percent of existing US commercial stocks.
Even the full 4.8 million tons, delivered over three months, would average around 400,000 barrels a day. The global diesel market consumes close to 29 million barrels daily.
Clayton Seigle, an energy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, put it bluntly. The agreement “probably won’t have much impact on prices” but represents “a tremendous benefit to Russia and Putin,” allowing Moscow to offload aging summer-grade diesel before winter demand shifts to a different blend.
One analyst’s note to clients went further: “We expect this deal to fail economically… We remain short US assets.”
If the economic case is thin, the political cost is not.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the move “a weak decision of strong partners” and warned that “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”
Rather than absorb the criticism, Trump told reporters that it might be time for Ukraine to find a new president who could strike a deal with Moscow. The remark landed in Kyiv exactly as intended: as pressure, not solidarity.
Behind the scenes, the bargain’s asymmetry was starker still. Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said that during the same call that produced the diesel agreement, Putin ruled out peace talks altogether. Russia, he insisted, would continue fighting until it had achieved “all its objectives.”
Washington surrendered sanctions leverage. Moscow surrendered nothing except diesel it could not use at home anyway.
Nor has the domestic reaction divided neatly along party lines. Critics in both parties have warned that the agreement would “only lead to more slaughter” by subsidising the Kremlin’s war chest while allowing Russia to dispose of surplus fuel.
Two days later, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, urging both sides to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure. Within hours, Russia struck a Ukrainian power plant.
The sequence captured the episode in miniature: a declaration made for effect, followed by a reality that refused to obey it.
This is not Washington’s first retreat from Russian energy sanctions this year. That is the deeper problem.
The administration had already eased restrictions on Russian oil in the spring, when the war with Iran strained global supply. Treasury’s new six-month waiver comes barely three weeks after Trump signed legislation on 18th September designed specifically to tighten sanctions on Russian energy exports.
READ: Putin says US-Iran ceasefire proved ‘too fragile,’ assures Tehran of support
A law intended to constrain Moscow’s revenue now coexists with a waiver that reopens a market for it. The contradiction diminishes the credibility of both.
The sanctions regime assembled after 2022 was never a single wall. Price caps, shipping restrictions, insurance bans, and financial penalties formed a system of interlocking constraints. Each reinforced the others. Each depended on traders, insurers, and allied governments believing that the rules would hold.
The EU and the UK have kept their sanctions on Russian diesel in place, pointedly declining to follow Washington’s lead. An American carve-out now sits awkwardly within an otherwise intact European wall, creating an opening allied governments neither requested nor welcomed.
Every exemption, however “temporary” its label, teaches the market something: the wall has a door, and the right phone call can open it.
Traders price that lesson in. Insurers reassess the risk. Moscow learns which levers move Washington and files the knowledge away for the next shortage, the next election, the next moment of American impatience.
That is the true shortsightedness of the agreement. The diesel relief may be economically small. The precedent is not.
A sanctions regime survives on the expectation that it will not bend under short-term political pressure. Trump’s own Treasury has now demonstrated, twice in a single year, that it will.
The next time Moscow seeks leverage, it will not need to persuade Washington that sanctions relief is deserved. It need only wait for the next price spike that happens to coincide with an American election.
None of this resolves the diesel shortage. Its structural cause—refineries in two war zones operating below capacity—cannot be remedied by a phone call; however, it is “highly successful.”
It can only be papered over. The price will be measured not in barrels, but in the erosion of the one instrument the West built to make the invasion of Ukraine costly.
Three weeks from now, American voters may or may not notice a few cents missing from the price at the pump. Kyiv, and every government that joined the sanctions architecture in good faith, will remember exactly what those few cents cost.
