articles.body:
Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes
US president urges Zelenskyy, Putin to end ‘ridiculous war’ and insists the two nations have agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure.
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war.
Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday.
“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.”
When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.”
The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone.
“All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said.
Kyiv blindsided
Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin.
Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law. Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”.
But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply.
“Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.”
Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign.
“I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.
US midterms
Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised.
“He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said.
The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol.
An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.
Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion.
The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow.
“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

articles.title: Brexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them on | Rafael Behr
articles.body:
Russian territorial aggression against Ukraine didn’t feature much in the Brexit referendum campaign. It made headlines briefly when Boris Johnson blamed Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimea on the European Union.
According to the Vote Leave frontman, Vladimir Putin’s land grab was a consequence of Brussels making foreign policy “on the hoof” and having “pretensions to running a defence policy”.
The logic of that position was that Kyiv had no right to choose its own allies and that European democracies should never have supported Ukrainian aspirations to escape submission to Moscow. It is the appeasement fallacy: if only the west acquiesced to Putin’s conviction that Kyiv is a Russian city and that Ukraine is not a proper country, he would not want to suffocate his neighbour’s independence.
That notion is refuted by all the evidence of campaigns to coerce countries deemed by the Kremlin to be errant possessions since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
When Nigel Farage repeated the EU-provocation theory of the Ukraine war during the 2024 general election campaign, one prominent defender of Ukrainian sovereignty described the Reform UK leader’s assertions as “ahistorical drivel” and “Kremlin propaganda”. That stalwart friend of Kyiv was one Boris Johnson.
There is nothing unusual about Johnson contradicting himself. His talent as a political communicator came from the ability to hold whichever view was expedient to him in the moment and, for the duration of that moment, appear to hold it sincerely. In a more generous reading, he rose to the occasion of Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, understanding events in their proper geopolitical perspective (and with access to classified intelligence reports), which afforded a different reading of Putin’s motives.
In 2016, his focus had been wilfully myopic. The goal of maximising Eurosceptic votes meant reaching for any argument that presented Brussels in a negative light. If that involved narrating the cause of a conflict on the other side of the continent in warped terms that matched the Kremlin story, so be it.
Putin despised the EU for his reasons; the leave campaign despised it for theirs. Johnson was not minded to interrogate whether that alignment of enmities discredited his cause.
This is the context in which Andy Burnham’s recent assertion that Russia meddled in the referendum needs to be understood. The prime minister said it was inconceivable, given all the evidence of Kremlin interference in elections around the world, that the toolkit of subversion would not have been deployed in support of Brexit.
That is not a controversial claim to anyone with a glancing awareness of Russian foreign policy and the means by which it is pursued – the swarms of bot accounts flooding social media with falsehoods; dirty money channelled to extremists; industrial dissemination of conspiracy theories and stoking of intercommunal tensions to undermine social coherence, deplete trust in democracy and make it less functional.
No candidate who was knowingly complicit in that process will admit as much. But even those who were unaware that their cause was boosted by Kremlin troll farms have incentives to deny it. No one wants their heroic victory recast as useful idiocy in service of a hostile power.
Conservatives have called Burnham’s intervention “dangerous and divisive”, which could be interpreted as a denial that interference happened or just as a preference that it not be mentioned to protect delicate pro-Brexit sensibilities.
Farage’s feelings were certainly hurt. He called the prime minister a liar and described the whole thing as a “Russia hoax” – the formula Donald Trump applied to well-substantiated allegations that his 2016 presidential campaign got a helping hand from Moscow. The Reform leader can’t be too surprised by the idea of Kremlin influence in British politics. His party’s former leader in Wales is serving a jail term for taking bribes from Russian spies.
The backlash forced Downing Street to clarify that the prime minister didn’t mean to cast aspersions on the legitimacy of the referendum result. That is the right position when there is no way of knowing what impact, if any, foreign meddling might have had. The views that interference happened and also that the leave campaign would have prevailed anyway are compatible.
Some remainers might seek comfort in the idea that Britain’s democracy was hijacked and diverted through clouds of Russian-induced false consciousness to the wrong destination. The banal truth is that the Eurosceptic side won enough arguments and voters made their choice freely.
Brexiters didn’t need any outside help to turn latent anti-immigration sentiment into active hostility to free movement across European borders.
The Russia dimension is more relevant when it comes to a geopolitical argument that the pro-European side failed to land. In June 2016 it was hard to make the peril of strategic isolation for Britain, self-exiled from the club of European democracies, no longer confident in the transatlantic relationship, seem vivid or imminent.
Trump’s first presidential election was five months away. The full extent of his scorn for the US’s allies and his admiration for authoritarians would not be clear for years. His propensity to behave like a private client of the Putin regime can still shock, even if it no longer surprises, as with the sanctions-busting deal he struck last week to import billions of dollars of Russian diesel.
The hope, entirely vain, is to depress pump prices and assuage voter frustration ahead of midterm elections in November.
On top of the cash infusion for the Kremlin’s war effort, Trump added a bonus of rhetorical venom for Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for regime change in Kyiv. He blames Ukrainian targeting of Russian refining capacity for rising global energy costs because his narcissistic ego resists the truth – that his war in Iran has been a disaster for the US and a boon for its enemies. The fact that Russia is an Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence support to resist US military pressure, is no impediment to Trump’s commercial collaborations with the Kremlin.
The exact character and motive involved in that relationship may never be elucidated. But there is no need to seek out hidden levers of influence that may not even exist when publicly available data paints a full enough picture.
Trump and Putin are two greedy despots who recognise no boundary between national interest and self-enrichment. They see law not as a restraint on government but as an instrument to be wielded by powerful leaders against perceived enemies. Their approach to domestic politics is gangsterish, based on networks of patronage and tribute. Their view of foreign affairs is imperial, based on the belief that strong states have natural title to territory in their immediate vicinity, and that big countries can trade in the fate of smaller ones like casino chips.
It is as obvious to Trump that Moscow has a seigneurial right over Ukraine as it is that he should be allowed to decide who governs Venezuela and who sells its oil.
That ethos leads inevitably to competition for resources where rival spheres of influence meet and, if there is no international framework for resolving that competition, to war. This is the lesson, learned the hard way in the 20th century, that became the foundational idea of the European project – the principle of swapping nationalistic rivalry for mutually beneficial cooperation within a common framework of law. That is why Putin and Trump cannot understand the EU and why they hate it.
And that is why the error of Brexit is more pronounced today than it was when the question was put in a plebiscite, and why Burnham is right to draw attention to the fact that Russia had a preferred side. The prime minister is also right when he says that rejecting the possibility of restoring closer ties with the EU would be “a dereliction of duty”.
Many falsehoods were propagated in the referendum campaign, but none greater than the leavers’ boasts of patriotism, when their agenda was certain to make Britain poorer and weaker. A decade into the error, there is no patriotism in pretending that Brexit has worked or in crying betrayal when anyone suggests a reversal. Isolation from the rest of Europe is the result that Britain’s enemies wanted in 2016. Sticking to that path is the route they would choose for Britain again today if they had a vote.
- Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: Zelensky’s bullying worked on Europe. But Trump has the backbone to turn the screws back
articles.body:
Zelensky thinks he can bully Trump like he does EU leaders
Vladimir Zelensky has a pattern in dealing with Western partners who disappoint him: raise the disagreement in public, question the partner’s judgment and explain why the decision benefits Russia and Vladimir Putin.
Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz heard variations of that argument for years, and now US President Donald Trump is hearing them again. The question is whether Zelensky can keep increasing the political cost of refusing Kiev without increasing the cost to Ukraine.
On October 9, Zelensky described Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel as a “weak decision by strong partners.” The announcement came while Ukrainian officials were discussing an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict with their American counterparts in Miami. Zelensky argued that the arrangement would give Moscow additional resources to continue fighting. His criticism challenged the judgment of the government on which he still depends.
Kiev has an obvious interest in opposing measures that improve Russia’s economic position. But when a partner makes a decision Zelensky doesn’t like, he repeatedly turns a policy disagreement into a public test of that partner’s resolve and overall capabilities as a politician.
German leaders have been the target of this manipulation for years now.
In March 2022, addressing the Bundestag, Zelensky used the country’s own historical memory to indict its policy toward Russia. Invoking Ronald Reagan’s famous appeal in Berlin, he called on Scholz to tear down the new wall he saw dividing Europe – that is, to cut off economic ties with Russia, which had benefitted Germany for decades before.
By June, the demand was more explicit. In an interview with ZDF, Zelensky said Scholz and his government had to decide where they stood. Berlin, he argued, could not balance support for Ukraine against its relationship with Russia. He also criticized Germany’s delay in supplying weapons.
Germany’s government had to consider its own security, resources and voters. Zelensky’s tirades made that look like a choice between the ‘right’ and the ‘wrong’ side.
In November 2024, with Nord Stream already sabotaged and German industry in decline for a second consecutive year, even just talking to Putin earned Scholz another reprimand from Zelensky. The Russian and German leaders held a phone conversation, which Zelensky promptly called a “Pandora’s box,” because apparently it would help Russia escape international ‘isolation.’ That’s despite the fact that Scholz’s message for Putin was a demand for the withdrawal of Russian troops and a reaffirmation of German support for Ukraine. You can denounce Moscow and supply arms to Kiev, but even the most rudimentary attempt at keeping diplomatic channels open is a no-no.
The same approach extended beyond Berlin.
In May 2024, Zelensky warned that Putin would personally applaud Joe Biden’s absence from a planned ‘peace summit’ in Switzerland. Biden’s attendance was framed as a test with an audience in the Kremlin.
Poland received a similar message during a grain dispute in September 2023. Speaking at the UN, Zelensky accused some European partners of performing solidarity in a “political theater” that helped Moscow. He named no country, but Warsaw understood the implication, summoned Ukraine’s ambassador and protested. Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki subsequently told him never to insult Poles again.
With Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, Zelensky made it personal. In January 2025, amid a confrontation over Russian gas transit, he mocked Fico’s reported vacation in Vietnam and accused him of pursuing shadowy arrangements with Moscow.
Zelensky seems to assume that Ukraine’s supposed cause of being a barrier to Putin’s phantom Europe invasion plans gives him the authority to judge how other governments exercise their responsibilities. A leader who refuses Kiev’s nagging demands must then answer accusations of weakness, misplaced priorities or assistance to Russia.
Trump had already encountered this treatment even before returning to office in 2025.
In an interview published in September 2024, Zelensky questioned whether Trump understood how to end the conflict. He also described his running mate JD Vance as too radical and urged him to study the history of the Second World War. These were public judgments about the competence of men who might soon determine American policy.
In February 2025, responding to Trump’s statements about the conflict and his approval rating, Zelensky claimed the American president lived in a space of disinformation. Later that month, the Oval Office meeting turned into an argument in front of the cameras. Zelensky challenged Vance’s understanding of Ukraine and warned that Americans would eventually feel the consequences of the war despite their distance from it. Trump angrily rejected the suggestion that his guest could dictate what Americans would feel.
One would think Zelensky would take the hint: unlike the meek Europeans, the American president has the willpower to resist political blackmail, and is not liable to take personal insults and turn the other cheek. One would also think that with crucial wartime assets like weapon supplies and intelligence sharing in the balance, Zelensky would cool off and rethink his negotiation tactics. One would be wrong.
After Zelensky criticized the diesel arrangement, Trump suggested that Ukraine get a new leader capable of making a deal. That statement is not a formal policy to remove him, but it does raise the question whether Zelensky himself is the obstacle that prevents a settlement.
Zelensky may believe that confrontation will rally European support, improve his own optics at home or force Washington to offer better terms. Public pressure could be a viable last resort for a leader out of option, allowing him to appeal over the heads of foreign governments to their voters, lawmakers and media.
But that approach depends on those governments accepting the terms of the argument. They must feel that refusing Kiev carries a greater political cost than accommodating it. And some leaders, as misguided as that seems, may truly believe that – or may have painted themselves into a corner by submitting to Zelensky’s earlier bullying, sacrificing their own economies and losing their voters’ trust.
Trump is not one of those leaders. Instead of accepting Zelensky’s accusation of weakness, he has accused the Ukrainian leader of obstructing an agreement. It’s unclear if Zelensky understands that the potential consequences of their quarrel are much worse for Ukraine than for the US.
For Trump, lowering American fuel costs and pursuing an agreement with Moscow are stated objectives. Zelensky cannot assume that he can bully those objectives away. What he might achieve instead is an end to crucial lifelines propping up his crumbling military – like intelligence sharing.
Zelensky has repeatedly tried to make Western leaders pay a political price for saying no to Kiev. Except some of those leaders may have the backbone to turn that price right back on him.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 74 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow hits homes, railway infrastructure
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 80 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow hits homes, railway infrastructure
At least 10 people were killed and 80 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continued to target residential buildings in cities including Kyiv, regional authorities said on Oct. 13.
In Kharkiv Oblast over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, killing four people and injuring 36, including four children, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. President Volodymyr Zelensky later raised the number of injured in a missile strike on Kharkiv, meaning that 42 people were injured in the Oblast in total.
All four deaths occurred in residential buildings.
In Kyiv, at least two people were killed and 14 others injured in drone attacks throughout the day, including a strike on a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi District.
Kyiv also came under ballistic missile attack shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, with powerful explosions reported before an air raid alert was issued in the Ukrainian capital. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a warehouse and railway infrastructure had been damaged.
In Vinnytsia Oblast, Russia struck a production complex belonging to Ukrainian confectionery company Roshen, the company said.
"Thanks to the timely activation of the warning system and the prompt evacuation, the lives of employees were saved," Roshen said in a statement.
Overnight on Oct. 13, Russian forces launched five ballistic missiles, 108 Shahed-type attack drones, including 74 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, and nine Banderol missiles, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 88 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at seven locations, the Air Force said.
Air defenses were active in the far-western Lviv Oblast overnight as Russian drones "struck villages and private homes," Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said, though he reported no casualties.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, four people were killed and 11 others were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast, two people were injured in Russian strikes, regional authorities said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks injured six people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, over the past day, Russia carried out 910 attacks against 58 settlements in the region — five people were injured in the attacks, regional authorities said.
Dnipropetrovsk and Chernihiv oblasts also came under Russian attacks, but no injuries were reported.

articles.title: ADF neutralizes 88 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
ADF neutralizes 88 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram.
Beginning at 16:00 on Monday, October 12, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles launched from Russia's Bryansk region, nine Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and 108 attack drones, including Shahed drones (74 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody decoy drones. The attacks came from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The aerial assault was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Tuesday, October 13, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 88 drones.
Impacts were recorded at 17 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at seven locations.
In addition, impacts by loitering munitions were recorded in Kharkiv, although some of the weapons failed to reach their targets.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian forces attacked Kyiv on the evening of October 12, reportedly using six ballistic missiles, according to preliminary information.
In Kharkiv's Kholodnohirskyi district, the bodies of three people were found beneath the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian missile strike.

articles.title: MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
articles.body:
MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
LONDON, Oct 13 - MI5 spy chief Ken McCallum delivered his annual speech on Tuesday outlining his view of the threats to Britain, from hostile states such as Iran and Russia to the development of artificial intelligence.
Here is a summary of the main threats and issues he detailed in his speech and subsequent questions from media:
RUSSIA
McCallum called Russia, which denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain and other Western countries, "aggressor number one". He said it was escalating "hybrid" warfare, staying below the threshold that would trigger a direct NATO response.
He said Russia's capabilities had been reduced by the expulsion of 1,000 officials from embassies since the invasion of Ukraine, which meant it had to rely on native volunteers and criminal proxies.
IRAN
Tehran is also using criminal proxies - to target opponents, Iranian media organisations and Israeli interests in Britain - and has expanded its hybrid campaign in the last year, McCallum said.
He said operations connected to Iran had yielded more than 50 arrests in the UK, and that many had been aimed at Jewish communities.
The other shift had been "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites", he said.
Tehran also rejects accusations of malign activity in Britain.
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
McCallum said AI was "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders", producing tailored propaganda and material for individuals.
MI5 has caught potential attackers using it to try to improve reconnaissance and attack methodologies. AI-enabled drones added a new challenge, he said.
McCallum said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists developing bioweapons or even creating new pathogens.
AI also presented a risk in itself.
"Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are, is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel and deserves the serious attention it is getting."
TERRORISM
Britain in April raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe", meaning an attack within the next six months is highly likely.
McCallum said Al Qaeda and Islamic State continued to inspire plots, and MI5 was still having to respond to attempts to carry out mass-casualty attacks.
He said the most marked trend of the last year had been the increase in cases where extreme anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievances were tipping over into terrorist intent.
An investigation into one 13-year-old who had been radicalised by extreme right-wing ideology had led to an unnamed foreign partner thwarting a lethal attack on its soil, he said.
BREXIT
On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia had interfered in Britain's 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union, something Moscow has denied.
Asked about such interference, McCallum said it was public knowledge that Russian media such as Russia Today "came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum", and there had been a certain amount of activity from trolls and bots.
But he said Russian online trolling had been comparatively unimpressive. REUTERS

articles.title: UK Sanctions Dutch Businessman Allegedly Linked to Russian Arms Firms
articles.body:
Reported by
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Dutch businessman Alexander Tattersall and his Turkish company, Redwing Metal, following a joint investigation by The Kyiv Independent, OCCRP and IrpiMedia that exposed shipments of European industrial equipment to Russian factories supplying missile and fighter jet manufacturers.
Tattersall and Redwing Metal were among 38 individuals, companies and vessels targeted by the British government on October 8 as part of a broader effort to disrupt Russia’s military supply chains, oil revenues and financial networks.
The measures freeze assets under British jurisdiction and prohibit British individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with the designated parties.
The sanctions follow a June investigation by OCCRP, The Kyiv Independent and Italy’s IrpiMedia, which revealed that Redwing Metal had shipped more than $5 million worth of European-made industrial machinery to two Russian metallurgical plants in 2023 and 2024, despite EU export restrictions.
The equipment included computer-controlled lathes, metal heat-treatment furnaces, hydraulic presses and other machinery manufactured in Italy, Germany, Spain and the Czech Republic.
The recipients, Aluminum Metallurg Rus (AMR) and Stupino Metallurgical Company (SMK), produce specialized metal alloys used by Russia’s defense industry.
Financial records examined by journalists showed that the two plants had supplied more than 40 Russian defense manufacturers since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including companies producing cruise missiles, fighter jets, tanks and artillery.
Both plants are controlled by Russian businessman Nikolay Timokhin, the son-in-law of Igor Zavyalov, a senior executive at Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec.
The investigation also found that Redwing Metal had shipped another $1.3 million worth of European-made shipbuilding equipment to a company in Timokhin’s business group. The equipment was intended for two vessels associated with Russian naval programs.
According to corporate records, Tattersall, a Dutch national residing in Switzerland, owns 40 percent of Redwing Metal, which was established in Turkey shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
When contacted before the investigation was published, Tattersall acknowledged his ownership stake but described himself as a part-time consultant with limited knowledge of the company’s operations. He denied knowing of any involvement in schemes to ship sanctioned goods to Russia.
The European Union sanctioned AMR in July, but Tattersall, Redwing Metal and the other Russian companies identified in the investigation remain outside the bloc’s sanctions list.
Roman Steblivskyi, director of policy and advocacy at Ukraine’s Economic Security Council, told The Kyiv Independent that the British designation would likely disrupt Redwing Metal’s supply chain and discourage European banks and companies from doing business with it.
He said the sanctions could also affect the company’s relationships with Turkish partners.

articles.title: Yemen: Taiz faces humanitarian disaster as Houthis tighten siege
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Taiz faces humanitarian disaster as Houthis tighten siege
Yemeni government forces are managing to stall the Houthi offensive on the besieged city of Taiz, analysts told The New Arab, as residents increasingly fear a repeat of previous sieges earlier in the war.
Ameneh Mehvar, Senior Analyst for the Middle East at ACLED, told The New Arab that, despite the recent encirclement by the Houthis and continued gains, "government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, appear to have stalled further significant Houthi advances in recent days."
Fighting around the city's suburbs and hills has continued in recent days, with Houthi attempts to advance along the western and southern approaches, including around al-Misrakh, where government-aligned fighters reportedly fended off a Houthi infiltration attempt, according to Yemeni analyst Muhammad al-Bashar.
However, the Houthis tightened their siege on Monday after closing all four exits from the government-held city, according to military sources cited by AFP.
A Yemeni government field officer said Houthi forces had established fire control over the exits and were shooting at vehicles attempting to pass through them.
The Houthis also attacked government positions defending the city's southern and western approaches, seizing new positions despite Saudi airstrikes.
Government-aligned forces lost 22 fighters in 24 hours of fighting, while the Houthis lost at least 40, according to AFP, citing military sources from both sides.
Mehvar noted, however, that the battle for the city highlights the limits of the government's recent offensive on the coast, which has been offset by the Houthis' stranglehold on Taiz.
"The Houthis do not need to capture Taiz outright to weaken government control, as prolonged isolation could erode the defenders' ability to sustain their positions while further deepening a humanitarian crisis."
The Houthi encirclement of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, was effectively completed after the group took the town of al-Turbah, severing the supply road to Aden, on 4 October.
It is not the first time the Houthis have occupied and encircled the city. The group previously captured Taiz in 2015 and laid siege to it until 2016, when government forces pushed them out, although the Houthis retained positions around the city.
Baraa Shiban, an Associate Fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that the Houthis' strategy in Taiz is informed by their previous attempts to capture the city, with fighting now focused on its surrounding suburbs and hills.
"The Houthis had before tried to take control of the city itself, and then it proved to be very costly," he said, noting that urban fighting eventually forced the group out.
"What they did instead is that they then placed snipers and artillery on the hills overlooking the city, and that was what the situation [was like] when I was there. So, the bombing of the city was constant."
With urban fighting proving costly, Houthi advances have concentrated on the hills and peaks surrounding the city and the wider province, eventually leading to its encirclement.
“There's fighting literally from one hill to the other, from one road to the other,” he said, adding, “the fight is really concentrated on trying to take control of the main road, because if you control the main road, then you effectively are in control of the district."
Humanitarian crisis deepens as Taiz is cut off
The encirclement has triggered a worsening humanitarian crisis, with the Studies and Economic Media Center (SEMC), a Taiz-based civil society group, warning in a recent report that the city is "facing near-total isolation from food, medicine, and energy supplies."
SEMC said petrol stations had run out of fuel, while wheat and flour stocks were sufficient for just 19 days of consumption.
Saeed Saif, the UN Population Fund's (UNFPA) West Coast and Taiz Coordinator, told The New Arab that roads into the city had been completely cut off, with prices for basic commodities doubling and fuel prices tripling.
He warned of critical shortages of medical supplies, with only two of the eight UNFPA-supported health facilities inside the city still operational.
"High transportation costs prevent women, girls, and vulnerable populations, particularly pregnant women from accessing essential services," Saif said.
The deteriorating security situation has forced UNFPA to suspend some of its activities, leaving vulnerable residents with even fewer options for healthcare.
Saif, who returned to his hometown of Taiz in April after 25 years away, was himself forced to flee as fighting intensified.
He left the city on 13 September, travelling at night to al-Turbah along deserted roads and through military checkpoints.
During his six days there, he visited displacement sites just five kilometres from the front lines, where artillery shelling could be clearly heard.
On 18 September, following an emergency relief distribution, security warnings prompted him to evacuate again, this time with his family to Aden.
The journey took more than five hours through difficult terrain amid heavy rain and flash flood warnings, with the sound of bombardment along the way.
Saif said the experience was particularly distressing for his 13-year-old daughter and brought back memories of the family's evacuation from Sanaa during intense airstrikes in 2018.
"There is widespread fear and anxiety," he said, warning that a further wave of displacement could affect up to 100,000 households.
According to the UN's migration office, 57% of the more than 200,000 people displaced by the recent fighting across Yemen have come from Taiz province.
Yemen's Human Rights Ministry also warned on Monday that the tightening siege threatened to disrupt life-saving medical services, including emergency surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal care.
In a statement carried by the official Saba news agency, the ministry held the Houthis responsible for blocking supply routes and called on the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations to intervene urgently to secure access to food, medicine and fuel.
Shiban said conditions in the city were reminiscent of earlier sieges during the war.
"There is a genuine fear, and that reflects itself on the prices of goods, food, and other main materials."
Can government forces break the siege?
Although Houthi advances have slowed, government forces lack the firepower needed to reverse the group's gains around Taiz.
Government troops and newly formed local resistance forces are largely equipped with unarmoured pick-up trucks and Kalashnikov rifles, while the Houthis possess drones, artillery and tanks.
Shiban said "the situation doesn't play in their favour."
He argued that the government's best chance of breaking the siege could depend on the success of its parallel offensive along Yemen's western coast.
"If their [government] operation on the West Coast succeeds, pushing from the Bab al-Mandab up and then to the Mokha port, then they can enter [the city] using the same road that the Houthis entered into Taiz districts," Shiban said.
Such an advance could allow government forces to bring heavier weaponry into the city and challenge the Houthi encirclement.
"Other than that, it's going to be difficult because now the city is encircled."

articles.title: The unthinkable becomes thinkable: Ukraine’s politicians begin discussing compromise
articles.body:
The unthinkable becomes thinkable: Ukraine’s politicians begin discussing compromise
Russia’s campaign of large-scale strikes against Ukraine’s economic infrastructure, underway since August, appears to be producing political consequences as, in Kiev, the possibility of peace is once again being discussed, and not simply in terms of negotiations from a position of strength.
For perhaps the first time since the conflict began in 2022, some Ukrainian politicians are openly considering serious compromises with Moscow, including concessions previously regarded as politically unthinkable.
Remarkably, one of the most prominent voices in this emerging debate belongs to Alexei Goncharenko, a Ukrainian MP long associated with the most uncompromising wing of the country’s political establishment.
Until recently, Goncharenko treated virtually any compromise with Moscow as treason and his position was effectively that Ukraine should continue fighting regardless of the human cost.
On October 2, however, he published what amounted to a political manifesto acknowledging that Ukraine was losing and insisting that negotiations with Russia should begin wherever possible.
Nothing, he suggested, should be excluded from discussion, including neutrality, the removal of sanctions against Russia, the status of the Russian language, and other contentious issues because sacrificing an entire nation for the increasingly remote prospect of NATO membership was, in his view, unacceptable.
The reaction was immediate. Goncharenko was branded a Kremlin sympathizer, expelled from Petro Poroshenko’s European Solidarity party and added to the ‘kill list’ database maintained by the controversial Ukrainian website Myrotvorets.
Yet he wasn’t entirely isolated because other political figures, including parliamentary committee chairman Daniil Getmantsev and Kharkov Mayor Igor Terekhov, have expressed positions suggesting a growing willingness to reconsider Ukraine’s approach and MP Anna Skorokhod also introduced legislation proposing neutrality.
For now, these politicians represent only a small minority of the Ukrainian establishment, therefore they possess neither the influence nor the institutional resources necessary to alter government policy.
Nevertheless, their emergence is significant as for the first time in years, an identifiable group within Ukrainian politics is openly challenging the prevailing assumption that the conflict must continue until Kiev achieves its stated objectives.
Previously, there was little meaningful political alternative, given how Zelensky’s principal rivals, including Poroshenko and former military commander Valery Zaluzhny, have offered different personalities and political styles, but little fundamental disagreement over the conflict itself.
The notable exception was Alexey Arestovich, the former presidential adviser who resigned in early 2023 and subsequently left Ukraine after he became an outspoken critic of Zelensky and advocated a different future for Ukraine, including some form of peaceful coexistence with Russia.
His proposals initially attracted limited support, while speculation about his presidential ambitions gradually faded.
Three years later, however, the political environment has changed considerably as successive Ukrainian counteroffensives, peace initiatives, and victory plans have failed to produce the results promised by Kiev. Meanwhile, forced mobilization, corruption scandals, and declining foreign military assistance have increased public frustration.
Dissatisfaction was accumulating, but largely remained private because for many Ukrainians living far from the eastern front, the war’s consequences, although serious, were still less immediate than those experienced in frontline regions.
Russia’s intensified air campaign against Ukraine’s energy and economic infrastructure since August has changed that calculation as disruptions to electricity, transport, and economic activity have brought the consequences of the conflict more directly into everyday life. It would be surprising if this had no effect on public attitudes.
In this respect, Goncharenko may simply have articulated concerns that were already becoming more widespread and the nervous reaction of Ukraine’s political hawks is particularly revealing. Rather than acknowledge that their own policies may have contributed to growing dissatisfaction, they have sought explanations involving Russian influence and political betrayal.
The fact that Goncharenko himself was previously among the most uncompromising supporters of the war makes his change of position especially uncomfortable for them and this presents a potential danger for Zelensky.
His continued hold on power rests partly on the argument that political leadership shouldn’t change during wartime, even as the prolonged suspension of normal electoral politics raises increasingly difficult constitutional questions.
But if discussion of peace becomes more widespread, it may eventually lead Ukrainians to question whether the present leadership is capable of delivering it.
The familiar argument against changing horses in midstream loses some of its force when people begin to suspect that the horse can’t reach the opposite bank, but for the moment, however, any suggestion of an imminent political transformation would be premature.
Ukraine’s emerging peace camp remains politically weak and far from achieving the influence necessary to challenge the government, also is there no guarantee that public frustration will translate into an organized political movement.
As long as the existing leadership retains control of the principal state institutions, the security apparatus, and much of the political agenda, fundamental changes in Kiev’s approach remain unlikely.
Nevertheless, something important has happened because arguments that were once confined largely to private conversations are beginning to appear in public political debate.
Whether this develops into a genuine challenge to Zelensky remains uncertain, but the political monopoly enjoyed by advocates of continuing the conflict is, at least, beginning to face open dissent.
This article was first published by the online newspaper Gazeta.ru and was translated and edited by the RT team

articles.title: ‘You’re Not Winning This Fight’: Kellogg Says Putin Shows Weakness as War Drags On
articles.body:
Keith Kellogg, former US envoy and general, said Ukraine should determine how it fights Russia, including whether to strike Russian refineries, while dismissing public tensions between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as rhetoric that should not be overinterpreted.
Speaking to Bloomberg Television on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum, Kellogg argued that Ukraine’s military decisions should be left to Kyiv and that Russia should not be allowed to treat its fuel infrastructure as a sanctuary from attack.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We should all need to step back and let Ukraine make determinations of what it’s going to do, how it’s going to attack,” Kellogg said.
He also pushed back against concerns that recent exchanges between Trump and Zelensky could signal a return to the tensions that culminated in their contentious Oval Office meeting in early 2025.
Kellogg described the two presidents as stubborn leaders who speak their minds, adding that differences in language and the nuances of translation could contribute to misunderstandings.
“I think people ought to take a step back and just assume it’s noise level, even from the President of the United States,” he said.
Kellogg says Ukrainians should be the ones who decide on elections
Kellogg said decisions about holding elections in Ukraine should rest with Ukrainians, not Washington or other foreign governments.
He acknowledged that democratic legitimacy was an important concern, noting that Ukraine’s presidential term is five years and that Zelensky has remained in office beyond that period. However, he also pointed out that Ukraine is under martial law, during which national elections are not held.
Russian Missile Strike Destroys Kharkiv Apartment Entrance, Killing 3 and Injuring 15
“It’s up to the Ukrainian people, not the United States, nor is it for anybody else,” Kellogg said.
Putin has failed to achieve strategic goals
Kellogg argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin is trying to outlast Ukraine and its international supporters, betting that public fatigue after years of war will eventually weaken their resolve.
He said continued pressure on Moscow was necessary because Russia had not achieved its strategic objectives despite the territory it had seized.
Kellogg also cited estimates of between 1.2 million and 1.5 million Russian military casualties and said Russia was losing around 30,000 troops a month.
To illustrate the scale of Russia’s losses, he compared them with the Soviet Union’s experience in Afghanistan, saying the Soviet military lost around 18,000 people during that war before withdrawing.
Kellogg described Putin’s current approach as a sign of weakness rather than strength and said Western countries should continue supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary.
“We just need to keep pressure on him [Putin] and the constancy of saying, ‘You’re not winning this fight.’ We’re going to be here as long as it takes to do so and keep putting the pressure on him. I think his response right now is a response of weakness, not of strength.”
Kellogg also criticized Putin’s approach to a diesel deal with the US.
“And what he’s trying to say with the diesel deal with the United States – that’s not really a good deal. It’s not really all-encompassing out there, and it shows me his weakness, not his strength,” Kellogg said.
He added that Putin was trying to capitalize on the upcoming US elections and Trump’s presidency:
“He’s trying to capitalize on elections coming up in the United States. He’s trying to capitalize on President Trump right now, and most people see through it.”
Kellogg defends strikes on Russian refineries
Kellogg once again defended Ukraine’s attacks on Russian military targets and fuel infrastructure, rejecting the idea that such facilities should be off-limits.
He argued that allowing an adversary to maintain sanctuaries during a war could be a strategic mistake, pointing to fuel production and refineries as examples.
Kellogg said the impact on the global diesel market had been limited, adding that Ukraine had demonstrated an ability to strike targets inside Russia while Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian cities and civilian areas.

articles.title: Americans urged to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia over Iranian, Houthi attack threats
articles.body:
The US Mission in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday urged Americans to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing risks from Iranian and Houthi missile and drone attacks, armed conflict and terrorism, Anadolu reports.
In a post on US social media company X, the mission shared a travel advisory maintaining Saudi Arabia at Level 3, or reconsider travel, while designating the area along the Yemen border Level 4, or do not travel.
The US travel advisory system has two lower levels: Level 1, which calls for normal precautions and Level 2 for increased caution.
Under the advisory, US government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use any airport in the country and are prohibited from traveling within 20 miles (32 kilometers) of the Yemeni border. They also require special authorization to travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Taif and Yanbu.
The mission advised Americans in Saudi Arabia to take similar precautions.
The advisory said that since the outbreak of hostilities between the US and Iran on Feb. 28, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. It said commercial flights remain operational from Saudi Arabia but have at times faced significant disruptions.
It said Iran and the Iran-backed Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks into Saudi Arabia, targeting cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic sites and energy facilities.
The advisory said falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk and warned US citizens against photographing, filming or sharing information about interceptions or affected sites.
READ: Saudi-led coalition launches airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s Sanaa
It cited terrorism, exit bans and the enforcement of Saudi laws governing social media activity among the risks facing travelers.
The advisory follows security alerts issued by the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia in recent days amid attacks and threats targeting the kingdom.
The embassy renewed its security alert on Monday for a third consecutive day following attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The embassy warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions and urged US citizens to exercise caution at major airports.
Saudi authorities have reported missile and drone attacks targeting airports and other sites in the kingdom in recent days, while the Houthis have threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.
A Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has intensified military operations against Houthi positions in Yemen, including airstrikes in the capital, Sanaa.

articles.title: Two ships struck by drones in Black Sea off Bulgaria
articles.body:
Eleven sailors are missing after drone strikes hit two cargo ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on Tuesday, 13 October, sinking one vessel and damaging another. Bulgaria has summoned Russia's ambassador and requested assistance from NATO and the European Union.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev condemned the attacks, which occurred near the country's territorial waters, and convened an emergency meeting with security officials.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The vessel that sank was identified by Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity. It went down approximately 31 kilometres east of the coastal village of Krapets.
Reuters reported that five crew members had been rescued, while 11 remained missing. Other initial reports gave a lower number of survivors. Search and rescue operations continued on Tuesday.
The second vessel, the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, was struck by three drones approximately 33 kilometres off the coastal town of Byala at around 1.30am local time.
The Maltese-flagged cargo ship, registered in Ukraine's Odesa, was travelling from Turkey to Moldova when the attack occurred.
All 15 crew members, comprising seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, were rescued by Bulgarian border authorities and transported to Varna. Five received treatment for minor injuries.
"This is absolutely unacceptable — another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.
Bulgarian authorities have not established who launched the drones. Radev said there was no conclusive evidence identifying those responsible, although he suggested that the attacks benefited Russia.
Following the incident, Bulgaria summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova for discussions in Sofia.
According to Reuters, Mitrofanova said she had received no information from Russia's Defence Ministry concerning attacks on commercial vessels. She also raised the possibility that a third party had staged the incidents as a provocation.
The attacks prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from NATO and the EU to strengthen maritime monitoring, airspace surveillance and investigations into the strikes.
Radev discussed the situation with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Rutte said NATO would continue monitoring security developments in the Black Sea and adjust its military presence along the alliance's eastern flank when necessary.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," von der Leyen wrote on X, condemning the attacks and calling for those responsible to face accountability.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha directly accused Moscow of targeting civilian shipping and threatening international food supplies.
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security," Sybiha wrote on X, accusing Russia of using attacks on commercial shipping to disrupt food transportation.
The incidents follow drone attacks against commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone on 6 October.
One of those ships, the Alfa Watan, sank, leaving 10 sailors, including nine Syrians and one Egyptian, missing and presumed dead. Another vessel sustained damage, but its crew survived.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted maritime infrastructure and vessels during the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Russian forces have struck Ukrainian ports and shipping facilities, while Ukraine has attacked Russian vessels and maritime infrastructure in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
The attacks have affected commercial routes used to transport grain and other goods, including shipping corridors near Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members.

The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries.
Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries.
Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.
“The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.”
The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”.
Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors.
Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe.
“Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukrainian scouts used a captured Russian soldier’s radio to gather intelligence for four days
articles.body:
Ukrainian reconnaissance troops used a captured Russian soldier’s radio for four days to listen to Russian military communications and relay important intelligence to their command, according to a report by ArmyInform, which covered the episode. The soldiers serve in the 23rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, which operates in the Oleksandrivka sector, the report noted.
Russia uses infiltration tactics involving small groups to slip through Ukrainian positions undetected, establish themselves into the rear of Ukrainian positionse, and create conditions for the further advance of its main forces. They are countered not only by reconnaissance drones but also by specialized reconnaissance teams, which sometimes cover several dozen kilometers on foot to reach their designated targets.
Ukrainian scouts capture Russian soldier in the grey zone
Ukrainian reconnaissance troops captured a Russian soldier in the grey zone as he was trying to enter a neighboring house, the report said.
“He took off his body armour and set his rifle aside. He felt right at home. Our commander went over and offered him a chance to surrender, and he agreed. He then stayed with us for four days. He told us everything he knew,” a soldier with the call sign Kubik said in the report.
The soldiers’ hideout was later discovered. Fleeing a Ukrainian drone, a Russian infantryman ran into the building where the reconnaissance troops were staying. The position was subsequently attacked by FPV drones, followed by an artillery barrage.
One Ukrainian soldier sustained a minor injury, but the group managed to withdraw without suffering serious losses.
Reconnaissance soldier Kubik spent 23 days on a combat mission
For reconnaissance troops, the journey to their positions and the return trip remain perhaps the most dangerous parts of a mission. During his year of service, Kubik has completed five combat missions, one of which lasted 23 days, according to the report.
During their most recent mission, the soldiers covered 20 kilometers on foot in one direction, moving mostly through tree lines, Kubik said. He added that they had to run across open areas and destroy enemy drones lying in wait before quickly retreating to cover.
Because of the constant threat from the air, the length of time reconnaissance troops can remain at their positions depends on the weather and the situation, the report noted. Sometimes, staying in place longer is safer than risking exposure while a team is being replaced.
Dzhus’s first mission: 20-year-old reconnaissance soldier chooses infantry
Twenty-year-old Mykyta, whose call sign is Dzhus, is preparing for his first combat mission as part of the 23rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the report said. He joined the military under the “18–24 Contract” program after leaving the police force.
“Many people who join under the ‘18–24’ contract go into UAV operations, but I’m more interested in infantry work. We have many experienced reconnaissance soldiers, and the guys are constantly giving advice and sharing their experience,” Dzhus said.
He is heading out on the mission under the guidance of an experienced commander, he said. The soldiers prepare thoroughly for every mission, practicing at the training ground and rehearsing procedures tailored to the specific task, the media outlet noted.
Russian troops seek new hiding places for infiltration along the front
Russian forces continue to use small-group infiltration tactics. For example, the Russian army is likely increasing its infiltration efforts in Kharkiv Oblast, taking advantage of the remaining summer foliage for concealment, the Institute for the Study of War reported on 9 October. In particular, Russian forces are seeking to infiltrate the city of Kupiansk in small groups, according to an RBC-Ukraine report published on 7 October.
Similar incidents have also been reported in Donetsk Oblast. Russian troops are attempting to infiltrate the gaps between Ukrainian observation posts in small groups and establish positions there, Artem Prybilnov, spokesperson for the 155th Separate Mechanized Brigade, said during a broadcast on Suspilne.Studio on 7 October, NV reported. Their aim is to build up forces for a further advance toward Dobropillia. Ukrainian infantry, working alongside drone operators, is repelling the ongoing Russian attacks and preventing them from achieving this goal, Prybilnov added.
As autumn sets in and vegetation becomes thinner, Russian troops find it increasingly difficult to conceal themselves in tree lines, Prybilnov noted. During the summer, they used these areas for cover and to accumulate personnel, ammunition, and equipment, the spokesperson said. Russian forces are now attempting to infiltrate villages, where they can hide in buildings and basements and establish positions, he added.

articles.title: US envoys say "diesel deal" is attempt to coax Russia into negotiations – Reuters
articles.body:
US envoys say "diesel deal" is attempt to coax Russia into negotiations – Reuters
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, envoys of the US president, have informed the Ukrainian delegation at negotiations in Miami on 9 October that the agreement permitting the export of Russian diesel fuel is part of an effort to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.
Source: Reuters, quoting its sources, as reported by European Pravda
Quote from a source: "The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say 'See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you this deal. Now it's your turn to do something.'"
Details: Reuters' sources said that Witkoff and Kushner informed the Ukrainians during the Miami meeting that Russian leader Vladimir Putin is not currently prepared to negotiate on ending the war.
Therefore, according to the special envoys, the diesel deal announced last week could help restart trilateral talks.
Another source said that the US assured the Ukrainian side that the diesel fuel agreement might help "soften" Moscow's stance, in part because it "sends a signal" regarding US President Donald Trump's willingness to cooperate with Russia.
During the Miami meeting, Kushner reportedly brought up Trump's request for Ukraine to cease strikes against Russian oil refineries once again.
One source familiar with the course of the meeting noted that the diesel fuel deal is merely one component of a broader discussion on how to bring Ukraine and Russia back to the table and bring an end to the war.
According to this Reuters source, security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed during the meeting, though no further details were provided.
However, Ukrainian officials who participated in the Miami talks remained sceptical of this American approach.
Meanwhile, Kushner and Witkoff emphasised "all that the US has done for Ukraine", including military and intelligence support provided to the Ukrainian armed forces.
Nevertheless, the Americans did not threaten to cut off support if the Ukrainians refused to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, according to three sources, one of whom was present at the meeting.
Background:
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement with him on supplying Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: FSB foils drone attack on military airfield in Voronezh Region
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) detained a Russian woman suspected of preparing a drone attack on a military airfield on orders from the Security Service of Ukraine, the FSB said in a statement.
TASS has compiled the key details available so far.
Foiled attack
- The Federal Security Service in the Voronezh Region foiled a large-scale act of sabotage and terrorism orchestrated by the Security Service of Ukraine, which planned to attack the Russian Defense Ministry’s Baltimor military airfield with short-range drones, the agency said.
- Law enforcement operations made it possible to expose and disrupt the illegal activities of a Russian woman who had been recruited by a Ukrainian intelligence officer during a trip to Ukraine in 2022.
- Acting on instructions from her handler, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage, where she planned to assemble and launch drones meant to be used to destroy infrastructure and aircraft, as well as kill military airfield staff," the FSB said.
- The drones were supposed to be operated remotely by personnel based in Ukraine.
- According to the FSB, the woman retrieved nine drones equipped with explosive devices, along with drone control equipment, from previously established caches and took them to the garage. Each drone carried 500 grams of foreign-made explosives.
- FSB officers responded immediately after receiving intel, promptly detaining the accomplice of Ukrainian intelligence agencies and preventing the act of sabotage before it was carried out, thus containing the potential consequences of the Kiev regime’s actions against the military facility, the FSB said.
Confessions
- The woman confessed to cooperating with the Ukrainian intelligence service, according to a video released by the FSB.
- She said she had been living in Ukraine when Russia launched its special military operation.
- According to the suspect, a Ukrainian intelligence officer recruited her and suggested that she travel to Russia to carry out his orders in exchange for a cash reward.
- On his instructions, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage near the military airfield, the woman said.
- She added that she had retrieved drones and explosives from caches, brought them to the garage and assembled them as instructed by her handler.
- The woman also said that she had planned to return to Ukraine after completing her mission.
Investigation
- The suspect has been taken into custody.
- Efforts are ongoing to establish all circumstances of the crime and identify all those involved," the FSB said.

He now faces murder and extortion charges in a military court in temporarily occupied Donetsk.
The shooting reportedly occurred on October 25, 2025, near Lyman Pershyi, during Russia’s offensive operations around Kupiansk.
According to Ukraine’s I Want to Live project, the confrontation began after a Russian FPV drone mistakenly struck an all-terrain vehicle belonging to another Russian unit.
Several soldiers assaulted reconnaissance personnel and seized their drone-control equipment. When the reconnaissance unit attempted to recover it the following morning, another confrontation erupted.
Korolev opened fire after a fellow serviceman referred to his criminal past and threatened him with sexual violence. Six Russian soldiers were killed and two others wounded.
Among the dead was 22-year-old Rodion Kravets, whose banking records identified him as a specialist at military unit 71330, which corresponds to the FSB’s highly classified 16th Center.
According to The Insider, the unit specializes in signals intelligence, including intercepting and decrypting electronic communications, penetrating foreign computer networks, and conducting cyber espionage operations.
The UK government has linked the 16th Center to Russian intelligence cyber activities, while the European Union has also attributed cyberattacks to the unit.
Kravets reportedly began working there in June 2023 before later appearing in military records as a soldier of Russia’s 27th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade. It remains unclear whether he had permanently left the FSB or was temporarily assigned to combat operations in Ukraine.
Another victim, 28-year-old Vadim Petukhov, was reportedly associated with Russia’s elite Rubikon drone warfare center, although investigators could not independently verify the connection.
Court records reviewed by The Insider show that Korolev had previously been convicted of robbery, theft, fraud, hooliganism, and drug-related crimes.
His case reached the Southern District Military Court in March 2026. His lawyer confirmed that the proceedings are being held behind closed doors but declined to provide further details.
Earlier, in February 2026, a Russian soldier who had twice been released from prison to fight in Ukraine was arrested on suspicion of another murder. The suspect, Viktor Savvinov, had previously been convicted of three killings but was repeatedly allowed to join the Russian military despite his criminal record.

articles.title: Zelensky prolonging fighting to avoid answering for corruption – Polish MEP
articles.body:
Zelensky prolonging fighting to avoid answering for corruption – Polish MEP
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky is deliberately prolonging the conflict with Russia to avoid being held accountable for his policies and rampant corruption within his inner circle, Polish MEP Ewa Zajaczkowska-Hernik has said.
Zajaczkowska-Hernik’s remarks came after Zelensky demanded a 60-day “total truce” to prepare for a presidential election, which he has repeatedly postponed since his term expired in spring 2024, citing martial law. Moscow dismissed the request as a pretext to buy time to rearm Ukrainian forces and prolong the conflict.
“Vladimir Zelensky’s term in office expired long ago, yet by dragging out the war, he manages to evade accountability, specifically for corruption,” Zajaczkowska-Hernik told Poland’s Zet Radio on Monday.
According to Zajaczkowska-Hernik, the Ukrainian leader had many opportunities to make peace but “rejected [them] every time precisely to avoid facing the consequences, since he knew that [peace] would necessitate holding elections, which Vladimir Zelensky might lose.”
Zelensky’s popularity at home is “not so great,” the MEP argued, attributing it not only to the prolonged fighting but also to “massive corruption” within his inner circle. “The Ukrainians see it,” Zajaczkowska-Hernik said.
Ukraine has been rocked by a series of high-profile corruption scandals since last year, with the largest centering on a $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Zelensky. Other recent graft probes have targeted former Ukrainian ministers, prosecutors, diplomats, and senior officials.
Zajaczkowska-Hernik has been a vocal critic of the Ukrainian government, particularly Kiev’s glorification of Nazi collaborators. In July, she tore up a flag of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) during a debate on Kiev’s bid to join the EU. UPA fighters massacred up to 100,000 ethnic Poles in one of World War II’s worst atrocities. The move landed the MEP on Ukraine’s notorious Mirotvorets ‘kill list’.
Zajaczkowska-Hernik’s remarks on Monday came just days after US President Donald Trump called for Zelensky to be replaced, accusing him of creating “problems for the world” by continuing to target Russian oil refineries and ignoring Washington’s objections. Trump blamed the strikes for contributing to rising global fuel prices and declared that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Zelensky hit back by telling ABC that, if Trump “really wants some changes,” he should “tell [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, give us two months, 60 days off.”
Moscow, however, said it was ready to suspend strikes on Ukraine only on the election day itself, despite Kiev having launched an “unprecedented” drone attack on Moscow during Russia’s parliamentary elections last month. Russian officials also said Ukrainian strikes had damaged or destroyed 74 buildings housing election commissions.
Zelensky’s goal is “very simple: to bargain for time in order to secure a respite,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Monday. During that period, Europe would be able to supply him “with new weapons to continue the terrorist war against the Russian people.”

articles.title: US and Europe prepare peace plan to improve post-war state of Ukraine and Russia – The Washington Post
articles.body:
US and Europe preparing peace plan to improve post-war state of Ukraine and Russia – Washington Post
The United States and Europe are discussing a joint four-point peace plan that envisages both territorial concessions from Ukraine and Russia, as well as security guarantees and agreements aimed at improving the post-war situation of both countries.
Source: The Washington Post, citing comments from a US official familiar with the negotiations
Quote from The Washington Post: "The package would have four basic components, according to the US official. The message to Putin would be: Don't just end the war with Ukraine. Make an economic and security deal with Europe that would restore stability to the region after an upward spiral of escalation."
Details: The Washington Post explains that the peace plan currently being developed by the US and European nations relies on the principle of "whenever you run into a problem you can't solve, make it bigger".
As part of their diplomatic efforts, US Presidential Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner organised a meeting in Miami on 9 October between representatives from Ukraine, the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany. During the session, they asked the Ukrainians to cease strikes against Russian oil refineries and briefed them on Trump's deal with Russia regarding diesel fuel.
Quote from the official: "We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the post-war situation would be – and then make concessions."
Details: As part of the US-European peace settlement, the US is seeking to put together a package of measures that takes account of the post-war needs of both Ukraine and Russia in such a way as to improve their situation following a territorial compromise that will be unpalatable to both sides.
According to the official, the package will consist of four core components. First will be the reconstruction of Ukraine. The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock are seeking to establish a financial mechanism to rebuild the country's devastated regions, provide assistance to families of fallen and wounded soldiers and restore the shattered economy. Negotiators have already requested detailed cost estimates from Kyiv, along with guarantees that these funds will not be embezzled post-war. The Ukrainian side has not yet provided exact figures but is expected to do so in the coming days.
The second component of the peace settlement will be security guarantees. Ukraine would receive commitments from the US and European nations regarding military intervention in the event of a new Russian attack – which the US official stated is equivalent to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty. They noted that Russia would also enter into agreements with Europe addressing Moscow's security concerns, though the specific terms of this remain unclear.
The third strand will be the economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy agreement. One proposed aspect could be a pipeline transporting Russian oil and gas to Europe, with revenues split between Russia and Ukraine. Such a pipeline could drastically reduce European energy costs, as the official noted.
Aside from granting Russia long-term access to the European energy market, the peace agreement would also define how and when current economic sanctions against Russia will be lifted.
The fourth point of the plan will prove the most unacceptable to both sides, the official claims. It envisages that Russia, which launched the war in the hope of conquering the whole of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the current front line. For Ukraine, this would mean allowing Russia to control occupied territory.
However, a major hurdle for such an agreement is that the "line of control", as negotiators call it, remains fluid due to small daily shifts along the front line.
Background: According to media reports, Witkoff and Kushner informed the Ukrainian delegation at negotiations in Miami that the agreement permitting the export of Russian diesel fuel is part of an effort to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.
