articles.title: Ukraine's Air Force comments on delay of air-raid warning in Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukraine's Air Force comments on delay of air-raid warning in Kyiv
Ukraine's Air Force has expressed hope that Ukraine and its international partners will establish why information regarding Russia's launch of ballistic missiles towards Kyiv on 12 October was not received in time, noting that such incidents have occurred before.
Source: Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the national joint 24/7 newscast
Details: Amid foreign media reports referencing sources that the US might halt intelligence sharing, the presenter asked: "Can you confirm the delay in notification and what specifically caused it?"
Ihnat confirmed that this time the air-raid warning indeed was issued only whilst the Russian ballistic attack was already underway but noted that this was not the first such instance. This has happened not only in Kyiv Oblast but also in frontline cities. In this case, the Air Force spokesperson expressed hope that Ukrainian intelligence together with foreign partners will determine the cause of the delay.
Quote: "The intelligence data that everyone is talking about now varies. There is intelligence utilising satellite communications that not only the US but also other NATO countries share with Ukraine. This covers the activity of enemy strategic aviation at their home airfields, ship movements in the Black or Caspian Seas and ballistic missile launches.
There are moments when this information fails to arrive. This is not the first case... If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the experts can sort it out. And we will resolve this problem together with our partners."
Background:
- At 22:10 on 12 October, Russia struck the capital of Ukraine with five ballistic missiles. Radar systems detected the incoming missiles only once the attack on Kyiv was underway.
- Ukraine's Air Force reported that no information regarding launches from Russian territory had been received.

Russia Moves to Arm Mi-8 Helicopters With Cruise Missiles and Jet-Powered Drones
Russia is testing redesigned weapon mounting systems on its Mi-8AMTSh-VN military helicopters, potentially expanding their ability to carry small cruise missiles and jet-powered drones. The modifications have been spotted on aircraft used by Russian special operations forces.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the aviation-focused Telegram channel Vertical Team, the new mounting structures replace the Soviet-era BD3-57KrV weapon racks and feature a more aerodynamic design.
The modified helicopters are reportedly undergoing testing with new external weapon mounts that could support additional types of air-launched munitions, including compact cruise missiles and Dan-M jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles. However, their intended use has not been officially confirmed.
One of the main changes involves reducing the number of external weapon attachment points from six to four. Despite this reduction, each mounting point retains a maximum payload capacity of 500 kilograms, comparable to the previous system.
The older BD3-57KrV racks had remained in service for decades despite operational limitations. Their design made it difficult to fully equip B8V20 unguided rocket pods mounted closest to the helicopter’s fuselage.
The redesigned structures appear intended to address these limitations while improving aerodynamic performance and potentially accommodating different weapon configurations.
The Mi-8AMTSh-VN, also known as the Sapsan, is a specialized version of Russia’s Mi-8 transport helicopter developed to support special operations missions, including troop deployments in difficult environments.
First unveiled at Russia’s Army military exhibition in 2017, the helicopter completed development between 2019 and 2020, incorporating operational lessons from Russia’s military campaign in Syria.
Earlier, Russia was reported to be equipping its Mi-28N attack helicopters with Strelets launch systems designed to fire Igla surface-to-air missiles. The modification was believed to be aimed at countering Ukrainian long-range drones, although its effectiveness against small aerial targets remained uncertain.

articles.title: Houthis warn of fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia after Sanaa strike
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis warn of fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia after Sanaa strike
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi Arabia struck an oil facility in Sanaa on Tuesday, after the Riyadh-led coalition told civilians to leave the surrounding area in its first evacuation order for the Yemeni capital since the war flared up again.
After a series of strikes on the kingdom's airports and energy sites, the coalition's spokesman said people should leave an oil facility belonging to the Yemen Petroleum Company on the western outskirts of Sanaa before it was attacked.
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported hearing an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression targets the oil company in Al-Sabaha, west of Sanaa".
The Saudi-led coalition is yet to confirm the reported strike.
Swiftly responding to the earlier coalition warning, the Houthis had issued a threat to target Riyadh's international airport, a refinery, and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces urge all citizens to immediately evacuate and move away from targets that our forces will strike should the Saudi enemy target," military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X, identifying the three targets.
An attack at Riyadh's airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended, rocking the world's top crude oil exporter and deepening the war in Yemen, where the kingdom backs the internationally recognised government.
An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa fearing shortages rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.
The Yemen Petroleum Company sought to reassure the public, saying it had taken all necessary precautions in the event of an emergency to "meet people's needs".
Petroleum stocks were "available in safe facilities and locations, and in sufficient quantities" to meet demand for long periods, it said.
Saudi Arabia was still weathering fresh attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of the kingdom's capital Riyadh.
Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday.
The Saudi coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a humanitarian crisis.
Economic woes
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.
Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on the Hormuz strait, vital for oil and gas trade, since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the restart in July of Yemen's frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea - Saudi Arabia's alternative export route.
In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.
Houthi warning
Blasts were heard over the Saudi capital again late Monday, with the Saudi coalition saying it intercepted a Houthi missile and the group announcing it had again targeted the airport.
On Monday evening, Human Resources Minister Ahmad bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi remained defiant.
"We're not going out," he told the crowd at the Riyadh Economic Forum. "We are safe. With God's will. May God turn their plots back against them."
The Riyadh airport attack prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, after having reportedly rebuffed previous Saudi requests.
The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

articles.title: US insists "no change" to arms supplies to Ukraine via PURL
articles.body:
US insists "no change" to arms supplies to Ukraine via PURL
The US says it is continuing to supply weapons to Ukraine through the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL).
Source: US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker in comments to AFP, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Whitaker said he did not want to comment directly on "unconfirmed reports" that the Trump administration has threatened to halt arms supplies if Kyiv continues its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Quote: "I don't think that's consistent with what I know today, which is that the United States continues to sell our equipment and munitions to our European and Canadian allies that then provide it to Ukraine. I know of no change to that programme."
Details: Whitaker acknowledged, however, that equipment deliveries under the PURL programme are currently being delayed, particularly when it comes to air defence systems.
"Air defence largely is in high demand, and the availability is probably not as good as we would like," he explained.
He noted that companies are developing new approaches to intercepting incoming projectiles and expressed confidence that the problem can be resolved.
"I think it's a short-term challenge," the ambassador added.
He also warned that timing is critical as Ukraine approaches winter.
"Ukraine is facing a winter where, if there is not an energy ceasefire ... their electricity and heating infrastructure could be under a lot of pressure," he said.
Whitaker reported that Washington is working with allies that possess air defence systems to get them to Ukraine as quickly as possible.
"We'll continue to every day work on it, try to find available inventory, and then increase production on both sides of the Atlantic," he added.
Background:
- The Financial Times previously reported that the Trump administration is threatening to halt arms supplies through the PURL mechanism if Ukraine does not stop striking Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL programme, Ukraine receives US-made equipment purchased by NATO allies.
- NATO subsequently stated that deliveries of US weapons to Ukraine are continuing.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Iskander-M Repair Base, Threatening Its Ballistic Missile Operations
Ukrainian forces struck a repair base for Iskander-M missile systems, a radar station, logistics sites, and Russian troop concentrations on October 12 and overnight into October 13.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the strikes on October 13, noting that several Russian military facilities were hit in Russia and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The confirmed targets included:
- a repair base near Kondrinka in Russia’s Kursk region servicing Iskander-M self-propelled launchers and transporter-loader vehicles;
- a Russian radar station near Skryabine in Russia’s Bryansk region;
- a fuel and lubricants depot near Dovzhansk in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region;
- an ammunition depot near Rubizhne in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region;
- Russian troop concentrations near Selydove, Rozdolne, Suzhenka, and Myrnohrad in the Donetsk region;
- Russian personnel near Naberezhne in the Zaporizhzhia region and Kuzemivka in the Luhansk region.
The Iskander-M is a Russian mobile short-range ballistic missile system designed to strike high-value targets behind the front line. Its launchers and support vehicles allow Russian units to relocate quickly and conduct missile strikes from dispersed positions.
Damage to a repair base can reduce the availability of launchers and support vehicles by disrupting maintenance and the return of damaged equipment to service. The General Staff did not disclose the extent of the damage or Russian losses from the strikes.
Days earlier, Ukraine struck a similar set of Russian maintenance and supply sites across the temporarily occupied east.
Strikes on October 10 and overnight into October 11 hit a military repair unit near Chystiakove, also known as Torez, and logistics facilities near Makiivka and Horodyshche. Russian troop concentrations near Purdivka, Lysychansk, and Irmino were also targeted.
Earlier on October 10, Ukrainian forces hit command posts in the Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk regions, an electronic warfare station in Russia's Bryansk region, and a repair base near Sukhodilsk.

articles.title: USA and Europe drafting peace plan for Ukraine and Russia involving security guarantees and territorial compromise – media
articles.body:
The USA and European countries are developing a peace initiative to end Russia's war against Ukraine; the plan entails funding for Ukraine's reconstruction, security guarantees, economic cooperation with Russia, and a ceasefire along the current front line, The Washington Post reports, citing a US official familiar with the negotiations.
According to the ezine, the diplomatic push came during a six-hour meeting last Friday in Florida hosted by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The meeting, which included Ukrainian officials and representatives of Britain, France and Germany, was held at the Shell Bay Golf Club, a development owned by Witkoff in Hallandale Beach.
According to the Washington Post, U.S. negotiators are trying to frame a package that addresses Ukraine’s and Russia’s postwar needs in a way that ends the bloodbath and leaves both countries better off — as a sweetener for a territorial compromise neither side will like.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the publication quoted an American official as saying.
The peace plan comprises four main components. Ukraine’s reconstruction would be the first pillar. The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock want to create a framework for meeting Zelensky’s myriad cash needs — for rebuilding the devastated areas of the country, providing benefits to families of dead and wounded soldiers, and restoring a shattered economy.
Security guarantees would be the second essential component. Ukraine would get a pledge from the United States and European nations that they would respond militarily if Russia attacked again, which the U.S. official described as equivalent to NATO’s Article 5. The official said Russia would also negotiate agreements with Europe that would address its security concerns, though it’s not clear what this would involve.
A third pillar would be economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy deal. One aspect might be a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia splitting the profits. Such a pipeline could sharply reduce European energy costs, the official said. In addition to providing Russia with “long-term access to the European energy market,” a peace deal would specify how and when existing economic sanctions would be removed. The final, the fourth, piece of the deal would be the most unpalatable. Russia, which began the war hoping to conquer all of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the existing front line, or “line of control,” as negotiators describe it. For Ukraine, that would mean allowing Russia to control the territory it occupies — including the bitterly contested area known as Donbas. One hurdle is that the line of control is fuzzy, given small shifts in the front almost every day.
According to a European diplomat, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries are affecting Russia's economy and strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position.
“Clearly, the Ukrainians’ ability to strike refineries is having impact on Russia’s economy. It has increased Zelenskyy’s leverage,” the European diplomat is quoted by the publication as saying.

articles.title: Poland called on Europe to switch to a "war footing" due to the pace of weapons production in the russian federation
articles.body:
Poland called on Europe to switch to a "war footing" due to the pace of weapons production in the russian federation
Kyiv • UNN
Poland's Minister of Defence called on Europe to sharply increase the production of weapons and ammunition. russia is outpacing the EU in terms of arms production.
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that Europe must accelerate the production of ammunition and weapons in order not to fall behind Russia’s pace. He warned that failure to do so would have negative consequences for Europe. Euronews reports, writes UNN.
I am actually in favour of a wartime footing when it comes to production in the defence sector. That is exactly how the Russian Federation is operating now. We cannot ignore this fact
Russia switched to wartime production in the defence sector even before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. According to forecasts, in 2026 it will spend 7.5% of its gross domestic product on the armed forces.
According to a recent report by Estonian intelligence, in 2025 Russia produced approximately seven million artillery, mortar, tank and missile munitions. Russian forces are currently using approximately 10,000–15,000 munitions daily, continuing their aggression against Ukraine.
By contrast, Europe’s defence industry suffered from insufficient funding and fragmentation for decades.
Russia is outproducing the EU in terms of ammunition production. According to a leaked report on Europe’s defence readiness, the 27 EU member states and Norway are expected to produce only two million 150 mm artillery shells this year.
The efforts of European countries and NATO members to rearm have delivered the largest annual increase in defence spending since the Cold War. Despite this, total defence spending by EU member states in 2025 was estimated at €418 billion, or 2.2% of the European Union’s combined GDP, the report says.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said that it was “time” for Europe to prepare to defend itself independently by significantly increasing production in the defence sector.
He warned that failure to do so would be a “costly” mistake for Europeans, adding: “This is one of the shortcomings, but in the future it will also have a negative impact on us and future generations.”
As the publication notes, Poland is among the countries that spend the largest share of GDP on defence capabilities. According to US representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, the country allocates 4.7% of its GDP to core defence needs.

articles.title: Houthis and Saudis strike each other in latest escalation
articles.body:
Houthis and Saudis show no intent to stop fighting
October 13, 2026
Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Tuesday said that Saudi Arabia had carried out overnight airstrikes targeting border regions in Yemen.
Rebel-run satellite television said two strikes had hit the Red Sea island of Kamaran and a third targeted Qanawis, north of Hodeida port.
Further strikes were reported in Jawf and rebels said their forces had downed a Saudi drone over Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
The strikes came just hours after air-raid sirens blared and loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which has come under intense fire for the past several days as fighting between the two belligerents intensifies.
The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.
The rebels have pounded Saudi Arabia in recent days, repeatedly attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On Saturday, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.
On Tuesday, Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for an immediate end to Houthi attacks on the kingdom, telling Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi that there is "no justification for these attacks and they cannot be accepted."
Houthi attacks' economic impact on Saudi Arabia
Beyond reigniting fighting tied to Yemen's civil war, increased Houthi activity has come as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on February 28.
A regional proxy, the Houthis have helped Iran further destabilize the region by striking largely at the oil and transport infrastructure that brings oil and gas from US allies in the gulf to market.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter and Houthi attacks have not only raised security issues, they have greatly hampered the kingdom's ability to get its product to market.
In its latest annual World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Saudi GDP will contract by 3.3% on the year as a result, with Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz compounded by Houthi maneuvering in the Red Sea and attacks on Saudi oil refineries and tankers.
Saudi Arabia quickly diverted oil exports away from Hormuz as Iran's blockade dragged on, making use instead, of its overland pipelines and Red Sea access. Houthi attacks, however, have also dramatically impacted these.
Saudi Arabia stops issuing air raids
The devastation of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to seek help from Washington and US President Donald Trump.
Although he previously ignored Saudi requests for assistance, on Saturday Trump mused about joining the fight against the rebels.
News of this consideration drew a quick response from the Houthis, with a representative saying US interests in the region would be targeted should DC enter the fray.
Despite at least 18 people being killed and more than 300 injured in recent days, Saudi Arabia has stopped issuing air raid alerts in the kingdom.
The government has not spoken of the policy change but observers suggest it may be an effort to avoid stirring public panic as the country's security vulnerabilities come into focus.
Still, analysts warn that the change could have the opposite effect by amplifying uncertainty over the current situation.
Last week, prior to a string of airport attacks, government officials said the alerts had been halted due to citizens' complaints about being woken by them.
Further, Saudi government officials on Monday reminded residents of regulations issued in March that forbid sharing any images related to Houthi air attacks, including missile interceptions or impact craters.
Former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney told Reuters news agency that Riyadh — which initiated public warnings in May before halting them on September 29 — was trying to balance public messaging with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but that in his opinion leaders had ended up adding to a sense of unease about Houthi airstrikes.

articles.title: Gazan families fight to protect slain journalists' legacies
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Killed twice': Gaza families fight to clear the names of journalists branded militants by Israel
"Publishing my son’s name on that list is a second assassination," begins 70-year-old Bakr al-Louh. "The first time, they killed his body. Now they are killing his legacy and his career as a journalist. They are killing him in his grave."
His son, Ahmed al-Louh, was a photojournalist working for Al Jazeera. He was 39 when an Israeli strike hit a civil defence post in Nuseirat refugee camp, in central Gaza, on 15 December 2024. He had returned there shortly before, after filming ambulances carrying the bodies of people killed in an earlier Israeli strike nearby.
On 1 October, the family found Ahmed’s name and photograph in The Press Files, an online database published by the Israeli occupation. It names 170 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed in Gaza and claims they were members or fighters of armed factions.
"This news destroyed us," his father says. He says the allegations against Ahmed are "lies, with no basis in truth."
Ahmed’s page on the site lists him as a military operative in Hamas’s armed wing. When The New Arab viewed it on 11 October, it contained no supporting evidence. Its only image linked to an internal address and did not load.
The Israeli army claims the database is the product of an in-depth investigation, drawing on open-source information, documents seized in Gaza, interrogations of alleged militants and intelligence gathered during military operations.
But the evidence it presents varies widely, from cropped documents to old photographs.
In 49 cases, the main evidence is an obituary published by an armed group. An analysis by +972 Magazine found that 59 of the pages contain no evidence at all, only a line saying the claim is based on intelligence sources.
For Bakr al-Louh, the list is an extension of the war on Gaza’s journalists. Targeting them, he says, is "an attempt to silence the free word and the truth, because the occupation doesn’t want any voice or image to come out of Gaza that exposes its massacres."
The fear does not stop with the dead. "We have a real fear that these accusations will reach the rest of the family," he tells The New Arab. If any of them needs urgent medical treatment outside Gaza, he worries Israel could reject them on security grounds.
‘He moved in the open’
Ahmed Khaireddine, 30, was a cameraman for Al-Quds Al-Youm. He was killed on 27 December 2023, when an Israeli strike hit his home in Beit Lahia, in northern Gaza. His uncle Mohammed Khaireddine, a journalist with Al-Aqsa TV, died with him, along with 23 other members of the family.
The Press Files describes Ahmed as an Islamic Jihad commander and lists his employer as Al-Aqsa TV, the channel his uncle worked for. His brother Basel, 36, a journalist himself, says the photograph on the page is fabricated. He says he had never seen it in his life. He believes the way his brother died is the clearest proof the allegations are false.
"Before he was killed, Ahmed spent more than 80 days moving around with his camera and his blue vest, covering al-Shifa and the Indonesian hospitals," he tells The New Arab.
"If he had really been a military target, they would have picked him off in the streets and public squares, where he moved openly. But he was killed with his family, in a massacre that destroyed three adjoining houses at once and killed more than 30 civilians."
Many of the names on the list, he says, belong to colleagues he saw every day. "We saw them all the time where journalists gathered at hospitals and out in the field, and we never once saw them among gunmen or fighters. They were doing their work in the open, and the drones above them knew very well they were civilians doing their jobs," Basel says.
He says Israel is deliberately confusing political affiliation with combat. "A Palestinian is born with a political affiliation. That is nothing shameful, and it does not take a journalist out of the civilian work protected under international law."
'A ready-made warrant'
Photojournalist Bilal Abu Samak says the database’s real purpose is to justify the killing of journalists who covered the war. He and Mohammed both describe the accusations as a ready-made warrant, one that could be used against journalists who are still alive and still reporting.
Gaza’s journalists, Abu Samak says, are civilians who wear protective vests and carry no weapons.
"Through this list, they are trying to terrify us and force us to abandon journalism, especially as they keep barring international journalists from entering Gaza to document their violations," he says.
"We demand real protection for press crews, and that the professional legacy of our colleagues who were killed be preserved."
Israel has barred foreign reporters from Gaza since the start of the war, apart from brief visits escorted by the army, and denies deliberately targeting journalists.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) told The New Arab it was still reviewing all the claims in the database. When new information emerges about the killing of a journalist anywhere in the world, it said, it reviews each case independently and updates its records.
CPJ published the database a week after completing its own review.
On 24 September, the New York-based group removed 22 people from its list of journalists killed in Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory. It found that 19 of them had been militants or had taken part in combat, and that three could not be confirmed as journalists.
CPJ now counts 191 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed by Israeli forces. It said Israeli forces remain responsible for the large majority of journalist killings worldwide since 2023, and that each case in its review required interviews with at least two independent, credible sources as well as desk research.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate puts the toll higher, at more than 260. Its secretary-general, Ahed Farawneh, says the timing of the Israeli database is no accident.
"The occupation is trying to get around the huge numbers of journalists killed by levelling these false accusations of links to armed groups," he says, "to justify targeting them after a global outcry and strong condemnation from journalists’ unions and international organisations."
When the syndicate looks at the lives of those killed, he says, it finds that "they were working under the sun," in plain sight and far from any armed faction.
The syndicate says it applies criteria matching those of the International Federation of Journalists before recognising anyone as a journalist killed in the line of duty.
It is also building a case file of killings, injuries, arrests, destroyed offices and homes, and families wiped out and documenting the ban on foreign press and on bringing cameras and equipment into Gaza.
"We have obtained power of attorney from the families of those killed, and from injured journalists and former detainees, to file cases at the International Criminal Court," Ahed says.
"Unfortunately, the court is still stalling on opening this file. But together with the International Federation of Journalists, we insist on it, and on the families’ right to take the occupation to court."
He points to earlier legal efforts over the killings of journalists Shireen Abu Akleh, Ahmed Abu Hussein and Yaser Murtaja. The syndicate is also working with rights groups and legal experts to bring cases in countries whose laws allow prosecution of war crimes committed abroad.
'In case of doubt'
Hussein Hammad, a specialist in media and human rights, says the database deliberately blurs the line between political or institutional affiliation and taking a direct part in hostilities.
Working for a media outlet linked to a political faction, or sympathising with one, does not strip a journalist of civilian protection, he says.
International humanitarian law is clear on this. Article 79 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions states that journalists on dangerous professional missions in armed conflict are civilians and must be protected as such.
Under Article 51, civilians lose that protection only "for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities." Article 50 adds that "in case of doubt whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian."
Accusing journalists after they have been killed, with no chance to answer the charges, has no legal value, Hammad says, and amounts to a cover for extrajudicial killing.
International justice, he adds, does not accept military verdicts based on evidence the victim or their lawyer can never see or challenge. He says the response must be to document every violation, gather physical evidence and build cases for court.
For Bakr al-Louh, the fight is also about memory. His son’s last assignment was to document the dead of Nuseirat being carried to hospital. Shortly afterwards, he was among them.
Ismail Nofal is a Gaza-based journalist specialising in human interest stories
This article was published in collaboration with Egab

articles.title: NATO exercise involves potential countries for nuclear weapons deployment — expert
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Countries under consideration for expanding the program for hosting and storing US nuclear weapons in Europe (Nuclear Sharing) are participating in the NATO exercise Steadfast Noon, taking place in Italy, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security of the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"Italy is hosting the latest phase of the exercise, which brings together 17 participating nations, including countries potentially under consideration for expanding the Nuclear Sharing program in terms of nuclear weapons deployment," he said. The expert noted that these countries are primarily located along NATO's eastern flank--the Baltic states and Finland.
According to Stepanov, the exercise aims to ensure coordination during strategic operations, primarily involving the air force component. "These maneuvers involve 60 aircraft to provide both strategic reconnaissance capabilities and cover for the main delivery systems as part of a combined nuclear-use scenario across various sectors," the expert added.
Starting October 13, NATO is conducting nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy without the use of live munitions. Seventeen nations are participating, the NATO press service reported. It emphasized that "no live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country."
The Steadfast Noon exercise is held annually as "part of NATO’s efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the Alliance’s deterrence and defense." It involves dual-capable aircraft designed to carry both conventional and nuclear munitions.

articles.title: Govt approves changes to reservation system
articles.body:
The Cabinet of Ministers adopted a resolution On certain issues concerning the organization of reservations for conscripts during mobilization and wartime, MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak (from the Holos faction) said; a government source also confirmed this information to Interfax-Ukraine.
"The document was adopted after one day of revisions, and regarding the reservation percentage – after five days. However, my sources say that they apparently managed to remove this provision regarding the 50% calculation basis," Zhelezniak said on social media.
According to him, government officials retained the provision that employees with deferrals (students, caregivers, and parents of three children) can be included in the calculation basis for the quota, as is currently the case.
A government source speaking to the agency also said the calculation of the reservation base in the final document will most likely remain unchanged.
He noted that, in accordance with the approved resolution, a Coordination Center for Allocation Issues will be established, but its membership will include not only representatives of the security and law enforcement agencies but also representatives of the humanitarian sector.
Earlier, Zhelezniak had released a draft government resolution that called for reducing reservation limits for the defense industry and the energy sector from 100% to 85%, for utility companies – from 75% to 60% – as well as a change in the basis for calculating the 50% quota and the creation of a Coordination Center under the Cabinet of Ministers. According to him, it was proposed that the Coordination Center consist of 17 members, including representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the Main Intelligence Agency of Ukraine, the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, and the National Police. Without a positive recommendation from this body, companies will not be able to obtain "critically important" status or a reservation quota exceeding 50%; moreover, the center will also have the authority to recommend revoking such status, while the document lacks clear deadlines, criteria, and appeal mechanisms.
Interfax-Ukraine reached out to the Cabinet of Ministers for comment.
As previously reported, relevant defense associations – including NAUDI, the Technological Forces of Ukraine, and the Council of Arms Manufacturers – have called on the government to maintain a 100% procurement quota for defense industry enterprises, emphasizing the risks to the fulfillment of defense contracts. The Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs announced its intention to send an official request to the relevant ministry to clarify the details of the drafting of the document in question.
The European Business Association (EBA) also expressed concern over possible changes to the procedure for reserving employees subject to military service and called on the government to ensure an open dialogue with the business community before making any decisions.
Regarding the creation of the Coordination Center, Yulia Svyrydenko's government had already adopted a similar decision in July, shortly before her resignation, but it never took effect. At that time, it was envisaged that the Coordination Center would function as a temporary consultative and advisory body to the government, and its tasks would include: coordinating government agencies and finding solutions to problematic situations regarding conscription; reviewing proposals from government agencies regarding the designation of enterprises, institutions, and organizations as critical to the economy and the public's livelihood.

articles.title: Putin-Trump deal about ‘much more’ than diesel – Serbia’s Vucic to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Putin-Trump deal about ‘much more’ than diesel – Serbia’s Vucic to RT (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia is part of a broader geopolitical strategy to draw Moscow away from Beijing, Aleksandar Vucic has told RT Balkan in an exclusive interview.
According to Vucic, who recently stepped down as Serbian president to run for prime minister, Washington, which sees China as its main rival, hopes to weaken Beijing’s partnership with Russia by improving ties with Moscow.
Trump announced the deal following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 9. Moscow agreed to release more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and one million tons thereafter. Washington subsequently waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7, 2027.
Ahead of the deal, Trump blamed soaring fuel prices on Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries, although markets have also been disrupted by the US war with Iran, which has affected shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
“As far as Donald Trump is concerned, he is doing a smart thing for America, he is trying to do something to bring down the price per gallon… But I don’t think this is just about diesel,” Vucic said, noting that the initial 300,000 tons would cover less than a day’s US consumption.
With the US midterms approaching and Trump’s standoff with Tehran increasingly unpopular, Vucic suggested the deal could partly be aimed at winning over voters by lowering fuel prices. However, he suggested there was a larger geopolitical calculation behind the agreement.
“I think it is about something much more than this. Donald Trump knows that his main competitor is China. And is trying, in a sophisticated way, to move Russia somewhat away from China and bring it closer to the US.”
Asked whether Trump was seeking closer ties with Moscow, Vucic replied: “Of course.”
“If he is in conflict with Russia, he will only push Russia closer to China,” he explained. “Trump is trying, I assume, to draw Russia, China’s powerful and strong ally, at least a little away from that alliance.”
The Trump administration has long treated China as a major strategic rival. Its 2025 National Security Strategy calling for a rebalancing of economic ties with Beijing. Trump nevertheless hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington last month for talks on trade, Taiwan and Iran. The two sides agreed to extend their trade truce until January, but tensions over tariffs, technology and security persist.
Russia and China, meanwhile, have only deepened their strategic and energy cooperation in light of Ukraine-related Western sanctions on Moscow. Beijing has become Moscow’s biggest oil customer and a major buyer of Russian gas, with supplies expanding through the Power of Siberia pipeline as Russia redirected energy exports away from Europe.
Talking about Russia-US ties, Vucic also pointed to Washington’s diplomatic push to resolve the Ukraine conflict, saying its parallel negotiating channels with Moscow and Kiev show it is serious about reaching a settlement. However, he sees little prospect of an imminent breakthrough.
Vucic expressed hope that a peace deal could be reached within five to six months. Asked whether he fears that the conflict could evolve into a direct confrontation between Russia and the EU, Vucic replied: “I fear that, but I hope it won’t happen.”
Serbia has maintained close ties with Russia and, under Vucic, has resisted EU pressure to impose sanctions on Moscow over Ukraine, despite Belgrade’s ambitions to join the bloc. In the interview, Vucic again stressed the need to preserve Serbia’s traditional ties with Moscow despite external pressure, saying leaders must “keep a cool head and make rational and wise decisions.”
Vucic resigned during his second presidential term last month ahead of snap parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25. Barred by the Serbian constitution from seeking a third term, he is now seeking the prime minister’s post as a candidate for the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

articles.title: Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?
articles.body:
Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?
While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass muster
Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out at least three airstrikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian search engine company Yandex. Reports suggest at least two of these datacentres took significant damage, with Telegram footage appearing to show one on fire. Yandex acknowledged the strikes, and Russian media reported that several websites appeared affected by the downed datacentres.
On Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested the strikes had dampened Russia’s massive disinformation operation, saying: “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations.”
It is a commendable hope, but experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case.
Did Ukraine’s strikes lead to a decline in Russian disinformation?
Probably not. While a few graphs went viral on social media suggesting there had been a big decline in activity from Yandex bots, those graphs are unrelated to Russian disinformation.
“Our platforms are still monitoring Russian social networks across the world and there is no discernible change in their posting patterns,” said Amil Khan, the chief executive of Valent, a tech startup that tracks disinformation.
Khan and his team track about 40 disinformation networks around the world, from the UK to Australia to Syria, and monitor what narratives they put out and how publics respond to them. They have seen no drop in the volume of posts from these networks, saying: “Yandex datacentres have no practical connection to social media bot farms.”
So what exactly did happen?
Yandex is a search engine which also hosts websites and bots. Data from Cloudflare, which monitors worldwide internet traffic, shows a marked decline in activity from bots associated with the Yandex network on 8 October and 11 October, corresponding to the dates of two of the strikes.
The independent Russian news outlet Meduza reports that a number of websites in Russia are down: major banks, retailers, sports apps and Yandex’s services such as Yandex Go and Yandex Eats. It suggests the damage took out a large part of Yandex’s operation and could take months to fully repair.
Some online commentators have mistaken the Cloudflare data to mean that the decline in bot activity has led to a major drop in disinformation on social media. But this is not what experts have noticed.
What are these different kinds of bots?
“The term ‘bot’ can mean many different things,” said Michał ‘Rysiek’ Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. “When Cloudflare data shows a precipitous drop in ‘bot’ traffic, that does not mean ‘automated social media troll accounts’, it means ‘software that makes automated web requests on a large scale.’” What Cloudflare picked up was a decline in activity from Yandex’s web crawlers. These are used by search engines to index websites and help users to find them, said Khan.
State-sponsored disinformation networks – the kind of “bots” a lot of people misinterpreted this as – could still be affected by the strikes, said Woźniak. “But those effects are going to be much more indirect.”
Those networks are far more distributed, and more resilient, said Ned Mendez, the head of research at Alliance4Europe. “Platforms will routinely flag traffic from datacentres as likely automated, so serious bot operations run more through distributed methods, such as residential connections and phone farms, that airstrikes can’t really knock out.”
So how could Ukraine disrupt Russian disinformation in Europe?
“We can’t simply bomb the bots out of existence, however appealing that might sound,” said Mendez. “They aren’t really a single set of buildings that can be switched off.”
Khan said the Ukrainians could consider taking action against companies such as the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Wagner-linked troll farm that was engaged in influence operations until 2023. But another tactic could be to work with Europe to disrupt the supply chain and recruitment pipeline of private sector contractors used by the Kremlin.
Another tactic could be to pressure big social media companies to moderate disinformation on their platforms. Khan’s team has successfully worked with Meta to tamp down on inflammatory content in Sudan.
But, said Khan, the Trump administration would probably push back on this, hard. “I can see why blowing up datacentres is an easier option.”

articles.title: “We don’t need to hit the entire plant”—Ukraine’s drones go for refinery parts sanctions make hard to repair
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones have helped push Russia into its worst fuel crisis since the Soviet Union fell, The Washington Post (WaPo) reported on 11 October.
Diesel is where this war reaches American drivers. US President Donald Trump blames rising diesel prices mostly on Russia’s war in Ukraine, while experts blame mainly the US war with Iran. Some of his allies now accuse Kyiv of trying to sway the US midterms.
Drones go for the first stage of refining
The Washington Post looked at dozens of strikes between 1 April and 31 August. Three refinery experts then examined satellite images of 54 strikes with visible damage. In over half, the damage seems to be to the desalting and distillation units, known by the Russian acronym ELOU-AVT. These units clean the crude of water and salt, then split it into separate compounds, the first steps toward gasoline and diesel. More than a third appear to have hit secondary units, which turn those compounds into jet fuel, gasoline, and liquefied petroleum gas.
From April through August, drones struck two-thirds or more of the 36 big Russian refineries that S&P Global Energy tracks, a strike every third day. Some took as many as five hits. On 16 June, drones set the Moscow refinery’s distillation towers on fire. That strike and a second one days later kept the plant offline into September, WaPo reported, citing data firm Kpler. Ukraine targeted the refinery again on 20 September.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
“We don’t need to hit the entire plant,” a Ukrainian drone battalion commander with the call sign Tango told The Washington Post. Ukraine knows where to strike so that a refinery stops and stays down, he said. His unit, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems, runs long-range strikes deep inside Russia.
Sanctions slow the repairs
The EU banned exports of oil-refining equipment to Russia the day after the 2022 invasion, and the US followed days later. WaPo reported that the bans cover the distillation and secondary processing units Ukraine keeps hitting. The bans make spare parts hard to get, Alexander Kolyandr of Eurasia Group told the paper, and the strikes come faster than repairs.
Since last year, Ukraine has doubled the size of each wave, decoys included, a person involved in the strike campaign told WaPo. The decoys are unarmed and draw Russian fire, wasting air-defense ammunition, WaPo explained. Without them, the person said, Ukraine would simply lose expensive systems. András Rácz of the German Council on Foreign Relations told WaPo that even if only 2–3% of drones get through, the damage is significant.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Trump discussed possibility of renewing strikes against Iran before elections - report
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke to US President Donald Trump last week to discuss the possibility of a renewed military campaign against Iran before Knesset elections are held at the end of October, according to an Axios report on Tuesday.
The potential joint US-Israel operation could target Iran’s nuclear and military sites, sources reportedly said.
Senior US officials told Axios that Netanyahu cited alleged Iranian efforts to rebuild nuclear capacity as the reason for launching new strikes.
If military operations against Iran do reignite, it could have an impact on both the Israeli election and US midterm elections in early November.
Despite Trump’s earlier public statements that he has not yet decided how to proceed with Tehran, sources said both the IDF and US Central Command (CENTCOM) are on alert and are finalizing preparations in case he decides to order strikes.
One US official told Axios that Trump told Netanyahu to “go ahead and get ready,” but noted there was no firm commitment to restart military operations.
A White House official denied that the two leaders had talked about resuming the war and asserted that Trump has said that the US will not attack Iran before midterm elections.
The Prime Minister’s Office confirmed that Netanyahu maintains regular contact with Trump but did not comment to Axios on the content of their talks.
Support for renewed strikes mixed, officials say
One Israeli official said Trump initially seemed willing to join renewed strikes before growing hesitant, and another US official said Trump was still on the fence.
Additional sources familiar with the discussions told Axios that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM leadership are among the strongest backers of plans to resume the war.
Much of the Trump administration, however, reportedly favors maintaining economic and political pressure on Tehran over military action.
"They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," a US official told Axios.
Trump says decision on Iran coming 'very soon'
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Tuesday, Trump said the US would decide on its next move regarding Iran “very soon.”
"Iran is a failed country," Trump said. "They have no economy, they have 300% inflation, they have no money, they're not paying their troops, they're not paying anybody."

Palestine Action Canada targets Elbit-owned firm in Ontario
Pro-Palestine activists affiliated with Palestine Action Canada have targeted an Ontario-based subsidiary of Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems, citing the company's role in supplying military equipment amid Israel's military offensives in Gaza and Lebanon.
In a statement sent to The New Arab on Tuesday, the group said it had targeted GeoSpectrum Technologies in Peterborough, Ontario, in the early hours of Monday.
Video footage provided to The New Arab showed activists taking responsibility for damage to the premises.
The footage appeared to show red paint sprayed across the building, writing on its exterior and damage to an outdoor communications box.
It also showed a masked individual apparently tampering with unidentified equipment, while another masked person threatened to smash a window with a hammer.
The activists defended the action, describing Elbit as "the largest profiteer of the genocide of Palestinians."
"Dozens of Canadian companies across the country have been found to supply essential parts and components used in the tanks, drones, and munitions deployed to murder the Palestinian people, with full support of the Canadian state," Palestine Action Canada said.
"GeoSpectrum Technologies, Elbit's Canadian subsidiary, manufactures maritime surveillance and exploration technologies, regularly conducting performance trials with the Royal Canadian Navy and the Department of National Defense," the group added.
Palestine Action Canada has called on the Canadian government to end all trade and ties with Elbit Systems, demanding a full arms embargo and sanctions against Israel.
Local police have confirmed that they are investigating the incident.
They said footage of the incident, which has also circulated on social media, forms part of the investigation.
Police have also classified the incident as a hate- or bias-related crime, adding: "Hate has no place in our community."
According to its website, GeoSpectrum Technologies develops and manufactures marine acoustic systems, including sonar, underwater communications technology, submarine targets and surveillance systems for defence and other applications.
Palestine Action Canada's ongoing Arms Embargo Now campaign has identified several Canadian companies it alleges are involved in supplying components to Israel's defence industry.
The campaign has listed GeoSpectrum Technologies' Peterborough premises among the sites it has identified in connection with Elbit Systems.
The group has previously cited the International Court of Justice's July 2024 advisory opinion that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territiores is unlawful and a subsequent paper by a UN commission in its calls for Canada to comply with international law.
It argues that ending relations with Israel would demonstrate that the Canadian government is not contributing to the continuation of Israel's decades-long occupation or the commission of war crimes and genocide.
The latest development follows discussions at Montreal City Council last month over a motion calling on the Canadian city to suspend all institutional ties with the Israeli government.
However, Montreal ultimately only passed a motion expressing solidarity with Palestinians, removing a clause that called for the severing of institutional and diplomatic ties with Israel.

articles.title: Defense forces strike Iskander-M repair base and radar station inside Russia – General Staff
articles.body:
Units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a number of Russian military targets within Russia and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories on Monday and overnight into Tuesday, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports.
"A repair base for self-propelled launchers and transport-loader vehicles of the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system was struck near Kondrinka in Russia's Kursk region. Additionally, an enemy radar station was hit near the settlement of Shkryabino in Russia's Bryansk region," the General Staff said in a Telegram post.
Logistics facilities belonging to Russian units were also struck in the temporarily occupied territory of Luhansk region: a fuel and lubricant depot near Dovzhansk and an ammunition depot near Rubizhne.
"Ukrainian forces also struck areas where enemy personnel were concentrated. Concentrations of Russian troops were hit near Selydove, Razdolne, Suzhenka, and Myrnohrad in Donetsk region; Naberezhne in Zaporizhzhia region; and Kuzemivka in Luhansk region," the General Staff reported.
